1.title: Conceptual Design Generation Using Large Language Models
1.summary: The authors used large language models to generate solutions for 12 design problems and compared them with crowdsourced solutions to the same problems. Experts rated both sets and computational metrics measured their differences. LLM solutions were rated more feasible and useful, crowdsourced ones more novel, and few-shot prompting made the generated solutions more like the crowd's.

2.title: Emulating Cognitive Style in Large Language Models
2.summary: The authors tested whether large language models can imitate cognitive style as defined by Kirton's adaption-innovation theory. They prompted LLMs to solve three design problems in an adaptive or an innovative style and rated the solutions for feasibility and how much they changed the existing paradigm. Adaptive prompts gave more feasible, paradigm-preserving solutions and innovative prompts gave more paradigm-changing ones, as the theory predicts.

3.title: Examining the Longitudinal Psychological Safety of Mentored Senior Capstone Design Teams
3.summary: This study tracked psychological safety in senior capstone design teams over a two-semester course, with each team mentored by someone from industry or academia. Individual and team psychological safety were measured three times: at the outset, midway and at the end of the course. Psychological safety did not change significantly over time, for individuals or teams, and the type of mentor made no difference.

5.title: Incorporating Social, Policy, and Ethical Considerations in Engineering and Design Education: an Examination of Barriers and Resources
5.summary: This survey asked instructors of design courses in engineering and related fields how and why they include social, policy and ethical considerations. Responses show growing awareness that such content matters. Instructors who want to include it are held back by unclear relevance, lack of time and a shortage of teaching materials, which more resources and funding could address.

7.title: Gathering and Communicating Empathic User Understanding in Product Development
7.summary: The study looked at how insights about users are gathered and passed on to the wider team in a large global engineering and service company. The authors ran a thematic analysis of ten interviews with staff who either collect or receive user information. Communication broke down because of different disciplinary backgrounds, too little shared time and many handovers, and there was no good way to store and find user insights from past projects.

8.title: Towards a Theoretical Framework for Using “Context” in Engineering Design Processes for Global Health Applications
8.summary: Drawing on several studies, the paper sharpens what "context" means in engineering design for global health and proposes an early framework for working with it. The framework separates categories of context (contextual factors) from strategies for applying them at different design stages. The authors show how it could improve reporting in design research and help judge whether a solution will transfer to another setting.

10.title: TRIZ-GPT: An LLM-Augmented Method For Problem-Solving
10.summary: The paper presents TRIZ-GPT, a method that uses large language models to guide problem solving with TRIZ, the theory of inventive problem solving. The authors built a collection of TRIZ cases and a step-by-step prompting workflow that turns a concrete problem into a TRIZ problem and generates solutions. A mechanical engineering case study shows GPT-4 producing solutions close to the original ones and suggesting further ways to implement them.

13.title: Paper or Tablet? The Impact of Digital Tools on Sketching During Engineering Design Concept Generation
13.summary: This experiment compared sketching on a digital tablet with pen and paper during an engineering concept generation exercise. Sketches were scored for quantity, quality and how well they communicated the idea. Both tools produced similar numbers of equally understandable sketches, pen and paper gave higher-quality sketches, and no gender differences appeared.

14.title: Concept Chaining Patterns During Ideation Using Digital Tablets
14.summary: This controlled experiment compared concept chaining, meaning iterating on one concept in sequence, between sketching on iPads and on paper. Engineering participants generated concepts for prompts with one or several functional requirements. Tablet users chained concepts more despite producing a similar number of related ideas, and prompts with more requirements changed chaining patterns because not every idea addressed every requirement.

18.title: Identifying a Relationship Between Design Concept Representation Style and Consumer Product Preference
18.summary: The study tested whether the way a product concept is shown affects how consistently consumers state their preferences. Participants rated eyeglass frames shown as hand drawings, CAD models and realistic renderings, compared with physical models, while eye tracking recorded where they looked. Preferences for CAD models were the least consistent with preferences for the physical frames, though this difference vanished for participants with an engineering background.

20.title: Reverse Engineering Through a Product Teardown Activity and Component-Function Identification
20.summary: The study measured how a product teardown affects upper-level engineering students' mental models of everyday products. Students drew mental models of three products, disassembled a hair dryer, drew them again and identified the dryer's components and their functions. Mental model scores did not change and knowledge did not transfer between products; the teardown helped students identify components such as the motor but made their functional reasoning worse.

21.title: Identification of Design Strategies and Their Effects on Performance Outcomes in Pair Parameter Design Tasks
21.summary: Using data from an experiment in which pairs completed simple cooperative parameter design tasks, the authors looked for action patterns that make pairs faster. They applied principal component analysis and regression to 192 task observations. Pairs who made small, quick, consistent adjustments finished faster, likely because frequent feedback improved coordination, while lower English ability and less experience were linked to worse performance.

22.title: Towards Quantifying Interviews: Comparing Techniques to Evaluate the Quality of Design Interviews
22.summary: The authors developed and tested a scoring method for the quality of design research interviews conducted by novice interviewers. Twelve undergraduates trained in design ethnography interviewed people for a dialysis service project in Zimbabwe, and their interviews were scored and compared with expert ratings and the information gained. The scoring method did not align well with either benchmark, so the authors revised its metrics and offer recommendations.

23.title: Evaluating the Dynamics of Designers’ Moods Throughout the Collaborative Design Process
23.summary: This longitudinal study tracked the moods of student designers and their teams across a semester-long collaborative project. Sentiment analysis was applied to written self-reflections collected at three points in the project. Time significantly predicted changes in team mood but not individual mood, pointing to a complex link between individual and team emotion during design.

24.title: We’re All in This Together: Evaluating the Impact of Designers’ Mood Dynamics on Collaborative Design Project Outcomes
24.summary: Extending prior work, this study examined whether differences in team members' moods relate to the outcomes of student design projects. Sentiment in self-reflections collected at three points in a semester-long project was compared with project performance and collaboration quality. Teams whose members diverged more in tone, positive tone and negative emotion had worse project outcomes.

26.title: Assessing Pedestrian Trust in Autonomous Vehicles: a Comparative Study of Immersive Virtual Reality and Non-Immersive Video Media
26.summary: This within-subject experiment with 50 adults compared immersive virtual reality and ordinary video for studying pedestrian trust in autonomous vehicles. Participants watched seven vehicle behaviours in both media and rated trust, risk and how understandable the behaviours were. VR raised trust and risk ratings overall though understanding was the same, and both media ranked the vehicle behaviours similarly, so video is adequate for comparing behaviours.

28.title: Empathic Ability Vs. User Satisfaction: Evaluating the Role of Preference Accuracy in Engineering Design
28.summary: The authors explored whether preference accuracy, how well a designer predicts another person's preferences, could serve as a practical measure of empathy in design. Fourteen participants were paired up, interviewed their partner, and designed a chair for them, completing preference surveys for themselves and for their partner. Preference accuracy did not appear to be linked to the partner's satisfaction with the design, but it may help distinguish designers' empathic abilities.

29.title: Typology Development for Synthetic Chemistry Sub-Tasks: Towards Human-Robot Collaboration Task Design in the Wet Lab
29.summary: To inform human-robot collaboration in chemistry labs, the authors studied the manual tasks synthetic chemists perform. Based on observations and surveys, they identified 10 common tasks and analysed the two most frequent, liquid dispensing and solids handling, in detail. They found 40 types of liquid dispensing and 18 of solids handling and measured each one's workload with the NASA-TLX, as a basis for robots that support rather than replace researchers.

33.title: A Picture or a Thousand Words: Design Description Crafting to Replicate Human Similarity Judgments in Large Language Models
33.summary: This study asked whether large language model embeddings of design descriptions can reproduce how people judge the similarity of design sketches. LLM embeddings of crowdsourced text descriptions were compared with an embedding built from human triplet judgments of the same sketches, and descriptions written to a template focused on function, behaviour or structure were also tested. The comparison shows where human and LLM similarity disagree and which ways of describing designs bring the two closer.

34.title: Protocol Study: Patterns of Designer Behaviors When Describing Engineering Problem Domains Through Concept Maps
34.summary: A pilot protocol study of how designers describe an engineering problem domain by building concept maps. Ten participants each mapped one of three domains, and their actions were coded second by second, along with patterns of cross-links, grouping and clustering. The results show which parts of mapping are hardest, such as naming concepts and relating distant ones, and how information is generated within and across clusters.

35.title: Similarities and Differences in Human Vs. Computational Representations of Non-Semantic Inspirational Design Stimuli
35.summary: The study compared how people and AI models judge the visual and functional similarity of 3D part models used as design inspiration. Thirty-six participants judged similarity in triplets of parts, which were used to build embedding spaces compared with deep-learning embeddings of the same parts. Human and computational similarities largely agreed, especially for very dissimilar pairs, but diverged for similar pairs, and people used abstract cues the AI did not capture.

36.title: From Obstacles to Opportunities: How Perceptions of Psychological Safety Affect Founders’ Abilities to Identify Resources
36.summary: This mixed-methods study of 32 startup founders examined whether a team's psychological safety affects how well founders find resources to overcome obstacles. Founders' perceptions of psychological safety were measured alongside their ability to name useful resources for current problems. Founders who felt their team was more psychologically safe were better at identifying meaningful resources.

38.title: LLM4CAD: Multi-Modal Large Language Models for 3D Computer-Aided Design Generation
38.summary: The authors developed LLM4CAD, an approach that lets GPT-4 and GPT-4V generate 3D CAD models of mechanical parts such as gears and springs by writing CAD scripts. They created a dataset of parts, sketches and images with crowdsourced descriptions, and measured whether the scripts ran and how closely the resulting shapes matched. Both models showed promise: text-only input did best on average, but adding images helped more as the parts got more complex, such as springs and gears.

41.title: Gender Inclusivity: Exploring Design Dynamics and Psychological Safety in Virtual Engineering Design Dyads

43.title: Who Is This Design For? Promoting Consideration of People During Concept Generation
43.summary: This between-subjects experiment tested a simple prompt to make engineering students think about users during concept generation. Half of the mechanical engineering students were asked to draw people in their concept sketches, and afterwards everyone reflected on who each idea was for. Drawing people led to longer, deeper reflections that considered context of use and user values, and fewer claims that a design was "for everyone".

47.title: Factors Hindering the Implementation of Prototyping in the Early Stages of New Business Development
47.summary: Through a grounded theory study at a large Japanese manufacturer, the authors investigated what stops prototyping from working in early-stage new business development. They interviewed members of new technology business projects and analysed project documents. Two barriers emerged: prototyping skill depends on individuals and relies on tacit knowledge, and teams are reluctant to talk with customers, and the paper proposes countermeasures for both.

48.title: Open Quantum Models and Magnetoencephalography Derived Neural Correlates for Engineering Decision Dynamics
48.summary: The paper proposes modelling engineering decision making with open quantum systems, which can explain decision paradoxes that classical probability cannot. It argues that brain activity recorded with magnetoencephalography (MEG) could help set the parameters of such models. The authors outline possible experiments and give preliminary data on how this could work in practice.

49.title: Journey Mapping the Virtual Design Thinking Experience: Engaging Students Across Disciplines in Human-Centered Design
49.summary: The study mapped the experiences of six student teams over the phases of a design thinking course, a method the authors call journey mapping. Students' experiences were captured through assessments at each phase and reflections on the whole process. The early research phases were experienced less positively than later ones, and engineering and non-engineering students reflected on the process differently.

50.title: The Impact of Facilitation During Idea Generation in Engineering Design
50.summary: This experiment tested whether a trained facilitator improves group brainstorming in an engineering design task. Groups generated ideas with a morphological matrix under facilitated, unfacilitated and nominal (individuals working alone) conditions, with idea quantity, task load and psychological safety measured. Facilitated groups produced more ideas than unfacilitated groups but fewer than nominal groups, and facilitation also lowered perceived workload and raised psychological safety.

52.title: Understanding the State of Sanitation in India Through Qualitative Methods and a Septic Tank Sensing Device
52.summary: To design a sensor that tells households when to empty their septic tanks, the authors studied sanitation in three municipalities in Maharashtra, India. They combined interviews, questionnaires and measurements of septic tanks. The device only makes sense where a working sludge treatment plant exists, needs different stakeholders involved in each municipality, and should track how long waste is retained rather than years since the last emptying.

53.title: Adaptive Optimization of Subjective Design Attributes: Characterizing Individual and Aggregate Perceptions
53.summary: In a study with 56 participants, the authors used interactive Bayesian optimization to find the most comfortable mug design from each person's pairwise choices. Some participants trained the model alone, while others started from a model pre-trained on simulated data or on other people's choices. Combining aggregate and individual decisions produced designs that best matched people's perceptions of comfort.

57.title: Public Engagement and Participatory Design Preparedness: Adapting Participatory Technology Assessment Methods for Design Science
57.summary: This project tested whether participatory technology assessment, a public engagement method from science policy, can prepare teams for participatory design of complex sociotechnical systems such as fusion energy. The team of fusion and engagement experts ran two open dialogues with members of the public in Madison, Wisconsin. Early findings suggest the method reveals how the public frames the issue, what it knows and its hopes and concerns, which could shape later design engagements.

58.title: Steps Toward Development of a Comprehensive Set-Based Design Process Model: A Case Study
58.summary: This case study followed a U.S. Navy team applying set-based design to an entire large ship at system-of-systems scale. The researchers used participatory action research to document the process, how teams ruled out options and how they agreed on system-level choices. Reasoning across design representations at different levels of abstraction was especially hard, and the paper draws lessons for set-based design.

59.title: Exploring the Role of Individual Differences in System Interpretation
59.summary: The study tested whether two personal traits, confidence in one's own design ability (self-efficacy) and a preference for quick, firm answers (need for closure), shape how people group a system's parts for a fault-detection task. 147 first-year students from two universities clustered three products shown as component graphs, function graphs and function structures. Neither trait, nor university, gender or first language, was related to cluster size, though the similar complexity of the products limited the test.

60.title: Crack the Code: Impact of Engineering Design Prompt Objective and Linguistic Characteristics on Understanding and Creativity Perceptions of Students
60.summary: The study examined whether the objective and wording of engineering design prompts affect how understandable and creative students find them. The authors analysed 45 design prompts by objective and by linguistic features, alongside students' ratings. Prompts with different objectives differed only in word prevalence and were rated similarly, and neither objective nor linguistic features predicted students' ratings.

62.title: Should I Sketch or Should I CAD? Exploring Design Representation Strategies in Design for Additive Manufacturing Tasks
62.summary: This study looked at how fourth-year engineering students switch between sketching and CAD when designing for additive manufacturing. Participants completed a one-hour design task while eye tracking recorded which representations they used, and strategies were compared between high- and low-creativity and high- and low-performance solutions. Students with the most creative designs spent more time in CAD, especially late in the task, while those with the best-performing designs (less build time and material) sketched more.

63.title: Augmenting Engineering Design With AI: Introducing the AI Design Assistant (AIDA)
63.summary: The authors built AIDA, a web chatbot based on large language models that supports design ideation and rates users' ideas for validity, novelty and feasibility, using a sustainable washing machine as the example. A human-subjects experiment tested the first version. Participants used it smoothly and found it useful, enjoyable and trustworthy, though men and people under 25 trusted it less than other participants.

64.title: Co-Design in the Himalaya: Embracing Local Knowledge and User Innovation to Address Household Energy Challenges
64.summary: A case study of co-designing a cooking stove with someone who cooks on a traditional stove in a remote Himalayan village in India. The authors visited five villages to learn about cooking practices and then worked with this user as a design peer. The process revealed complex patterns of stove use and produced a design that cut household air pollution while keeping features users valued in the traditional stove.

66.title: Building Spaces for Design Justice: A Case Study on the Design Justice Pedagogy Summit
66.summary: A case study of the Design Justice Pedagogy Summit, held in August 2022 to help instructors bring design justice into their teaching. Participants were studied through surveys, interviews and design artifacts around the summit and four months later. They became more confident about embedding design justice in their work, valued the community it built, and planned to keep engaging, which the authors turn into guidance for similar spaces.

68.title: Form Attributes to Measure and Understand Aesthetic Preferences
68.summary: The study set out to define a vocabulary of objective form attributes and test whether people's aesthetic preferences carry over from one product to another. Participants rated vase and canopy designs built from combinations of four form attributes, and conjoint analysis measured their preferences. Individual form preferences were consistent between the two products about 61% of the time.

69.title: Thinking Beyond the Default User: The Impact of Gender and Stereotypes on Designers’ Interpretation of Users and Their Needs
69.summary: This survey experiment examined whether a user's gender and gender-stereotyped tasks change how engineering students interpret that user's needs. 151 undergraduates read a persona and a walkthrough of a makerspace user meeting obstacles, under six conditions, then recalled and rated the obstacles. The user's gender affected how the environment was perceived, and users of unspecified gender were assumed to be men.

70.title: Human-AI Collaboration Among Engineering and Design Professionals: Three Strategies of Generative AI Use
70.summary: This ethnographic study followed an early-stage NASA design team to see how professionals actually use generative AI during a speculative design workflow. The authors observed the team's process and interviewed members afterwards, coding the data inductively. They identified three strategies, intimate co-design with AI, selective delegation to AI and minimal use, along with factors that influenced each person's choice.

71.title: Dealing With Loss: How Do Designers’ Resilience and Perceptions of Scarcity Affect Perceptions of Design Performance?
71.summary: In a controlled study, the authors examined how designers' resilience and perceived resource scarcity affect how they judge their own design performance. Participants completed design work under induced resource scarcity, with measures of resilience and scarcity mindset. Feeling short of time in daily life predicted lower perceived design performance, and more resilient participants were less affected by the induced scarcity.

74.title: Effect of Reflection and Incubation on Artificial-Intelligence-Assisted Design Space Exploration
74.summary: This human-subjects study tested whether pausing to reflect, or pausing to step away (incubation), changes how designers explore a design space with an AI cognitive assistant. Participants explored design alternatives with the AI and had one of the two breaks partway through. Incubation improved design performance much more than reflection, and the two breaks led to different styles of human-AI collaboration.

75.title: Development and Evaluation of a Process to Advance Orphan Assistive Technology Prototypes for Small Batch Production
75.summary: The project developed and tested a process for taking one-off assistive technology prototypes, built for individual people with disabilities, to small-batch production when the user group is too small for normal commercial development. The four-step process screens each prototype against its target users and existing alternatives, then assesses its function and how best to manufacture it in small numbers. Applied to four devices and reviewed by three experienced assistive technology professionals, it appeared to be a practical, low-cost way to bring such devices to more users.

76.title: Understanding the User Perception Gap: Older Adults and Sit-to-Stand Assistance
76.summary: The study explored why older adults may not adopt sit-to-stand assistive devices. Participants did a standard mobility test, rated their own difficulty standing, were interviewed and reacted to look-and-feel prototypes, while a physical therapist rated videos of them standing. Self-ratings did not track measured mobility even when it signalled fall risk, and participants preferred discreet, light, flexible devices regardless of how much help they needed.

78.title: Triple Process Theory and EEG Frequency Band Power: Metacognitive Brain Activity in Open Design
78.summary: Using EEG, this study compared brain activity during spontaneous, deliberate and metacognitive thinking in open-ended design, based on Triple Process Theory. Frequency band power was compared across the three process types. Metacognitive processes showed higher alpha and beta power across all channels, suggesting they help balance effort between spontaneous and deliberate thinking.

79.title: A Task-Decomposed AI-Aided Approach for Generative Conceptual Design
79.summary: The paper proposes using large language models for concept generation by splitting the task into functional, behavioural and structural steps, following the Function-Behaviour-Structure model. Prompt templates guide the model at each step, and each step's output feeds the next, with designers choosing along the way. In a conceptual design experiment, this approach produced more reasonable and creative concepts than a baseline.

80.title: Inspired by AI? A Novel Generative AI System to Assist Conceptual Automotive Design
80.summary: The authors studied how experienced automotive designers draw inspiration from text and images, to build a generative AI tool that fits their concept design workflow. Through workshops and surveys with design teams, they examined current practice, the limits of off-the-shelf image generators (style bias, weak grasp of design meaning, poor fit with team processes) and how designers would like to interact with AI. They then built a diffusion-model system to support conceptual automotive design.

81.title: The Impact of Robotics Expertise on Iterative Robot Design Decisions and Vulnerability to Design Fixation
81.summary: This study examined how robotics expertise affects iterative robot design and susceptibility to design fixation. 39 attendees of a robotics conference, with 0 to 17 years of experience, designed a ground robot for rough terrain in a 15-minute task using a software tool that logged their decisions. Participants iterated often regardless of expertise, and at every level of experience they tended to fixate on their first concept even when it was not working.

82.title: Investigating Pro-Environmental Attitude for Designing Affective Eco-Feedback
82.summary: This study asked whether people's attitudes toward their own environmental behaviour shape how strongly they react emotionally to eco-feedback designs for saving electricity. Workshop content from 67 participants informed ten feedback sketches with positive, negative or neutral framing, which 60 participants then rated for emotional intensity. People with pro-environmental attitudes reacted most strongly to positively and negatively framed messages, and people with neutral or negative attitudes still reacted negatively to negative framing, suggesting feedback should be tailored to attitudes.

83.title: Facilitating Success: Exploring the Influence of Design Facilitators’ Behaviors on Team Members’ Responses and Perceptions of Team Climate and Trust
83.summary: Using data from a design thinking workshop, this mixed-methods study looked at how five facilitators' behaviours affect team conversation, trust and psychological safety. The authors modelled conversation sequences with Markov models and correlated facilitator behaviours with participants' perceptions. Facilitator engagement encouraged participation and support, clarifying prompted questions, engagement and promoting reflection were linked to greater psychological safety, rapport building was not, and participants trusted facilitators who gave more direction.

84.title: Evaluating and Developing Human-Centered Design Workshops for Engagement of Co-Designers Living and Working in Sub-Saharan Africa
84.summary: The authors studied how local co-designers experienced human-centered design workshops for global health projects, since methods for practicing and evaluating co-design are little studied. They qualitatively coded and thematically analysed survey responses from co-designers who took part in workshops in Kenya and Uganda. Co-designers gained knowledge and enjoyed the process, but time constraints and language barriers remained obstacles, pointing to a need for better curricula and evaluation tools.

85.title: Reading Users’ Minds from What They Say: An Investigation into LLM-based Empathic Mental Inference
85.summary: The study tested whether large language models can infer users' underlying goals and basic psychological needs from what users say, a task central to empathic design. The authors collected data from users and designers to build an empathic accuracy measure and compared several LLMs and prompting techniques against human designers. The LLMs inferred goals and needs about as accurately as the designers, suggesting a way to scale empathic understanding to larger groups of users.

89.title: An Analysis of the Content of Technical Information Used by Engineering Designers
89.summary: The authors examined what kinds of written technical information engineers at two aerospace companies actually rely on, to inform future design information systems. They analysed the text of sample documents and surveyed designers about which attributes help them search. Text documents such as correspondence, reports and manuals need a much richer set of descriptive attributes than drawings or CAD models, and the paper sketches a framework for building taxonomies to index them.

92.title: Activities in Collaborative Concept Selection Processes for Engineering Design
92.summary: The authors set out to identify what designers actually do when groups select among design concepts, as a basis for better decision-making support. In three workshops, groups of participants with differing experience were recorded performing concept selection tasks, and the transcripts were content-analysed. They identified 12 main activities, some with sub-activities, and made five observations about the processes from the time spent on each, which could underpin a descriptive model of concept selection.

104.title: Enhancing Product Development Efficiency Through Changes With a Holistic Strategy
104.summary: The author examined how companies in Northern California's Silicon Valley carried out product development, focusing on problems with collaboration and how to make development more efficient. The study, carried out in 1998, drew on thirty-six qualitative interviews in six companies. It described collaboration problems and the steps companies took to improve efficiency and teamwork, and proposed guidelines and a framework for building organisational support for collaborative work.

107.title: Theoretical Underpinnings of Functional Modeling: Preliminary Experimental Studies
107.summary: The authors set out to test experimentally whether formal methods for functional modeling, which describe what a product must do, give repeatable results, since such formalisms had rarely been tested. At three universities, design teams and individuals created functional models of products with and without the formal vocabulary and method. The models were highly repeatable for a toaster, a power screwdriver and a toy dart gun, and the experiments also exposed weaknesses in the current formalisms.

116.title: Information Handling and Social Interaction of Multi-Disciplinary Design Teams in Conceptual Design: A Classification Scheme Developed From Observed Activity Patterns
116.summary: The authors set out to understand how multidisciplinary teams use information and interact socially during early conceptual design. At a Stanford design charrette on technology-supported global learning spaces, participants from many disciplines were videotaped, and the authors developed a coding scheme to analyse their activity quantitatively. Two teams with apparently very different approaches showed similar activity patterns, each splitting its effort fairly evenly between introducing information and navigating the design process.

119.title: A Survey of Concurrent Engineering Design Practice in the Australian Automotive and Maritime Industries
119.summary: The authors wanted to compare everyday engineering design practice in industry with what research recommends, focusing on concurrent engineering, in which all stages of a product's life are considered together from the start. They reviewed design practice in two major Australian sectors, automotive and maritime, drawing on investigations made for two undergraduate theses in 1999. The review benchmarked the state of practice to help judge how far industry must shift to reach the state of research.

120.title: Learning From Experience of Peers: An Empirical Study of Knowledge Sharing in a Product Design Community
120.summary: The authors studied whether design teams learn from the archived experience of their peers, using a database of design notes, drawings, reports and emails gathered from a Stanford project-based course between 1994 and 1999. They analysed four years of web access records and interviewed users. Teams accessed process-related files far more than product-related ones, usage peaked around deliverables, and its link with team performance grew over time, but physical and psychological barriers limited learning from peers.

128.title: Student System Level Design Activities: An Empirical Pilot Study on Improving Design Outcomes
128.summary: The authors tested whether a laboratory experiment could show that system-level design, earlier found to be associated with better project outcomes, actually causes better results. In a pilot student lab exercise, they compared the outcome quality of design processes that used system-level design activities with those that did not, using simple statistical tests. The results supported an effect of system-level design on quality, but the protocol proved unable to test whole design processes, though it suited testing a specific tool.

130.title: Transforming Design Education by Design
130.summary: The authors treated a design course itself as a product to be designed, aiming to build the best possible project-based course for their setting using tools from design research. They analysed why student projects had failed in earlier courses and selected six design methods to address those failures, forming a mechatronics curriculum for high school students. A study with several groups, including a control group, showed that the redesigned course improved on the existing one.

139.title: Affordances in Product Architecture: Linking Technical Functions and Users’ Tasks
139.summary: The authors set out to help developers link what a product technically does with the tasks users perform with it, using the idea of affordances, the actions an object invites. They introduced a Function-Task Design Matrix and two affordance levels, functional and operational, to capture user-related requirements while generating a product's architecture. They explained the tools step by step and illustrated the method with a case study of a kitchen appliance.

142.title: Effects of Product Usage Context on Consumer Product Preferences
142.summary: The authors developed a framework for understanding how the context in which a product is used shapes customer needs and preferences. They interviewed customers about two sets of products, mobile lighting and food boiling, to identify distinct usage contexts, then measured product choices with interactive surveys. Preferences differed across the usage contexts, and attributes of the chosen products were related to contextual factors, such as product mass being related to how it is transported.

151.title: “Collaborating To Success”: An Experimental Study of Group Idea Generation Techniques
151.summary: This experiment compared the ingredients of four group idea generation methods (Brainsketching, Gallery, 6-3-5 and C-Sketch) by varying how ideas are shared and whether they are written, sketched or both. Teams of participants generated ideas under each combination, and the authors also propose a way to count ideas expressed in mixed sketches and words. Individuals picked up many ideas from teammates, passing subsets of ideas around produced more ideas than showing everything at once, and idea quality improved as teams built on each other's work.

152.title: Preference Consistency in Multiattribute Decision Making
152.summary: The authors addressed the problem of decision makers expressing inconsistent preferences when choosing among design alternatives with several competing attributes. They developed a Preference Consistency Check, demonstrated within the Hypothetical Equivalents and Inequivalents Method but applicable to any ranking or rating-based preference structure. Using a product selection case study in which the decision maker gave inconsistent preferences, they showed the check was effective and illustrated why consistent preferences are needed for a confident decision.

153.title: Does Sketching Skill Relate to Good Design?
153.summary: The authors explored whether a designer's sketching ability relates to how much they sketch and how good their final design is. In a preliminary study, students completed sketch tasks testing drawing facility, mechanical recall and visualization of new objects, and these scores were compared with sketch quantity and design outcomes. Drawing facility correlated positively with sketch quantity but mechanism visualization correlated negatively; sketching ability showed no notable link to design outcome, and students taught sketching tended to draw more.

154.title: Cognitive Characteristics and Design Creativity: An Experimental Study
154.summary: The authors set out to identify how various cognitive characteristics relate to design creativity, so that these links could guide design education. They evaluated cognitive characteristics and abilities in three groups of students with differing exposure to design education. Constructive perception, which combines perceiving and conceiving, and basic visual reasoning ability were both equally related to creative design ability, but no correlation was found between constructive perception and visual reasoning themselves.

160.title: Using Product Dissection to Integrate Product Family Design Research Into the Classroom and Improve Students’ Understanding of Platform Commonality
160.summary: The authors developed a product dissection activity for a graduate course to teach platform commonality, the sharing of parts across related products, and to involve students in research. Five teams took apart and analysed three product families of four products each, and their results were used to study the variability of a published commonality index. Variability came from different levels of dissection, omitted parts and differing factor values, and the activity significantly improved students' understanding of commonality.

188.title: Understanding Perceptual Gaps in Integrated Product Development Teams
188.summary: The authors explored why engineers, designers and marketing researchers think so differently about the same product, which they call perceptual gaps, as part of a model of interdisciplinary team performance. They carried out an in-depth study with engineers, designers (stylists) and marketing researchers in the auto industry. The gaps had a profound effect on the design process, revealing differing goals among the disciplines and leading to unhealthy conflict.

195.title: Functional Modeling Experimental Studies
195.summary: This study tested whether a published method for deriving functional models gives the same model when different designers apply it to the same product. Three experiments were run with participants of varying design experience. The method mostly produced repeatable models, and the authors identify where it works well and where it could be improved.

197.title: Re-Interpretation of Conceptual Design Sketches in Mechanical Engineering
197.summary: A case study of conceptual design sketching in mechanical engineering, focused on how designers reinterpret their own sketches. The authors analyse an example sketch and a sketching sequence, looking at how geometric and functional elements are drawn at different levels of abstraction. They find that reinterpreting a sketch can lead to major changes in the concept, but the mechanism was too rare to confirm, so the paper offers hypotheses for future work.

205.title: Influence of Design Representation on Effectiveness of Idea Generation
205.summary: The authors tested whether recording design ideas as sketches works better than recording them in words during idea generation, a common belief with little experimental evidence. They ran a statistically designed experiment, scoring the ideas produced with each representation for fluency, quality, novelty and variety, and examining how well each conveyed key design information. The results confirmed that graphical representation gave greater benefits for engineering idea generation than textual representation.

218.title: Improving Turbomachinery Design Process Management
218.summary: The authors aimed to help designers produce higher-performance turbomachinery designs more quickly, since getting a new product to market on time is critical to profitability. They combined an enhanced version of the Signposting design process management method with industry-standard analysis codes and computational fluid dynamics, allowing iteration across the whole process and automatic data handling. A laboratory experiment designing a large high-pressure steam turbine succeeded, and the approach was being extended to aero-engine compressor design with Rolls-Royce.

226.title: Creative Stimulation in Conceptual Design
226.summary: The authors set out to understand how designers' thinking is stimulated during conceptual design, since conventional design methods ignore human cognition. They developed a Cognitive Model of Creative Conceptual Design linking the properties that stimulate cognitive processes to the design operations that support them, and tested it through protocol analysis and cognitive experiments. Designers showed recognisable patterns of creative behaviour, and the authors concluded these patterns could be captured and built into the design process to promote creativity.

231.title: A Model of Learning in Design
231.summary: The authors set out to explain how designers learn while they design, because no comprehensive model of this existed to guide the development of computer design support systems. They developed a model called LinD that formally describes the thinking involved in designing and in learning. The model explains how the two activities interact through three kinds of links, which the authors called epistemic, teleological and temporal links.

238.title: Embedding Real Engineering Decisions and Sometimes-Consequent Errors in a Small Design Project Toward Reflective Learning
238.summary: The author described a new project-based design class for junior mechanical engineering students at Osaka University, in which students' own system-level decisions could lead to errors they would learn from. Over two months, students worked through every phase of a simplified but realistic design problem, built and used hardware, and analysed the results. Afterwards, students were seen to learn from their own experience how individual knowledge falls short in system-level design and how such failures can be avoided.

253.title: Modelling Design Interpretation as Interaction of Problem Framing and Problem Solving
253.summary: The authors set out to model how designers interpret and reframe ill-structured design problems, an aspect studied far less rigorously than problem solving. They presented a sequential model treating design as an interplay between specifying the problem and solving it, built around an operation they call framing. They described three reasoning patterns for reinterpreting design problems, supported by a framework based on abstracted similarity and illustrated with extracts from experimental studies.

269.title: Comparing Three Different Modularity Methods
269.summary: The authors compared three methods for dividing a product into modules, because little was known about which method to use and when. They applied the heuristic method, the design structure matrix and modular function deployment to four commercial products, including an intraoral camera and a pipette, and tested how repeatable each method was. Given the same inputs, the methods split the products differently and shared almost no module boundaries; repeatability ranged from 68% to nearly perfect.

283.title: A Collaborative Team-Based Approach to Computational Configuration Design: Initial Results
283.summary: The authors explored whether ideas about effective human teamwork can improve computer algorithms that generate designs. Drawing on organizational behavior research, they built a computational model of collaborative team-based design using multiple software agents and tested it on a manufacturing process-planning problem from the literature. Solution quality improved by 65% and successful solutions per unit time rose by an order of magnitude, with collaboration between agents being the strongest and most consistent source of the gains.

287.title: Representing Product Architecture
287.summary: The authors set out to give engineers a way to represent product architecture, the step that turns a product's functions into a physical layout, because current practice lacks such representations. They developed a vocabulary of core product architecture terms and a practical notation for applying them, intended to be simple enough for educational use. They illustrated the technique with an example and reported the results of a validation experiment.

296.title: Concept Generation and Sketching: Correlations With Design Outcome
296.summary: The author examined whether hard-to-measure parts of the design process are linked to design success, as groundwork for better information tools for designers. Using novice designers' sketches as evidence of their ideas, the study looked at how many concepts were generated, when, what type of sketch was made, and the designers' prior experience. Dimensioned drawings made early in the design process and prior fabrication and building experience were both significantly correlated with better design outcomes.

298.title: Empirical Studies of Design Ideation: Alignment of Design Experiments With Lab Experiments
298.summary: The authors aimed to build a model of how engineers generate ideas, linking realistic design experiments with tightly controlled cognitive psychology lab experiments. They aligned the two kinds of experiment using shared ideation components and uniform measures, and applied this to one component: incubation, or setting a problem aside for a while. Incubation had a positive effect on idea generation in both settings, and the alignment approach proved suitable for modelling individual ideation components.

299.title: Steps Towards Geographically Dispersed Collaborative Student Design Projects
299.summary: The authors wanted to teach undergraduates the skills needed to work in design teams spread across different locations. In January 2002 they set up a collaborative engineering design project between students at the University of Bath in the UK and the University of Canterbury in New Zealand, communicating mainly by email, project web pages and videoconferences. Despite different education programs and time zones, they found a way to fit the project into both curricula, providing a basis for further exchanges.

304.title: Evaluating a Functional Basis
304.summary: The authors evaluated whether two standard vocabularies for describing product functions are suitable for indexing design knowledge so engineers can find and reuse it. In eighteen interviews at two UK aerospace companies, engineering designers described the functions of assemblies or components they knew well, giving 207 function descriptions that were compared with the two taxonomies. Designers referred to functions in only 7% of their descriptions on average, though the most experienced active designers did so four times as often.

309.title: How Process Affects Performance: An Analysis of Student Design Productivity
309.summary: The authors set out to identify design processes that produce higher-quality results in less time. They coded the design journals of twelve student capstone projects for hours spent on different activities at three design levels, rated each project for client satisfaction and design quality, and used factor analysis and regression. A three-factor model explained 91% of the variation in productivity; generating ideas and defining the problem at the system level distinguished the more productive teams.

312.title: Use of Biological Phenomena in Design by Analogy
312.summary: The authors studied how designers use written descriptions of biological phenomena as analogies to solve engineering problems, an approach called biomimetic design. In two studies, participants developed solutions to an example problem from such descriptions, having been told about unhelpful kinds of similarity seen in an earlier study, and the second study aimed to reduce fixation. Misleading similarities and fixation on particular words or solutions declined, but participants still needed support in mapping biological strategies onto the problem.

314.title: Computer Support for Requirements Management in an International Product Development Project
314.summary: The authors examined how a software tool for managing requirements was actually used in practice, since complex products involve thousands of requirements and few studies had evaluated such tools. They studied an international defense materiel development project by taking part in the project team, conducting interviews and reviewing project documents. They mapped the requirements management process, identified different people's needs for tools and information, and described how the tool was introduced and used, ending with guidelines for introducing such tools.

325.title: Relating Design Activity to Quality of Outcome: A Regression Analysis of Student Projects
325.summary: The authors set out to understand how the way students carry out design affects the quality of their results. Using design journals from mechanical engineering student projects at Montana State University and quantitative outcome measures, they related time spent on different activities to outcomes with multivariate regression. Client satisfaction rose with time spent defining the problem and fell with concept-level analysis, while design quality, as judged by professional engineers, was most strongly linked to system-level idea generation and refinement.

330.title: Insights on Designers’ Sketching Activities in New Product Design Teams
330.summary: The authors studied how student designers in new product design teams use sketches, and whether sketching relates to design success. They defined a set of sketch metrics, judged their importance at different design stages, and correlated sketching activity and variety of concept sketches with design outcomes. The total number of sketches and of 3D sketches mattered more as projects moved toward detailed development and testing, and students who made more journal sketches tended to earn higher class grades.

337.title: A Grammar for Function Structures
337.summary: The authors aimed to provide a systematic language for building function structures, diagrams of the flows and functions in a product, which are hard to check, share and teach. They combined function structures with graph grammars, writing rules that capture the feasible ways a function structure can be created. The grammar provides a basis for computer tools that quickly draft function structures, a way to teach them, and a means of automatically generating them to help designers brainstorm new concepts.

349.title: Requirements as a Means to Drive Innovation: A Reason-Based Perspective
349.summary: The authors were concerned that industry's focus on efficiency, such as standard components and short lead times, can crowd out innovation and product value when managing requirements. They identified factors that help create innovative products and condensed them into a reason-based method that challenges requirements and solutions against innovation and value. They demonstrated how the method could be applied using an industrial product development case.

356.title: Enhancing Innovative Product Design by Explicating Tacit Knowledge
356.summary: The authors aimed to help designers bring their tacit knowledge, the experience-based know-how they use without being aware of it, into the open during demanding early stages of product development. They developed a method to make this knowledge explicit and tested it in a controlled study with sixty mechanical engineering students, then adapted it for practicality and used it in a real product design project with more students. The method had a positive influence on the quality of product innovation.

358.title: Multilevel Aligned Empirical Studies of Ideation: Final Results
358.summary: The authors set out to understand design ideation by testing which components of idea generation methods actually work. They ran experiments on several ideation components, such as provocative stimuli, suspending judgment, flexible representation, shifting frame of reference and incubation, at both an engineering design level and a cognitive psychology lab level. Some components had similar effects and could be grouped into broader principles, outcome measures were harder to improve than process measures, and idea quantity correlated with quality.

359.title: Design Activities and Personal Creativity Characteristics: A Case Study of Dual Protocol Analysis Using Design Information and Process
359.summary: The authors explored how designers' activities relate to their personal creativity characteristics, comparing expert and student designers. They analysed recorded design sessions of eight participants using two coding schemes, one for design information and one for the design process, alongside personal creativity tests. Expert designers had more effective design processes than students, participants' creativity traits varied widely, and many of those traits could be linked to their observed design activities.

360.title: Analysis of User Activity in an Engineering Design Task During the Evaluation of an Immersive Stereoscopic Design System
360.summary: The authors wanted to understand how engineers actually spend their time when using an immersive virtual reality system for cable harness design, so that such systems could be improved. Ten participants each completed three harness design tasks on the Co-Star system, and every interaction was recorded and sorted into activity classes. Navigation took about 41% of activity and system operation 23%, against 27% for design itself, while 7% of activity was unproductive and 28% of time was idle.

361.title: Structural Tendencies and Exposure Effects in Design Idea Generation
361.summary: The authors set out to understand how fixation on prior knowledge shapes the ideas designers generate. They ran two design experiments, one tracking the order in which ideas appeared and one showing participants pictorial example ideas at different times. Designers started with the most common categories of ideas and moved to more novel ones over time, and the timing of exposure to examples mattered more than whether the examples were common or unusual.

362.title: A Conceptual Framework for Understanding the Impact of Digital Libraries on Engineering Design Learning
362.summary: The authors set out to explain how the information designers find and use, including from digital libraries, shapes what they learn during a design project. They surveyed engineering students from Stanford, Olin College and Strathclyde who took part in a two-week international team exercise to build bicycles out of paper. From the survey they built a conceptual framework describing how information flows through a design process and feeds designers' learning.

363.title: Characterising in Detail the Information Requests of Engineering Designers
363.summary: Designers can spend up to a quarter of their time looking for information, so the authors set out to characterise in detail the questions that send them searching. Working with the aerospace group of a major power systems company, they combined ethnographic participation, a diary study and observation by shadowing designers. They developed six categories for classifying information requests, including objective, subject and direction of reasoning, analysed two large data sets with them, and derived a coding scheme.

364.title: Incorporating Affordances Into Product Architecture: Methodology and Case Study
364.summary: The authors aimed to bring users' tasks and product affordances into early product architecture decisions, which usually focus on technical functions. They reviewed their Function-Task-Interaction method and ran two studies: field research on end users' mental models of a product's architecture, and an investigation with design experts at a global mobile communications manufacturer. They extended the method with new questions and a user-centred vocabulary, and argued for a controlled vocabulary to describe affordances.

366.title: Identifying Customer Needs: Disabled Persons as Lead Users
366.summary: Ordinary users struggle to imagine needs beyond existing products, so the authors explored whether extraordinary users could act as lead users who sense future needs early. They carried out a case study on mobile phones that compared the needs of disabled persons with those of ordinary users. Disabled users shared the ordinary users' needs but also experienced and could express needs that ordinary users did not yet have, making them a valuable source of customer needs.

368.title: Representing Analogies: Increasing the Probability of Innovation
368.summary: Design by analogy is a powerful route to innovation, and the authors asked whether the way a product is stored in memory affects whether people later use it as an analogy. They ran experiments built around three analogy problems, such as an air mattress as a source for a water-filled travel weights product and a whisk for a flour sifter. How a product was represented in memory influenced people's ability to use it later for a design analogy.

369.title: A Validation Study of an Automated Concept Generator Design Tool
369.summary: The authors sought to test whether the Concept Generator, an early automated software tool for producing design concepts from functions, was a sound approach and to set goals for its development. Four undergraduate researchers from two universities used it in a series of activities, and the solutions they produced were later analysed quantitatively. Both analyses suggested the tool was a promising first step, and the students identified strengths and weaknesses to address.

375.title: Including Functional Models of Biological Phenomena as Design Stimuli
375.summary: The authors explored how best to present biological phenomena to engineers as inspiration for biomimetic design. Participants solved a micro-assembly problem using several representations of leaf abscission, including functional models, and their designs, observations, follow-up conversations and analogical reasoning were analysed. Designers needed an explicit list of all the strategies inherent in the biological phenomenon, extracted beforehand from function structures, and the authors outlined ways to improve such representations.

379.title: Increasing Innovation: A Trilogy of Experiments Towards a Design-by-Analogy Method
379.summary: The authors aimed to build a reliable design-by-analogy method by studying how the wording of products and problems affects designers' use of analogies. In three experiments covering six design problems, analogous products and design problems were described in either domain-general or domain-specific language. Designers more readily used analogous products described in general terms, and success was highest when the problem was stated in domain-specific language and the analogous product in general language.

380.title: Understanding the Use of Language Stimuli in Concept Generation

382.title: Analysis of Engineering Design Journal Sketches and Notations
382.summary: Engineering students rarely keep design journals, and the authors wanted to see whether journal entries could reveal how students learn and practise design. An undergraduate research team at the University of Maryland studied the design journals of 12 students in a senior capstone course, adapting existing coding schemes to infer cognitive activity. The journals revealed uneven time spent on design stages, preferences for sketching, differences in clarity, and varying buy-in to the design tools taught in class.

386.title: Design Methods, Tools, and Outcome Measures: A Survey of Practitioners
386.summary: The author wanted to learn which design methods, tools and success measures working designers and engineers actually use, to help steer design research. She ran a web-based survey of practitioners in fields from product development to aerospace, asking about 14 design methods, several outcome measures and 12 design tools. Respondents found need finding, storyboarding and brainstorming useful but knew less about systematic design, axiomatic design or TRIZ, valued positive customer feedback, and rated CAD tools highly.

390.title: Evaluating the Use of Cyberinfrastructure in the Classroom to Enhance Product Dissection
390.summary: The authors set out to support undergraduate engineering design education with shared digital resources built around product dissection, through a project called CIBER-U. It combined dissection activities at three universities with two digital design repositories, CAD modelling and animation, video, wiki tools and summer research experiences. Nearly 700 students took part in the first phase, which focused on generating and storing data, and the authors reported lessons learned from students and faculty and discussed scaling up nationally.

395.title: Improving Design Understanding by Analyzing Questions
395.summary: The authors set out to better understand design activity by studying the questions designers ask, bringing together research on reasoning questions and strategic questions. They examined transcripts from protocol analysis studies to identify both types of question and related them to a problem-solving model. They described how designers move their tasks forward by asking questions at both levels, with strategic questions forming part of how experienced designers approach a task.

410.title: Towards an Interactive Assessment Framework for Engineering Design Learning
410.summary: Learning in team design project courses is hard to assess, so the authors explored using text processing technology for online assessment in a capstone engineering design course. They ran a five-week classroom study and analysed students' conversations on the course discussion board to predict their productivity. Simple counts such as number or length of posts and files committed did not correlate with instructor grades, but simple linguistic patterns in the conversations predicted grades substantially better.

430.title: Use of Analogies by Novice and Experienced Design Engineers
430.summary: The authors set out to understand how design engineers with different levels of experience use analogies in real work. They analysed protocol data from twelve design engineers in the aerospace industry, classifying the purpose of each analogy and the reasoning behind it. Novices mostly transferred information without linking it to design issues, while experienced designers used analogies to solve or identify problems and reasoned about a component's function and predicted behaviour.

433.title: Effects of Dichotomous Lexical Stimuli in Concept Generation
433.summary: Continuing their work on words as design stimuli, the authors compared stimulus words that agree with a design problem with words that contradict it. In a think-aloud experiment, half the participants generated concepts with congruent stimuli and half with incongruent stimuli. Participants given incongruent words used them as verbs more often, which tends to bring new ideas into concept generation, and two independent raters agreed that their concepts were more novel.

434.title: Creative Stimulation in Conceptual Design: An Analysis of Industrial Case Studies
434.summary: To learn when the ideas behind promising concepts are conceived, the authors tracked several real industrial design projects through early conceptual design. They traced how ideas from initial group brainstorming meetings fed into concepts at the next stage gate meeting, and gave different groups different forms of stimulus against a control group. Idea production stayed steady for the first hour, but ideas that reached stage gate concepts fell sharply after 20 minutes, and stimuli increased such ideas.

440.title: Increasing Innovation: Presentation and Evaluation of the Wordtree Design-by-Analogy Method
440.summary: Design by analogy can spark innovation, but few methods guide engineers in finding useful analogies. The authors presented the WordTree Design-by-Analogy Method, which systematically re-expresses a design problem in new words to point to analogies and analogous domains, using a team's own knowledge rather than special databases. A controlled experiment and redesign projects showed the method helped engineers find analogies and led to unexpected and unique solutions, while also pointing to improvements.

444.title: Comparing Component Functional Template Modeling Experimental Results in an Undergraduate Level Engineering Design Course
444.summary: Component functional templates give novices ready-made function layouts for common electromechanical parts, and the authors wanted to test further whether they improve students' functional models. They ran an experiment across several sections of an undergraduate engineering design course, limiting how long students were exposed to the templates, and scored models on structure, number of functions, flow representation and product representation. Students using the templates consistently made fewer mistakes in every category and produced better, more accurate models.

456.title: Mapping Shape Geometry and Emotions Using Fuzzy Logic
456.summary: Designers asked to create a shape that evokes an emotion such as aggressive or friendly each interpret it differently, so the authors sought to formalise the link between 3D geometry and intended emotion. They analysed 3D shapes made by design engineering students to match a set of emotion words and built a fuzzy logic model with if-then rules linking geometric features to each emotion. A study of how users perceived the shapes showed a high correlation with the model's predictions.

457.title: Quantifying Aesthetic Form Preference in a Utility Function
457.summary: Designers struggle to translate consumers' vague aesthetic wishes, such as wanting a product to look strong, into an actual form. The authors set out to show how a qualitative attribute like product form can be represented quantitatively, building it into a utility function whose values are captured for each person through designed experiments. Once a person's preference is captured this way, the utility function can guide the generation, modification or verification of product forms.

458.title: Overcoming Blocks in Conceptual Design: The Effects of Open Goals and Analogical Similarity on Idea Generation
458.summary: The authors asked which kinds of analogies most help designers and when during problem solving they should be sought. In an experiment, participants received information either closely or distantly related to a design problem, given either before they started or during a break after they had begun. Closely related information influenced solutions whenever it was given, but distantly related information only helped when given during a break, supporting the idea that unfinished goals help people absorb distant ideas.

459.title: Design Team Framing: Paths and Principles
459.summary: New product teams must both frame a design around a real customer need and get everyone on the team to agree on that framing, and the authors studied how these two challenges interact. They introduced a framework for tracing a team's path along both dimensions and, using interviews and survey data from graduate multidisciplinary product development teams, illustrated the three most common paths. These case studies yielded four themes to help teams navigate the new product development process.

469.title: WeDesign: A Forum-Based Tool for Managing User-Generated Content in Engineering Design and Product Development
469.summary: The authors built a web forum-based tool that lets large groups, including customers, contribute ideas to engineering design and product development in a crowdsourcing approach. They tested an early version in a mechanical engineering senior capstone design course, comparing a control mode with a parliamentary mode that encouraged discussion and negotiation and let participants design their own work processes. The designs produced and survey responses showed the system was well received and allowed a group to generate and select concepts.

472.title: An Industrial Case Study of Design Methodology and Decision Making for Automotive Electronics
472.summary: Growing product complexity in the automotive industry puts new demands on how engineers make design decisions, so the authors investigated the decision methods used in the research and development department of an international vehicle manufacturer. Through interviews and surveys, they identified the methods used by individual roles in different development teams. Most respondents used unstructured methods but wanted more structured ones, such as expert support, guidelines and methods training, and the study identified the company's best practice.

476.title: Design Team Convergence: The Influence of Example Solution Quality
476.summary: The authors examined how engineering design teams come to a shared understanding of a problem and its solution, and how example solutions shown beforehand affect this. In a cognitive study, teams received a poor example solution, a good example solution or none before solving a design problem, and Latent Semantic Analysis of their language tracked their convergence. A poor example slowed convergence and lowered design quality, while a good example did not change convergence but led to higher quality solutions.

480.title: Investigation of the Interpretability of Three Function Structure Representations: A User Study
480.summary: Function models describe what a product does regardless of form, and the authors asked how easily people can recognise a product from such models at different levels of abstraction. Sixteen mechanical engineering graduate students tried to identify products from function models at three levels, noting time taken and helpful keywords. Models were much easier to interpret when they used free-language terms and described the product's environment rather than a limited function vocabulary, and more functions helped identify similar products.

481.title: Four Dimensions of Design Similarity
481.summary: Brands need product families with a coherent look, but it is unclear which design elements make products seem similar. The authors proposed a framework of design elements in four dimensions, such as colour, texture, shape and form, and ran a two-phase survey with 52 participants who judged the similarity of pairs of simplified shapes and then of real products. Sharing the same shape, texture, colour and pattern significantly increased how similar a pair of products appeared.

486.title: A Methodology for Quantifying the Perceived Environmental Friendliness of Vehicle Silhouettes in Engineering Design
486.summary: People judge products on subjective qualities such as how eco-friendly a car looks, but such perceptual attributes are hard to include in design optimisation. The authors combined methods from psychology and engineering into a modelling framework that covers designing stimuli through design of experiments, survey design and statistical analysis. They demonstrated the method on vehicle silhouettes, quantifying an attribute they called perceived environmental friendliness and examining which design features influenced it.

490.title: Lean Thinking and Product Innovation in the Furniture Industry
490.summary: The authors asked whether lean thinking principles, methods and tools could be applied to product development in a traditional, largely family-owned sector like furniture making. They designed a cross-case research programme with in-depth case studies of one furniture firm in Portugal and one in Brazil, starting with how each company was organised. Preliminary results showed neither company had a formal product development system, leading to poor information flow and many sources of waste.

495.title: Metrics for Evaluating and Optimizing the Barrier and Time to Reverse Engineer a Product
495.summary: Reverse engineering is common in industry, and both original designers and imitators would benefit from knowing how hard and slow it is. The authors developed a set of quantitative metrics and parameters, drawing an analogy with Ohm's law, to calculate the barrier to reverse engineering any product and the time needed. Original designers could use the metrics to make products harder to copy, while competitors could target the most rewarding products.

496.title: Concept Diagramming Software for Engineering Design Support: A Review and Synthesis of Studies
496.summary: Engineers think by combining ideas spatially across levels of abstraction, which digital tools rarely support, so the authors summarised years of experience with diagramming software that supports such thinking. They synthesised three studies spanning conceptual to embodiment design, each centred on a tool: Cambridge's DRed design rationale editor, IHMC's CmapTools and the Open University's Compendium. Hypermedia diagrams offered many unique, valuable functions but had practical limits, and the authors called for more diagram literacy, industry studies and better interfaces.

497.title: A Testing Method and Cognitive Model of Human Diagram Understanding for Automating Design Sketch Recognition
497.summary: Computer design tools handle sketches poorly, even though people recognise them easily, so the authors set out to learn how humans interpret mechanical engineering diagrams as a step towards automated sketch recognition. They presented a testing method that probes human diagram recognition using techniques analogous to peripheral vision and attention. From this they proposed a cognitive model of human diagram understanding that future computational design tools could emulate.

498.title: Sketching in Design: Easily Influencing Behavior
498.summary: Engineering students rarely sketch during design, often preferring CAD tools, and the authors wanted to see whether a short intervention could change this. In a senior capstone design course at the University of Maryland, they reviewed students' sketches before and after a lesson on the importance of sketching in mechanical design, and compared them with a control group. The lesson changed the content of the students' sketches compared with the control group.

504.title: Effective Analogical Transfer Using Biological Descriptions Retrieved With Functional and Biologically Meaningful Keywords
504.summary: Biology is a rich source of design analogies, and having earlier helped engineers find relevant biological phenomena using keywords, the authors turned to how well designers apply them. They studied novice designers transferring analogies from biological descriptions retrieved with functional and biologically meaningful keywords. Transfer was poor when cause-and-effect relations were hard to spot, especially when descriptions had many action words or used the passive voice, so the authors proposed a template to help designers recognise these relations.

508.title: Framing Sustainability in Human-Centered Product Design
508.summary: Engineers want to design sustainable products, but many consumers do not yet prioritise or clearly express sustainability needs. The authors examined user research carried out by students in a graduate product design course, looking at how users describe sustainability, how it interacts with other needs and what trade-offs they make, and presented a case study of one team. They showed how the team's findings shaped its mission statement and product strategy, and proposed recommendations for designing innovative, sustainable consumer products.

510.title: A Stochastic Graph Grammar Algorithm for Interactive Search
510.summary: Generative grammars can describe very different design concepts, but these are hard to evaluate by computer, so the authors developed a search method that asks the user instead. The method limits users to at most thirty pairwise comparisons of candidates and uses a stochastic decision process to infer which solutions best match their preferences; they applied it to a grammar for tying neckties. In 21 user experiments and 4000 automated runs, it consistently found solutions in the top 0.2 percent.

512.title: Support for the Use of Hierarchical Temporal Memory Systems in Automated Design Evaluation: A First Experiment
512.summary: Automated design synthesis tools are rarely used in industry, partly because they cannot judge design quality the way people do. The authors proposed hierarchical temporal memory systems, which learn from examples, as a way to capture qualitative design quality, and in a first experiment trained them to recognise the visual styles of Hepplewhite, Stickley, and Greene and Greene chair backs.
