The systems stored style information similarly to humans, making them a promising option for future design automation.

519.title: Acceptance and Divergence From Engineering Design Procedures Implicating Knowledge Flow
519.summary: Companies develop design procedures, methods and tools, but engineers do not always follow them, and the authors set out to understand why. They carried out semi-structured interviews with 20 people at a company that develops large, complex equipment for oil rigs, focusing on its product development process model, methods and handling of knowledge. They uncovered three types of unwritten, implicit procedures, argued these must be recognised and managed alongside official ones, and proposed corrective actions that managers then evaluated.

520.title: How Cultural Characteristics Influence Design Processes: An Empirical Study
520.summary: The authors investigated whether designers' cultural backgrounds shape how they approach a design task, as product development increasingly brings together people from different countries. Designers from industry in Germany, India and China were observed solving the same design problem in a laboratory, and their processes were analysed against cultural characteristics drawn from the literature. The design processes differed, for example in how problems, sub-functions, selection criteria and improvements were handled, and these differences could be linked to cultural characteristics.

521.title: Relations Between Design Activities and Interactional Characteristics in Novice-Expert Design Consultations: ‘What’ is Done ‘How’
521.summary: The authors studied what happens in consultation meetings between novice and expert designers, since much design knowledge is shared face to face rather than written down. At Rolls-Royce Aerospace Engineering they recorded seven meetings between trainees and experts across three trainee team projects, and related a coding of design activities to a coding of conversational flow. Some activities were mostly carried out by novices or by experts, while others were done collaboratively, leading to suggestions for practice and further research.

522.title: Relationship Conflict and Feeling Communication in Design Teams
522.summary: The authors explored whether the feeling words design team members use in their messages could reveal team conflict early enough for instructors or managers to step in. They analysed 1,926 messages sent by 13 teams in a new product development class at UC Berkeley, comparing feeling language with conflict levels and team performance. High-performing and low-conflict teams used a lot of feeling language, high-conflict teams often suppressed it after feedback, and medium-conflict teams built up to normal levels over time.

523.title: Increasing Innovation in Multi-Function Systems: Evaluation and Experimentation of Two Ideation Methods for Design
523.summary: The authors tested two recently developed concept generation methods: WordTree Design-by-Analogy, which uses related words to find distant analogies, and Transformation Design, which draws on principles of reconfigurable products. Forty-one mechanical engineering students worked in groups on a problem of tagging and tracking vehicles, in a full-factorial experiment analysed with ANOVA. Transformation Design raised the number of concepts by 25-30%, while WordTree did not increase the count but produced distinctly novel and diverse solutions.

525.title: Design Fixation on Non-Verbal Stimuli: The Influence of Simple vs. Rich Pictorial Information on Design Problem-Solving
525.summary: The authors examined how pictures of existing solutions influence designers when they generate new ideas, a form of over-reliance known as design fixation. Industrial design students generated ideas during an ideation task after being shown either simple or rich pictorial representations of an existing solution. Both kinds of pictures caused high levels of fixation, with both harmful and helpful effects on idea quality, and the originality of ideas from groups shown examples was significantly reduced.

535.title: Evaluating Relative Instructional Effectiveness and Efficiencies of Design Activities for Product Platform Planning
535.summary: The authors wanted a way to measure how well an online teaching resource on product platform planning, built around power tool case studies, actually helped students learn. They proposed two quantitative methods, linked in one model, that use Data Envelopment Analysis to rate the learning effectiveness and delivery efficiency of each case assignment, and tested them with five undergraduates at Virginia Tech. The work gave an improved, relative picture of how effective and efficient each learning activity was.

537.title: An Approach to Educating Team Work
537.summary: Students on team design projects are tempted to contribute less while sharing the same grade, a problem known as free-riding. To see whether students could be taught the benefits of contributing, the authors ran a pilot experiment using a repeated prisoner's dilemma game. Grades were used in the game's payoff matrix to mimic an academic setting, as a first step towards a way of reducing free-riding in team-based design classes.

538.title: Concept Exploration Through Morphological Charts: An Experimental Study
538.summary: Morphological charts list a design's functions and possible ways to achieve each one, and the authors asked whether the shape of such a chart affects the quality of the concepts designers draw from it. Undergraduate mechanical engineering students worked with one of two charts holding the same number of cells: five functions with three options each, or three functions with five options each. The chart with fewer functions and more options per function helped students produce higher quality concepts.

544.title: Develop Pleasurable Automotive Switch-Feel Through Perceptual Design
544.summary: Car switches are usually designed for looks, ergonomics and function rather than how pleasant they feel, so the authors developed a perceptual design approach to engineer switch-feel. Using haptic simulators, they ran psychophysical studies with multidimensional scaling, sensitivity thresholds and preference experiments to link physical switch parameters to perceived quality, and built a system to measure real switches. Applied to the climate control switches of a production vehicle, the approach delivered pleasurable switch-feel and improved engineering efficiency.

548.title: Frontier Design: A Product Usage Context Method
548.summary: Engineers often design for unfamiliar settings, such as high human-need projects, and existing methods do little to capture this context. The authors built a contextual needs assessment method, centred on a template of context questions about how, where and by whom a product is used, and tested it in experiments, an inventive design application and student projects. The method proved usable and useful, and students rated it as valuable as established methods such as black box and activity diagrams.

550.title: Investigating the Affective Force on Creating Shared Understanding
550.summary: Psychology links emotion to thinking, and the authors asked how affect shapes the shared understanding that design teams build. They combined a framework for analysing shared understanding with a linguistic technique for extracting favourable and unfavourable attitudes from speech, and applied both to a transcript of collaborative design. The method allowed affect to be observed alongside cognitive processing and showed how the emotional content of designers' communication shifted design activities.

554.title: Empathic Lead Users: The Effects of Extraordinary User Experiences on Customer Needs Analysis and Product Redesign
554.summary: The authors tested whether ordinary customers could be turned into lead users, able to reveal hidden needs, by having them use a product under extraordinary conditions. In a trial study with a two-person tent, they compared these empathic lead user interviews with verbal interviews and with interviews where people used a prototype normally. Empathic lead user interviews uncovered five times as many latent needs as normal-use interviews and twenty times as many as verbal interviews.

557.title: Study of Argumentative Negotiation in Collaborative Design
557.summary: Engineers on design teams from different disciplines often struggle to reach agreement, and the authors had earlier proposed an argumentation-based negotiation framework to help. Here they ran an experiment to assess how this negotiation support affected both the process and the outcome of collaborative design. The results showed that the approach had positive effects on collaborative design but also revealed limitations.

567.title: Analysis of Team Interaction and Team Creativity of Student Design Teams Based on Personal Creativity Modes
567.summary: The authors studied whether knowing team members' personal creativity modes could improve how student design teams interact and how creative their designs are. Experimental teams learned their creativity modes and practised teamwork before a conceptual design task, and their designs were scored for novelty and resolution against control teams; one diverse and one uniform team were also analysed in detail. Experimental teams scored higher, and members of the diverse team interacted in very different ways reflecting their creativity modes.

575.title: Corporate Decision Making and Part Differentiation: A Strategy for Customer-Driven Product Development Planning
575.summary: The authors studied how corporate decisions at each stage of product development affect cost control and customer appeal, often treated as competing goals. They built a model of strategic planning from observations and interviews with everyone from top executives to design team members at a large automobile company. Mapping parts by complexity and value to customers showed which decisions matter most, helping companies balance cost against customers' emotional response.

576.title: Cognitive Modeling of Iteration in Conceptual Design
576.summary: The authors set out to understand the mental iterations designers go through during conceptual design, which affect design performance but were poorly understood. They built a cognitive model identifying three iteration loops, problem redefinition, idea stimulation and concept reuse, and tested it in an experiment comparing creative and routine design tasks. Iteration occurred more in creative design, with far more problem redefinition and idea stimulation loops, while concept reuse loops made up a larger share in routine design.

582.title: A Study of the Mechanical Designer’s Strategies and Tactics During the Later Phases of the Engineering Design Process
582.summary: The authors explored the strategies and tactics mechanical designers use in the later phases of design, after the concept is chosen. They ran six experiments covering basic design tasks, use of rules and guidelines, and additional factors, and analysed what designers said aloud as they worked. Although individuals differed, the experts followed similar strategies: they reasoned early in terms of concrete parts and quickly solved interface problems, but often treated evaluation and checking as secondary.

590.title: An Empirical Evaluation of Novelty-SAPPhIRE Relationship

593.title: An Examination of Prototyping and Design Outcome
593.summary: The author examined whether features of prototyping, such as the number of parts and the time spent on design and fabrication, relate to the success of a design. The study followed teams designing and building electro-mechanical devices in a mechanical engineering design course, tracking these factors over the project. Prototypes with fewer parts, and with fewer parts added during development, were linked to better outcomes, while spending more time on a project was not necessarily associated with success.

594.title: A Methodology for Integrating Customers’ Assessments During the Conceptual Design
594.summary: The authors aimed to give designers one consistent framework for understanding customer needs, carrying them into product concepts and assessing those concepts. They combined established methods from psychophysics, marketing and decision theory, such as multidimensional scaling and the Analytic Hierarchy Process, and applied them with user tests on the design of drinking glasses. The tool helped define the semantic side of the need, ranked prototypes against an ideal product, and highlighted dimensions to improve.

605.title: The Effect of Functional Modeling on Understanding Complex Biological Systems
605.summary: The authors asked which external representations best help people understand complex biological systems well enough to use them as analogies in engineering design. In a pilot cognitive study, they compared how well Structure-Behavior-Function (SBF) models, plain text, and text with diagrams supported people in making inferences about biological systems. SBF models appeared to support more accurate inferences for complex and abstract questions, although no single representation was best for every type of inference.

606.title: A Computer Aided Approach for Reformulating “Ill-Defined” Problems

608.title: Design Fixation in Physical Modeling: An Investigation on the Role of Sunk Cost
608.summary: The authors investigated why some studies found that building physical models makes designers fixate on early ideas while others did not, testing whether the sunk cost effect explains it. They ran a controlled between-subjects idea generation experiment, also testing whether physical models improve designers' mental models. The cost of building played a vital role in fixation, which did not seem inherent to physical models, and models helped designers produce higher-quality ideas.

609.title: Biologically Inspired Design: A Macrocognitive Account
609.summary: The authors aimed to describe, at a high level, how designers think when they adapt functions and mechanisms from nature to solve engineering problems. Drawing on an in situ study of designers working on biologically inspired design projects, they built a macrocognitive information-processing model of the activity. They then compared and contrasted the model with other accounts of analogical design, such as TRIZ, case-based design and design patterns, as a step towards better methods and support tools.

610.title: A Study of the Effectiveness of Empathic Experience Design as a Creativity Technique

613.title: Characterizing the Effect of Domain Distance in Design-by-Analogy
613.summary: The authors tested whether analogies from distant domains lead designers to think more abstractly and produce more creative designs than analogies from closely related domains. In a between-subjects experiment, 17 engineering students received analogies from the problem domain and from a domain of varying distance, then solved a design problem. Designers rated distant analogies and their resulting solutions as less useful and practical, yet analysis of their solutions found distant domains at least as useful as close ones.

614.title: Extraction and Transfer of Biological Analogies for Creative Concept Generation
614.summary: The authors developed tools to help novice designers borrow ideas from nature, since novices struggle to extract and apply the strategies in biological phenomena. They tested a causal relation template for retrieving strategies from biological descriptions, plus instructional mapping rules for transferring them to design concepts. Participants using both tools produced concepts where correct analogical transfer was significantly linked to creativity, unlike those using only the template, who often left concepts underdeveloped.

616.title: Understanding of Emotions and Reasoning During Consumer Tradeoff Between Function and Aesthetics in Product Design
616.summary: The authors investigated how consumers decide between products when weighing both looks and function, expecting such choices to involve both reasoning and emotion. They built a two-stage conjoint preference model, which correlated at about 0.56 with ratings from 14 participants, and used fMRI brain scans of 7 participants choosing between options varying in form, function or both. Choices involving both form and function used some unique brain networks and activated emotion-related regions when form and function conflicted.

619.title: Foraging for Inspiration: Understanding and Supporting the Online Information Seeking Practices of Biologically Inspired Designers
619.summary: The authors studied how designers search the web for biological systems to imitate, a key early step in biologically inspired design that poses its own difficulties. Based on observations of design teams, they built an information-processing model of this search and analysed the costs of designers' information foraging behaviour. They proposed adding conceptual models to online biology resources to make relevant ones easier to find, and described Biologue, an interactive online environment that puts this approach into practice.

622.title: Form Function Fidelity
622.summary: The authors studied how well people's judgments of a car's performance based on its shape match the shape's actual measured performance, since first impressions of products often come from appearance. Participants rated computer-generated car designs on how aerodynamic, sporty, fuel efficient and rugged they looked, and ratings were compared with measured aerodynamics, centre of gravity and wheel stance. The authors identified which shape features most influenced judgments and compared them with their effect on real performance.

623.title: A Descriptive Study of Designers’ Tools for Capturing, Reflecting on, and Sharing User Needs and Conceptual Designs
623.summary: The authors examined the tools designers use to capture user needs and early design concepts on their own and to share them with collaborators. They drew on interviews with practising designers and design researchers, plus documents from undergraduate and graduate new product development courses, and analysed the tools by how formal they were and how they supported sharing. They proposed a model of sharing as a cycle of capture, reflect and share, and offered recommendations for future design information tools.

627.title: Redefining User Perception: A Method for Fully Capturing the User Perspective of a Product Concept
627.summary: The authors set out to capture how users, as opposed to designers, fundamentally perceive a product, because understanding users' real needs is crucial but hard for designers. They developed and tested a Participatory 3D modeling method in which users and designers model their view of an existing product or service concept. Users' perceptions were not only opposite to the designers' but much wider, as users modeled their whole experience around the product rather than the product itself.

628.title: More Space to Think: Eight Years of Visual Support for Rationale Capture, Creativity and Knowledge Management in Aerospace Engineering
628.summary: The authors drew lessons from eight years of industrial use of DRed, a concept mapping tool for capturing design rationale on which over 700 Rolls-Royce engineers were trained. They interviewed 11 professionals, from junior engineers to chief designers, and qualitatively analysed transcripts and sample maps. Mapping was often the easiest way to organise unstructured ideas and conflicting views, but its flexibility made methods hard to standardise, and features must balance simplicity, learnability and functionality.

630.title: Environment-Based Design (EBD)
630.summary: The author summarised Environment-Based Design, a design methodology developed over two decades on the idea that design changes an existing environment into a desired one by creating a new artefact. The paper set out four requirements for an effective design methodology, then presented the mathematical, semantic and algorithmic foundations of the method's three activities: environment analysis, conflict identification and solution generation. Experimental validation and industrial applications were summarised to show the method's effectiveness, and open research questions were listed.

632.title: When to Transform? Development of Indicators for Design Context Evaluation
632.summary: The authors addressed when it makes sense to design a transformable product, one with two or more functional states, a question earlier research had left open. After reviewing how prior work categorises transformers, they used both deductive and inductive studies to identify transformation indicators, key context properties and usage factors. The result was a set of basic transformation indicators, which can show whether transformation suits a design problem and help develop new transformers by examining a usage environment or process.

636.title: Towards a Formal Representation Model of Problem Formulation in Design
636.summary: The authors aimed to better understand how designers formulate problems, as a step towards a computer system that supports this creative stage of design. They ran exploratory protocol studies of novice designers and interviewed an expert, all working on a model aircraft for an AIAA student competition, and proposed a formal representation called a problem map. The maps showed how problem and solution spaces evolved over time, with the expert attending to richer attributes and relations than the novices.

638.title: A User Study to Evaluate the Function Model and Function Interaction Model for Concept Generation
638.summary: The authors compared traditional function models with a function interaction model that also captures non-functional requirements and interactions with users and other products, to see how each affects concept generation. Forty students were split into two groups, each using one model to generate solutions to a design problem, and an external panel rated the concepts for quantity and quality. The traditional function model group produced more concepts, but the function interaction model group produced higher-quality ones.

639.title: Analysis of Design Activities Using EEG Signals
639.summary: The authors introduced a way of studying designers' thinking by measuring brain activity directly with EEG, as an alternative to protocol analysis, which is prone to subjectivity. They recorded six EEG channels from a designer working on a design task and calculated the power in four frequency bands. For the given problem, the designer spent more effort on visual thinking while generating solutions than while evaluating them, a preliminary result that lays a foundation for further study.

641.title: Potential Limitations of Verbal Protocols in Design Experiments
641.summary: The authors re-examined the talk-out-loud (verbal protocol) method after their own experiment found that design stimuli did not increase concept creativity, contradicting much of the literature. Having ruled out other possible errors, they reviewed the literature and their experience to identify limitations of verbal protocols that are specific to design studies. They proposed design-specific guidelines for using the method and outlined future work, concluding that verbal protocols remain a valuable, practical tool for studying design cognition.

642.title: A Comparison of Formal Methods for Evaluating the Language of Preference in Engineering Design
642.summary: The authors explored how design teams' preferences for alternatives can be measured from what they say, since design decisions are usually discussed rather than formally modelled. They compared two formal methods for assessing preferences from team discussion transcripts, APPRAISAL and Preferential Probabilities from Transcripts (PPT), and examined how consistently teams judged design attributes. The two methods gave comparable assessments of preference, and a team's assessment of an attribute could change substantially over time.

644.title: Exploring the Meaning of Success in Outsourced Product Development
644.summary: The authors examined what success and failure actually mean when companies outsource product development, because earlier studies reported high failure rates without agreeing on definitions. Based on in-depth interviews with thirty design consultants and clients, they reviewed the strengths and weaknesses of different success measures. They proposed the client's willingness to recommend the consultant as a common outcome measure, found that it varied widely, and identified several common ways client expectations and deliverables diverge.

646.title: Using Symbol Emergence to Discover Multi-Lingual Translations in Design
646.summary: The authors explored how design terms can be translated between languages by grounding them in the design context, since terms and their meanings vary across international design groups. They used an embodied approach in which compact characterisations of functional designs, called image schemas, are learned from performance on a task and then linked to words from human commentary. They demonstrated the approach on insertion tasks and fits, learning both the schemas and their labels in English and Telugu.

649.title: Physical Models in Idea Generation: Hindrance or Help?
649.summary: The authors tested whether building physical models during idea generation causes designers to fixate on early ideas or instead helps them, since the literature offers conflicting advice. They ran a between-subjects experiment with four conditions: sketching only, building, building and testing, and constrained sketching. No evidence of design fixation was found, and physical models appeared to supplement designers' mental models, leading to a higher fraction of functional ideas.

653.title: Forming Creative Teams: An Experimental Approach
653.summary: The authors proposed a structured way to help managers choose who should work together on a team expected to produce creative ideas, assuming past creative interactions predict future ones. Executive MBA participants rated how easily they generated creative ideas with each classmate, then were randomly assigned to teams for a product design exercise and rated teammates again. Creative interactions were predicted by both past creative interactions and classmates' views of a person's ability to spark ideas in others.

654.title: A Framework of Design for Affordances Using Affordance Feature Repositories
654.summary: The authors proposed a systematic way to design affordances, the features of products that naturally invite people to use them in certain ways. In their framework, affordances are identified through function-task interaction matrices or observation, matching features are retrieved from a repository according to design constraints and context, and new features are designed by analogy. They illustrated the framework with a case in which various designers designed affordance features for a tumbler coffee cup using such a repository.

655.title: Identifying Enablers and Barriers to Successful Platform-Based Product Development: A Case Study From Business-to-Business Products
655.summary: The authors sought to identify what helps and hinders platform-based product development, a common strategy for developing more products with fewer resources. They combined a comprehensive literature review with an exploratory case study of business-to-business companies with very different cultures and experience of platforms. Key enablers included institutionalising systems engineering, developing and communicating product roadmaps, strengthening phase gate reviews and characterising critical parameters, and the recommendations could be implemented without major organisational change.

656.title: Study of Existing Metrics Used in Measurement of Ideation Effectiveness

658.title: Towards a Decentralised Approach to Modelling Connectivity in Complex Products
658.summary: The authors looked for ways to reduce the heavy effort of building connectivity models, which map how the components of complex products depend on each other and help avoid unexpected rework. They broke the Design Structure Matrix into L-shaped or cross-shaped sub-sections, or modules, so that each person's effort is limited to a single module. Mathematical models were used to estimate the effort saved by this decentralised approach, and an experiment assessed its effect on model quality.

661.title: Applied Tests of Design Skills: Divergent Thinking Data Analysis and Reliability Studies
661.summary: The authors analysed data from a standardised test of divergent thinking, one of several tests they developed for cognitive skills relevant to conceptual design. The test was given to over 500 engineering students and some practising engineers, and 23 measured variables were examined with exploratory and confirmatory factor analysis. A four-factor solution fit reasonably well, but the factors matched individual test questions rather than measures such as fluency or originality, and several indirect measures did not load meaningfully.

664.title: Assessing the Quality of Ideas From Prolific, Early-Stage Product Ideation
664.summary: The authors developed and tested quick metrics for screening the large numbers of rough sketches produced in brainstorming, to pick out the most promising product ideas. They used 1,767 idea sketches for three product themes as a test bed and had reviewers rate them. Creativity ratings correlated strongly with novelty but barely with usefulness, clearer sketches were rated more creative, and people who produced more ideas had higher creativity and novelty scores.

666.title: A Validation Regarding Effectiveness of Scenario Graph
666.summary: The authors set out to validate Scenario Graph, a structured mind mapping method that helps design teams imagine scenarios for new products and services, since design methods are hard to validate. They proposed a validation framework and ran an experiment in which 43 people used Scenario Graph and 44 used brainstorming on the same problem. The number of ideas did not differ significantly, but the Scenario Graph group produced ideas that were significantly more novel, feasible and abstract.

668.title: Exploring the Collective Categorization of Biological Information for Biomimetic Design
668.summary: The authors explored combining several people's categorisations of biological information, because sorting it for use in design databases is subjective and ambiguous. Four participants independently grouped 163 examples of biological transformation using their own approaches, and a computational algorithm measured how related their groups were. Participants interpreted the information differently, but combining their categorisations revealed meaningful hierarchical, synonymous and causal relations that could support formal representations of biological phenomena.

672.title: Evaluating the Directed Method for Bioinspired Design
672.summary: The authors tested whether simply asking designers to consider how nature would solve a problem, the so-called directed method, improves idea generation, to provide a baseline for more systematic bioinspired design methods. A group of 121 novice designers tackled one of two design problems, either prompted to think about nature or given no method. The directed method gave no advantage in the number, quality, novelty or variety of ideas, so the authors recommended pursuing more systematic bioinspired methods.

674.title: Towards a Tool for Characterizing the Progression of Academic Research
674.summary: The authors began developing a tool to measure the progress of academic research, inspired by industry tools such as technology readiness levels, to help researchers and funders plan and communicate. Their proposed Research Maturity Levels divide research into background knowledge, problem and question formulation, procedures and results, and resources, each with increasing maturity levels and ways to record iterations and 'eureka' moments. A preliminary evaluation suggested the tool shows promise as a comprehensive measure of research progress.

675.title: Time-Based Modeling of Linguistic Preference to Preferential Probability
675.summary: The authors developed a way to predict which concept a committee of designers will choose based on how they talk about each alternative, since preferences are often spoken rather than formally recorded. They modelled the intensity and uncertainty of preferences expressed in natural language, converted these into probability distributions, and used a Markov model to track how preferences change over time. A case study was presented to illustrate the validity of the method.

676.title: Systematic Ideation Effectiveness Study of TRIZ
676.summary: The authors tested whether TRIZ, a structured method for inventive problem solving, makes the people who use it more creative. Students at the University of Texas at El Paso and the University of Maryland redesigned an LED traffic light that, unlike incandescent ones, does not melt accumulated snow, and their ideas were scored for quantity, novelty and variety. At both institutions, using TRIZ improved the novelty and variety of the concepts generated.

678.title: On Measuring Engineering Risk Attitudes
678.summary: The authors developed a test to measure how willing engineers are to take or avoid risk, because attitudes to risk can bias design decisions. The Engineering-Domain-Specific Risk-Taking (E-DOSPERT) test covers risk identification, analysis, evaluation and treatment, and its reliability was assessed by surveying undergraduate engineering students in Australia and the United States. The test reliably measured risk aversion and risk seeking, including for risk identification and treatment, but factor analysis suggested four other domains may better describe engineers' risk attitudes.

679.title: Comparing the Contribution of the Group to the Initial Idea in Progressive Idea Generation
679.summary: The authors examined what group members add to an individual's initial idea in progressive idea generation methods such as 6-3-5/C-Sketch, where ideas are passed around and built on. Participants developed concepts for alarm clocks or litter grabbers, and initial ideas were compared statistically with the final group results, rated at feature level for originality, innovation characteristics and feasibility. The group generally improved the originality and innovativeness of initial ideas, including highly original ones, while feasibility dropped slightly but not significantly.

682.title: The Structure of Creative Design: What Problem Maps Can Tell Us About Problem Formulation and Creative Designers
682.summary: The authors explored what the way designers formulate problems can reveal about creativity in design, a stage of the design process that has received little study. They used the problem map model, a flexible ontology of requirements, functions, artifacts, behaviors and issues, to code and analyse protocols from eight expert designers. They discussed how effective problem maps are for coding design protocols, what the maps reveal about designers' problem formulation, and changes the ontology may need.

685.title: Advances in Transformational Design: Correlating Context Evaluation to Quality Feasibility and Novelty
685.summary: The authors set out to help designers decide whether a problem calls for a transformer, a device with several functional states, or a single-state product. They developed an Indicators method that classifies the design context and recommends one of these two archetypes, and tested it in a series of experiments. Using the method was linked to a significantly higher chance of producing concepts with greater quality, novelty and feasibility than a standard design method.

688.title: Encouraging Environmentally Conscious Behaviour Through Product Design: The Principle of Discretization
688.summary: The authors used lead user methods to find product design principles that encourage people to conserve resources, studying Old Order Mennonites because of their low-consumption lifestyles. Ethnographic analysis showed that breaking resource use into discrete units helped Mennonites conserve, and an experiment tested whether this discretization reduced water consumption. Discretization was effective at reducing water use, and the authors described several ways it encourages conservation and how it could be built into modern products.

693.title: Opportunities and Barriers to Straw Construction
693.summary: The authors examined when straw-built houses are an appropriate choice, given growing interest in healthy, low-impact and affordable building materials. They reviewed the literature on straw construction and interviewed stakeholders from earlier straw-build housing projects to identify motives, barriers and key considerations, then produced a design guide for clients and consultants. Straw building turned out not to be harder or more uncertain than conventional methods; its problems are simply less familiar and so are seen as barriers.

698.title: Creativity and Long-Term Potentiation: Implications for Design
698.summary: The authors proposed a brain-based explanation of creativity built on long-term potentiation, the strengthening of connections between neurons that is already linked to learning and memory. Drawing on cognitive psychology and neuroscience literature, they used the model to explain known creativity phenomena such as fixation, incubation and difficulties in design-by-analogy. They used the model to describe existing methods and propose new ones for overcoming obstacles to creativity, and discussed a study testing whether physical activity affects fixation.

701.title: Understanding Innovation: A Study of Perspectives and Perceptions in Engineering

706.title: Detecting Design Trends Using Perceptive Tests Based on an Interactive Genetic Algorithm
706.summary: The authors proposed an interactive genetic algorithm to capture how users perceive product shapes, aiming to detect design trends quickly and reduce the risk of product flops. Linked to CATIA CAD software, the algorithm generates parameterised designs in real time for users to evaluate, and the authors studied how its convergence depends on tuning parameters and problem size. An experiment with 20 users evaluating table glasses showed how the algorithm can elicit user perceptions and detect design trends.

707.title: The Repeatability of High Definition Design Structure Matrix (HDDSM) Models for Representing Product Architecture
707.summary: The authors tested whether the High Definition Design Structure Matrix, a model that records specific types of interactions between product components, gives consistent results when built by different people. Pairs of examiners created models of a set of electromechanical products, and their agreement was measured with the kappa index for each type of interaction. Agreement between examiners was very encouraging across product types, and the authors offered recommendations for building objective product architecture models.

708.title: Modeling Product Form Preference Using Gestalt Principles, Semantic Space, and Kansei
708.summary: The authors asked how different descriptions of a product's form, from engineering design variables to the meanings and emotions users attach to it, could be combined to predict how much people like it. They created sixteen wheel rim designs from four design variables, and sixty-four participants rated each rim on semantic dimensions, Kansei emotional attributes and overall liking. Preference was predicted most reliably by higher-order Gestalt variables combined with the meaning and emotion users attached to the product.

718.title: The Role of Sketch Finish and Style in User Responses to Early Stage Design Concepts
718.summary: The authors studied how the finish and style of concept sketches affect users' responses, since sketches are often used to get feedback on early designs. Respondents judged three objects drawn in styles from rough hand sketches to CAD drawings, and the time needed to make each was recorded. Respondents generally preferred realistic, clean hand sketches, which took longer than other hand sketches but far less time than CAD renderings, and object complexity and familiarity also mattered.

719.title: Comparison of Problem Solving From Engineering Design to Software Design
719.summary: The authors compared how software designers and engineering designers solve ill-defined design problems, so that each field could learn from the other. They analysed observational recordings of two professional software design sessions and compared them with earlier findings from engineering design, mapping engineering design activities onto a general model of software design. The software designers moved quickly to detailed design, developed problem and solution together, and mostly worked depth-first on their solutions.

721.title: Mapping for Design Decision Support in Industry
721.summary: The authors studied how map-based software can restore the visual, spatial thinking support that engineers lost in the move from paper to computers. They interviewed 13 engineers at a company where 700 engineers had been trained on the Decision Rationale editor (DRed) over nine years, and analysed their examples of use. Maps were mostly used to sort out problems with several poorly defined options, and their varied uses point to a need for flexible visual thinking tools.

726.title: A Pilot Study of Engineering Design-Decision Methods in Practice
726.summary: The authors set out to gather empirical evidence on which formal design-decision methods work best and whether designers will adopt them. They built a framework for studying decision methods in practice and piloted it with undergraduate engineering students, comparing Pugh's Controlled Convergence and the Group Hypothetical Equivalent and Inequivalent Method with informal group decisions, using observation, interviews and surveys. They documented decision traps in each group, student attitudes to formal methods, and where such methods seem most useful.

727.title: The Impact of Product Dissection Activities on the Novelty of Design Outcomes
727.summary: The authors investigated whether taking apart an existing product affects how novel engineering students' later design ideas are, and how personality plays a role. They ran an experiment in which design teams carried out a product dissection activity, measuring each member's exposure to the activity, their personality traits and the novelty of the ideas they generated. Extraverted participants engaged more with the dissection activity and produced more novel ideas than those who were not extraverts.

728.title: Does Using Different Concept Generation Techniques Change the Design Cognition of Design Students?
728.summary: The authors wanted to know whether teaching engineering students different idea generation techniques changes how they think while designing. Twenty-two mechanical engineering students were taught brainstorming, morphological analysis and TRIZ, and worked in pairs on three 45-minute design tasks, one per technique, while being video recorded; their talk was analysed with the FBS coding scheme. Preliminary results showed statistically significant differences in students' design thinking depending on the technique used.

729.title: Assessing the Use of Function Models and Interaction Models Through Concept Sketching
729.summary: The authors examined how much functional detail a model of a product should contain to best guide designers when generating concepts. In a user study, participants designed a new device after being randomly given a function model, an interaction model, a pruned function model or no model, and a conformance metric measured how far their sketches used the model. Participants given a pruned model showed about 40% higher functional conformance than those given a full function model.

734.title: The Effectiveness of Design and Innovation Consulting
734.summary: The authors set out to provide hard data on how well outsourced product design projects turn out, since earlier claims of high failure rates rested on weak evidence. They used novel random sampling techniques to find domestic design consulting projects and measure the spread of their outcomes. Outcomes were generally good but varied widely between projects and firms, with commercialisation and market success rates comparing favourably with in-house design and client satisfaction similar to other service industries.

737.title: Improving Failure Mode and Effects Analysis as a Cognitive Simulation
737.summary: The author treated failure mode and effects analysis (FMEA), in which engineers predict how a product might fail, as a simulation carried out by human judgment, and examined its cognitive weaknesses. Over two dozen real FMEAs from mechanical and fluid dynamics work, containing 7,900 predictions by twenty people, were reviewed for consistency, correlation and accuracy, focusing on availability bias and poor self-insight. The author proposed individual pooled scoring and a return to the criticality index to improve the process.

739.title: Representation in Early Stage Design: An Analysis of the Influence of Sketching and Prototyping in Design Projects
739.summary: The authors revisited earlier findings on how the use and timing of sketching and prototyping relate to the success of early stage design. They examined these tools in the setting of student team design projects, looking at trends in intensive sketching sessions ("sketchstorming") and prototyping over time. In constrained settings, the quality of the information generated mattered more than its quantity, and teams benefited from starting to prototype as early as possible.

741.title: Impact of Product Design Representation on Customer Judgment With Associated Eye Gaze Patterns
741.summary: The authors questioned whether the simplified sketches and silhouettes researchers use to study customer preferences reflect how people judge the realistic products they actually buy. Two groups of people were shown either computer sketches and silhouettes or simplified and realistic renderings of cars and coffee carafes, and gave opinions, objective evaluations and inferences while an eye-tracker recorded where they looked. The results revealed inconsistent preferences across representations and effects of viewing order, which the gaze data helped explain.

743.title: Perception and Interpretation: Points of Focus in Design Sketches
743.summary: The authors examined whether people who view a designer's concept sketch notice and interpret the aspects the designer intends, such as shape or function. They had 163 participants view and respond to four different product sketches, also considering how aesthetic preference and concrete information shaped their opinions. Viewers tended to recall an object's texture, material or apparent efficiency more than its name, function or shape, and preferred more informative images over more attractive ones.

755.title: The Meaning of “Near” and “Far”: The Impact of Structuring Design Databases and the Effect of Distance of Analogy on Design Output
755.summary: The authors explored what "near" and "far" analogies really mean in design and how the distance of an analogy affects the solutions designers produce. They grouped US patents into clusters of similar inventions using text analysis and a Bayesian algorithm, used these to pick near and far examples for a design study, and mapped stimuli from earlier studies into the same structure. Near and far proved to be relative terms, and examples that were too distant harmed the design process.

757.title: A Study on the Role of Expertise in Design Fixation and its Mitigation
757.summary: The authors tested whether expert designers, though they copy features of example solutions like novices, still generate more ideas thanks to their experience. They repeated an earlier experiment with experts on novice designers, who generated ideas either with a fixating example, with the example plus alternative representations of the problem, or with the problem alone. Both groups fixated on the example, but experts produced more non-redundant ideas, and the alternative representations reduced fixation for experts but not novices.

758.title: Confirmation and Cognitive Bias in Design Cognition
758.summary: The authors examined confirmation bias, the tendency to seek and interpret evidence that supports existing beliefs, in how designers think. They ran two studies: a protocol analysis of novice designers working on a biology-inspired design task, and a controlled experiment in which participants evaluated design concepts. Confirmation bias was present during concept generation, and decision matrices proved effective at reducing it during concept evaluation.

762.title: Understanding Abstraction in Design: A Comparison of Three Functional Analysis Methods for Product Dissection
762.summary: The authors set out to find which of three common approaches to functional analysis, top-down, energy-flow or unstructured, helps students most, since many students struggle with it. In a within-subject study, 26 students dissected a hair dryer, a power drill and a NERF pistol and built function trees, which were scored on several measures. There was no statistical or practical difference between the approaches, suggesting formal methods may be no better than an unstructured one for novices.

765.title: Capturing Consumer Preference Through Experiential Conjoint Analysis
765.summary: The authors wanted to model consumer preference based not only on how a product looks and what it does but on how it feels to use. They introduced experiential conjoint analysis, in which people judge products after using or simulating their use, and used virtual reality to provide an immersive product experience at low cost. Judgments made in virtual reality produced accurate preference models that differed from those based on 2D images, and gave participants more confidence, information or realism.

767.title: An Experimental Investigation of Analogy Formation Using the Engineering-to-Biology Thesaurus
767.summary: The authors tested how well an Engineering-to-Biology thesaurus, which links engineering function terms to biological keywords, helps designers find useful biological inspiration. 100 mechanical engineering students tackled a corn-husking design problem, marking which biology passages containing thesaurus keywords prompted ideas. Design training did not affect how many analogies students found; passages that rarely helped were too technical or lacked information about a biological system, and very specialised or very common keywords seldom led to inspiring sentences.

768.title: Shape Spirit: Deciphering Form Characteristics and Emotional Associations Through Geometric Abstraction
768.summary: The authors studied how a product's form relates to the emotions it evokes, asking whether people need fine details or only the overall shape to judge a product's look. They developed a method that produces increasingly simplified versions of a 3D product model, and statistically compared consumer responses across products and levels of simplification. Emotional responses to coarse product impressions were strongly correlated with responses to the final models, underlining the value of early aesthetic exploration.

769.title: The Effect of Collaborative Stimulation on Design Novelty
769.summary: The authors investigated whether ideas sparked by collaborators, known as collaborative stimulation, are more novel than ideas people produce alone. They measured the novelty of ideas generated in collaborative design sessions and compared those resulting directly from four types of stimulation, prompting, seeding, clarifying and correcting, with those created by individuals working alone. Seeding and correcting produced the largest increases in novelty, and the authors suggested interventions to encourage them.

771.title: Visual Inspection or Product Dissection? The Impact of Designer-Product Interactions on Engineering Design Creativity

772.title: An Exploratory Study on the Effectiveness of an Inclusive Design Tool With a Metric to Evaluate Inclusivity of Conceptual Designs
772.summary: The authors tested whether a method that applies inclusive design rules to a product's action-function diagram helps designers create products usable by people of all abilities. In an experiment, trained participants generated ideas for an inclusive product with and without the representation scheme, and the authors introduced and validated a new metric for rating how inclusive an idea is. The scheme helped designers produce inclusive designs only to a limited extent, though it and the metric showed promise.

773.title: Getting to the Novel Ideas: Exploring the Alternative Uses Test of Divergent Thinking
773.summary: The authors explored how people arrive at novel ideas using the Alternative Uses Test, in which participants list unusual uses for a common object. From over 2000 participants, including engineering professionals and students, they evaluated 293 people's lists of uses for a paperclip produced in three minutes, rating novelty by how rare each response was. Later responses were significantly more novel, and participants typically listed about nine ideas before reaching highly novel ones.

782.title: Building Fast to Think Faster: Exploiting Rapid Prototyping to Accelerate Ideation During Early Stage Design
782.summary: The authors explored whether individual designers benefit from building many quick prototypes early on instead of committing to a single design. In a design challenge, engineering students were required to make either one prototype or several in the same amount of time during their first iteration. Those making several felt more time pressure and less satisfied at first, but their prototypes performed better, improved more between iterations, and their satisfaction rose by the end.

783.title: The Influence of Timing in Exploratory Prototyping and Other Activities in Design Projects
783.summary: The authors examined when quick "throwaway" prototypes should be built during the early phase of a design project, a question that had received little attention. They studied design projects by mid-career professional graduate students, relating the timing of prototyping, benchmarking and user interaction to the quality of the final designs. Building prototypes early, or doing extra rounds of benchmarking and user interaction later, was linked to better outcomes, while the total time spent on these activities was not.

784.title: Eye-Tracking Data Predicts Importance of Product Features and Saliency of Size Change
784.summary: The authors tested whether eye-tracking data can reveal which visible product features matter most to customers and how much a feature's size must change before people notice. They recorded viewers' gaze on product images while they judged features and spotted size changes, and built logistic models from the data. Feature importance correlated significantly with several gaze measures, noticed size changes drew longer and more frequent fixations, and the models could predict both importance and noticeable size changes.

785.title: Testing the Basis for an Automated Design-by-Analogy Tool Through Comparison to Expert Thinking
785.summary: The authors checked whether their earlier computational method for organising patent databases makes sense to human experts, as a basis for an automated tool that suggests design analogies. They compared the structure the method produced for 45 patents with expert designers' mental models of how those patents relate to each other. The computer-generated structure grouped and organised patents sensibly, reflected common ground among experts, and still kept an element of surprise useful for inspiration.

786.title: Rethinking the Comprehensive Test on Qualitative Reasoning for Designers
786.summary: The authors revisited the first version of their test of qualitative reasoning, part of a set of tests of thinking skills needed for conceptual design. They wrote problems for deductive, inductive, analogical and abductive reasoning, checked them in a protocol study, and gave them to senior undergraduate and graduate engineering students, collecting scores and feedback on clarity, timing and difficulty. Based on the correlations, average performance, validity and reliability observed, they built an improved beta version of the test.

787.title: How Should an Electric Vehicle Sound? User and Expert Perception

788.title: Evaluating Cognitive Efficiency by Measuring Information Contained in Designers’ Cognitive Processes
788.summary: The authors set out to measure how efficiently designers use their limited mental resources, an area little studied for lack of quantitative methods. They used Kolmogorov complexity, a measure of information content, to quantify changes in sketches based on designers' cognitive actions, analysing sketches and think-aloud recordings from 15 participants and judging efficiency by design quality and mental effort. Higher Kolmogorov complexity went with lower cognitive efficiency.

789.title: A Nested Multivariate Utility Copulas Approach to Aggregating User Experience Partworths for Aircraft Cabin Interior Design
789.summary: The authors sought a better way to combine users' experience of individual design features into an overall rating of a product, since the usual weighted sum ignores how these experiences depend on each other. They built single-attribute utility functions based on cumulative prospect theory and joined them with nested multivariate utility copulas, a statistical tool for modelling dependence, organised by groups of related attributes. A case study of aircraft cabin interior design demonstrated that the approach is feasible and promising.

790.title: Analyzing Transdisciplinary Design Processes in Industry: An Overview
790.summary: The authors examined how well design process models from the academic literature fit the real design of products that combine several engineering and design disciplines. They carried out an empirical interview study of design processes for integrated products in different industries, using a framework built from earlier consolidations of design process models across disciplines. They asked whether the literature-based process applies in industry, whether organisations share common stages and design states, and where practice departs from the framework.

792.title: Methods for Prototyping Strategies in Conceptual Phases of Design: Framework and Experimental Assessment
792.summary: The authors set out to give designers a structured method for planning prototypes, an important part of design with few published methods. Drawing on an extensive literature review of best practices in engineering prototyping, they built a method of guiding questions, flowcharts and basic equations that help designers choose how to approach prototyping, and tested it in a controlled design experiment. Using the method improved the performance of the prototypes designers produced.

793.title: Exploring the Utility of Product Dissection for Early-Phase Idea Generation
793.summary: The authors asked how different ways of taking apart existing products affect the creativity of the ideas designers generate afterwards. They ran a controlled experiment varying the type and number of products dissected and the structure and medium of the task, electronic or physical, and combined statistical analysis with interviews. The structure, medium and number of products affected the variety of concepts, while the analogical distance and number of products affected their novelty.

794.title: Prioritizing the Many Measures of Success in Outsourced Design
794.summary: The authors set out to clarify what counts as success when companies outsource product design. They gathered perspectives from the literature and from interviews with design consultants and their clients, organised them into seven dimensions of success, and ranked the key measures with a survey of 194 more practitioners. Past research had focused on the wrong measures, overstating development problems and return on investment, and different measures did not always agree; client satisfaction emerged as a promising summary measure.

800.title: Stakeholder and Constraint-Driven Innovation of a Novel, Lever-Propelled, All-Terrain Wheelchair
800.summary: The author described the Leveraged Freedom Chair, a low-cost, lever-propelled wheelchair for rural users in developing countries, where existing chairs cannot cope with rough terrain. Its drivetrain, built from cheap bicycle parts, lets users change gear by moving their hands along the levers, and feedback from user trials in East Africa, Guatemala and India refined it. The final chair was lighter and narrower, and was 76 percent faster and 41 percent more efficient than conventional wheelchairs on a typical commute.

801.title: Design for Micro-Enterprise: An Approach to Product Design for Emerging Markets
801.summary: The authors aimed to help designers create products for emerging markets in the developing world, where economic, cultural and other constraints make design especially challenging. They drew on existing literature and interviews with practising designers of products for these markets, and presented four case studies across several product categories. From this they documented current best practices and proposed a framework for designing products that support small-scale local businesses, known as micro-enterprises.

802.title: Trigger Features on Prototypes Increase Preference for Sustainability
802.summary: The authors tested whether design features that prompt thoughts of sustainability can help close the gap between customers saying they prefer green products and actually buying them. They built such features into realistic toaster prototypes and ran a purchase experiment in which some participants saw toasters with these features and others did not, followed by a written email task, interviews and ratings. Exposure to the features significantly increased participants' use of sustainability as a purchase criterion.

804.title: Validating Perceived Sustainable Design Features Using a Novel Collage Approach
804.summary: The authors tested whether product features that online reviews suggest people see as sustainable actually resonate with customers, using French press coffee makers. Participants placed products on a collage according to perceived sustainability and likeability and labelled them with descriptive features. Participants picked the sustainable-seeming features more often for products they rated as more sustainable, sustainability and likeability were measured separately, and perceptions differed across demographic groups.

805.title: A Study of the Exploratory Creativity Performance Between Machine and Human Designers
805.summary: The authors compared how creative a machine and human designers are when exploring a space of ideas, a gap that had not been well studied. They had the image-generation model DALL·E and novice designers produce imagery, and expert designers rated the creativity of both. Humans scored higher on overall creativity but the machine scored higher on exploratory creativity, and humans' text-based exploratory creativity exceeded their image-based results, while the machine showed the opposite.

808.title: Reducing Waste Outflow to Motivate Water Conservation
808.summary: The authors explored whether slowing the drainage of waste water, so that water builds up visibly, could prompt people to use less water. In an online study, 74 Amazon Mechanical Turk workers completed three handwashing simulations with different sink drainage rates. Participants used about 14% less water at lower drainage rates, regardless of how environmentally minded they reported being, suggesting the intervention relies less on user intention.

810.title: Assessing Early Stage Design Sketches and Reflections on Prototyping
810.summary: The authors developed ways to assess novice designers' early-stage sketches and their reflections on prototyping. They proposed a sketch quality rubric covering line smoothness, proportion and understandability, and a tool for capturing what designers learn after each prototype iteration. The number of sketches was linked to design outcomes but sketch quality largely was not, and novices often lost focus on users in their prototyping reflections and presentations.

811.title: Concreate: Using Data Physicalization to Increase The Understanding and Inspirational Use of Quantitative Data In Data-Driven Design Scenarios
811.summary: The authors explored whether turning numbers into physical, touchable objects helps designers use quantitative data as creative inspiration, something organizations struggle with. At a multinational automotive company, a preliminary study gathered requirements for a toolkit and a follow-up study compared it with conventional data visualization. The resulting toolkit, Concreate, appeared to stimulate creative thinking by encouraging intense hands-on interaction with data, more reflection while working and a deeper understanding of the data.

812.title: Quantifying the Predictive Abilities of Speculative Fiction: A Feasibility Study

813.title: Tablets, Pens, and Pencils: The Influence of Tools on Sketching in Early Stage Design
813.summary: The authors examined whether sketching on a tablet rather than with pen or pencil on paper changes early concept sketches, and whether gender plays a role. Three mixed-gender groups using pen, pencil or a tablet sketched concepts for an open-ended design prompt. Pencil sketches were of the highest quality, more novel concepts were harder to understand, many participants missed paper's friction on the tablet, and women and gender minorities produced more sketches with no difference in quality or style.

815.title: Objects of Collaboration: Roles of Objects in Spanning Knowledge Boundaries in a Design Company
815.summary: The authors investigated how objects such as prototypes, kanban boards and process maps help cross-functional design teams work across differences in knowledge and language. In a two-year ethnographic study at a turbomachinery design company, they observed 70 cross-functional meetings and conducted 52 interviews. Objects routinized interaction, translated information and prompted joint negotiation or discovery, with the last two roles leading to jointly discovering risks or bottlenecks and jointly designing integrated solutions.

816.title: Lessons Learned From Three Iterative Studies on Creativity Interventions
816.summary: The authors compared three of their studies on whether conflict-processing tasks boost creativity, after two online follow-ups failed to replicate an earlier in-person result. They examined differences between the studies in setting, instructions, intervention tasks and participant backgrounds. They concluded that in-person results may not carry over online, where distraction and low motivation are harder to control, and recommended minimum correct responses, better feedback and ways for participants to ask questions.

817.title: Where Next?: Exploring Opportunity Areas and Tool Functions for Sustainable Product Design
817.summary: The authors wanted to understand why sustainable design tools are adopted slowly by asking what designers find useful. They surveyed 42 hardware product design professionals and interviewed 12 about their control over, and the impact of, sustainability strategies and the tool functions they want. Designers felt least control over manufacturing and rated it low-impact, felt most control over design practice and business models, and wanted tools that improve transparency, support decisions, predict results, share knowledge and reveal user needs.

819.title: Visual Reasoning for Design by Analogy: Fuse Visual and Semantic Knowledge
819.summary: The authors aimed to support design by analogy with a computer method that, like people, combines what objects look like with what they mean. Their framework used a convolutional neural network to learn visual knowledge from familiar object categories and a hierarchy-based graph convolutional network to transfer it to unfamiliar categories based on semantic distance. Experiments on a benchmark dataset of mechanical components showed favorable recognition performance for the proposed methods.

822.title: The Use of Analogies and the Design Brief Information: Impact on Creative Outcomes
822.summary: The authors tested whether instructing design students to use analogies in a design brief improves the novelty and usefulness of their solutions. One hundred and seven first-year undergraduates received a brief with typical examples, a brief with word pairs and instructions to use textual analogies, or the same brief with instructions to first identify negative features. Instructions to use textual analogies led to highly novel outcomes, while starting from negative features led to more useful ones.

823.title: Reconfigurable Robot Design Aided With Design Cards
823.summary: The authors set out to help designers choose suitable mechanisms early in the design of reconfigurable robots, which change shape to perform different functions. Building on known transformation principles and facilitators, they observed motions produced by mechanisms across domains and mapped them onto a set of design cards. A limited-scale pilot study compared solutions generated with and without the cards to establish their usefulness and limitations.

825.title: Aerial Robot Design Principles in Creative Idea Generation and Evolution
825.summary: The authors tested whether a set of design principles for innovative aerial robots actually helps people produce more original ideas, since most design principles are unvalidated. They rated concepts generated with the principles using a decision-tree originality assessment and examined differences by domain expertise, problem novelty and how ideas evolved. Originality was significantly higher for a more novel problem and always higher for evolved ideas, while domain expertise made no significant difference to idea quantity or originality.

826.title: Exploration of the Dynamics of Neuro-Cognition During TRIZ
826.summary: The authors explored how brain activity differs across the steps of TRIZ, a structured method for inventive problem solving in engineering design. They measured activation in the prefrontal cortex of 30 engineering students as they completed a design task using TRIZ. Defining the problem engaged mostly the left side, searching for parameters and principles shifted activity to the right side, and generating solutions engaged the middle region linked to making associations.

827.title: Exploring Rules of Sustainable Design With Compositional Manufacturing
827.summary: The authors explored compositional manufacturing, a way of turning non-functional scrap or waste pieces into working products, as a new approach to sustainable design. In an exploratory case study with casting, they took risers, gates and miscast parts and created parts with arbitrary functions from their geometric properties instead of remelting them. They identified a few heuristics, notably that sets of scrap parts with greater geometric differences yielded final parts with more varied functions.

830.title: Can Gratitude Promote More Creative Engineering Design?
830.summary: The authors investigated whether feeling gratitude can make engineers more creative, linking psychology research on positive emotions with engineering design. In a pre-registered study, engineering students and working engineers (49 in a pilot and 329 in the full study) received gratitude, positive-emotion or neutral inductions, then completed an alternate uses task and a wind-turbine-blade repurposing task. No differences appeared on the alternate uses task, the gratitude manipulation succeeded only in the pilot, and the blade task results warranted further study.

831.title: Generative Pre-Trained Transformers for Biologically Inspired Design
831.summary: The authors aimed to help designers bridge the gap between biology and engineering when borrowing ideas from nature. They fine-tuned the GPT-3 language model into three kinds of design concept generators, plus machine evaluators to judge how well biological and engineering domains were linked in the generated text. In a case study generating lightweight flying car concepts inspired by nature, the approach produced bio-inspired design concepts with good performance.

832.title: Sustainable Creativity: Overcoming the Challenge of Scale When Repurposing Wind-Turbine Blades
832.summary: The authors tested whether a modified creativity exercise could help designers deal with the huge size of wind-turbine blades when proposing ways to reuse them. Twenty-eight fourth-year engineering students completed either a scaled version of the Alternate Uses Task or the standard version before a wind-turbine-blade repurposing task. The scaled task was harder, suggesting scale rather than unfamiliarity is the main obstacle, and it significantly increased the number of correctly scaled blade reuse concepts.

833.title: Investigating the Roles of Expertise and Modality in Designers’ Search for Inspirational Stimuli
833.summary: The authors studied how designers search for inspirational examples, and how expertise and search mode, such as text versus images, shape that search. Seven students and eight professionals searched for 3D-model parts on a new multi-modal search platform while thinking aloud, and their searches were described as activities, behaviors and pathways. Expertise and search modality both influenced search behavior, with examples of designers fixating on particular results or benefiting from unintended inspiration.

836.title: Effects of Structured Prototyping Support on Novice Designers’ Prototyping Plans
836.summary: The authors investigated how a structured support tool, the Prototyping Planner, changes the prototyping plans of novice designers. They compared plans made by 33 student design teams with minimal guidance against plans made with the tool, looking at questions addressed, testing purpose and structure. Unsupported plans varied widely, while the tool gave every team a clear, narrow purpose and an execution plan, and 81% of students judged their supported plans better.

838.title: Getting Beyond the Hairy House: Using Structure-Function-Mechanism to Advance Biologically Inspired Design Pedagogy
838.summary: The authors examined how well high school engineering teachers could learn biologically inspired design using Structure-Function-Mechanism, a version of a functional design theory aligned with US science standards. In a case study, they taught the approach and its teaching methods to four high school engineering teachers. The teachers grasped the structural concepts but sought clear boundaries between mechanism and function, which were often subjective because biological systems are nested systems.

839.title: Role of Representation in Subsystem Clustering: Effects of Distance Between Elements
839.summary: The authors examined how three ways of drawing an engineering system, as a component graph, function graph or function structure, affect how people understand it. Undergraduate students grouped system elements into subsystems, and the authors related these groupings to connective, physical and semantic distances between elements. Participants grouped closer elements together, with clear trends for connective and physical distance but not semantic distance, suggesting that visual layout itself shapes system understanding.

840.title: Investigating Mind-Mapping as a Tool for Problem Exploration in Early Design
840.summary: The authors studied whether mind-mapping helps designers explore a problem and identify design opportunities better than free writing. In a between-subjects study with 28 participants, they compared the two techniques and proposed new metrics to score the resulting design opportunity statements. They reported quantitative results, exploration behaviours and user feedback, and discussed implications for problem identification and future digital mind-mapping tools.

841.title: Investigating Priming Effects of Sketch Evaluation Instructions on Idea Generation Productivity
841.summary: The authors investigated whether designers' sketching skill, and worry about having their sketches judged, affect how many ideas they generate. In an entry-level engineering design and graphics course, they compared independent measures of sketching skill and idea generation, telling one group upfront that sketches would be evaluated and keeping another group unaware. Sketch quality and idea quantity were largely independent, and being told about sketch evaluation had small to negligible effects on productivity.

842.title: Multi-Modal Search for Inspirational Examples in Design
842.summary: The authors built a search platform that lets designers find inspirational 3D model parts by text, appearance and function at the same time, closer to how real designers search. In a study with 21 participants seeking inspiration for a design challenge, people searched by keyword, by curated parts and by parts they had assembled. The search mode affected how often people searched, how they used results and how broadly they covered the options available.

843.title: Computational Patterns of Team Interactions and Associations With Conflict Within New Product Development Teams
843.summary: The authors explored whether patterns in how new product development team members communicate reveal how much conflict a team has. Using social network analysis of team communication, they defined four interaction patterns, named central member, subgroup and aloof member, isolate member and pendant, and compared them with each team's assessed conflict level. The patterns captured the signatures of high versus low-to-medium conflict teams with a high level of accuracy.

844.title: Aligning Human and Computational Evaluations of Functional Design Similarity
844.summary: The authors compared how people judge the functional similarity of products with similarity computed from functional models, to see whether computational measures match human perception. They crowdsourced 1,360 triplet ratings at each of two levels: a product's overall purpose and how it works in detail. Different computational measures aligned best with human judgements at each level, and the line between similar and similar enough affected how the measures should be used.

845.title: Collaborative Design Decision-Making With Artificial Intelligence: Exploring the Evolution and Impact of Human Confidence in AI and in Themselves
845.summary: The authors studied how designers' confidence in an AI teammate and in themselves changes during collaboration, since misjudging either leads to poor reliance on AI. In a cognitive study, participants experienced AI performance that changed without notice and decided whether to accept AI suggestions. Confidence in the AI dropped with poor but not good performance, self-confidence fell whenever AI accuracy changed, and the two confidences pushed acceptance of AI input in opposite directions.
