846.title: Comparing Virtual and Face-to-Face Team Collaboration: Insights From an Agent-Based Simulation
846.summary: The authors investigated how virtual collaboration, accelerated by the COVID-19 pandemic, affects engineering design outcomes compared with face-to-face teamwork. They first ran an empirical study of human design teams to adjust the parameters of an agent-based team simulation, including self-efficacy, influence, trust and familiarity, then simulated both modes. Effective communication improved conflict resolution and task cohesion, and the simulations showed design outcomes differing between virtual and face-to-face collaboration.

847.title: Facial Expression Recognition as a Measure of User-Designer Empathy
847.summary: The authors explored whether automatic facial expression recognition during user interviews can capture a designer's empathy with a user in real time. They analysed mimicry of facial expressions, a known predictor of empathy in psychology, in 46 videotaped user-designer interviews about novel vehicle technology. Users and designers did mirror each other's expressions, but users' expressions did not always reflect their real emotional tone, and mimicry was not linked to how well designers understood users' thoughts.

849.title: Does Empathising With Users Contribute to Better Need Finding?
849.summary: The authors asked whether designers who empathize more accurately with users are better at identifying users' needs. Thirteen designers watched a standard video of a user interview, completed an empathic accuracy task and listed user needs, which were combined into 23 needs scored for quality, depth and latency. Designers who better read the user's emotional tone identified more important unmet needs, but accuracy about the user's thoughts, and need depth or latency, showed no such links.

850.title: “No, We’re Not!” the Classification and Impact of Blocking Behavior in Design Team Meetings
850.summary: The authors proposed a framework for classifying disagreements in design team meetings as either preserving or challenging the status quo, and tested how these affect productivity. They coded 104 blocking behaviours observed in 14 academic teams during ideation sessions using Interaction Dynamics Notation and Adaption-Innovation theory. Blocks were reliably classified and sometimes led to new ideas, neither style produced ideas more efficiently, and deflected blocks led to ideas more often than overcome or unresolved ones.

851.title: Comparing Nominal and Interacting Sub-Structured Teams in an Interdisciplinary Engineering Design Task
851.summary: The authors tested whether large interdisciplinary teams do better when their sub-teams work independently rather than interacting, extending earlier findings that individuals can outperform collaborative teams. Teams tackled a complex drone design and path-planning problem on the HyForm research platform, which tracked their communication and actions. Sub-teams working independently outperformed interacting ones and communicated much less, though their managers, being more central to information flow, reported higher cognitive load and workload.

852.title: Challenges and Strategies in Remote Design Collaboration During Pandemic: A Case Study in Engineering Education
852.summary: The authors set out to understand the challenges students faced, and the strategies they used, in remote design collaboration after the COVID-19 pandemic moved teaching online. They analysed bi-weekly and final reflections from 11 teams (42 students) in a semester-long introductory undergraduate engineering design course. The findings offered insights for building effective remote design education and showed that reflections are a useful way to capture students' learning.

853.title: Hit, Miss, or Error? Predicting Errors in Design Decision Making for Radically Innovative Ideas Using Individual Attributes
853.summary: The authors examined how personality and creativity preferences affect whether people correctly pick radically innovative ideas. Using 2,252 idea evaluations by student designers, they classified decisions with signal detection theory as hits, misses, false alarms or correct rejections and related them to individual attributes. Lower risk tolerance made hits more likely, higher neuroticism and motivation made rejecting good ideas more likely, and higher risk tolerance with lower motivation made backing weak ideas more likely.

854.title: Some (Team) Assembly Required: An Analysis of Collaborative Computer-Aided Design Assembly
854.summary: The authors studied how teams assemble pre-made parts in multi-user CAD software, an area of collaborative CAD that had received little attention. Twenty participants assembled parts of varying complexity alone or in teams of two, three or four, and the authors analysed audio recordings, team activity and surveys. Teams finished assemblies in less calendar time than individuals, but individuals were more efficient per person-hour because of communication and coordination overheads, while pairs showed an unexpected bonus effect.

855.title: Does Synchronous Collaboration Improve Collaborative Computer-Aided Design Output: Results From a Large-Scale Competition
855.summary: The authors examined whether working at the same time in cloud-based multi-user CAD helps teams produce better designs. They analysed backend action logs from 101 teams in a large virtual robotics design competition, using regression and mediation analyses to find factors linked to success. Larger teams performed more CAD actions and scored higher, but once team size was accounted for, more frequent real-time simultaneous collaboration was associated with lower performance.

856.title: Measuring Designers’ Empathic Understanding of Users by a Quick Empathic Accuracy (QEA)
856.summary: The authors wanted a faster way to measure how accurately designers understand users' thoughts and feelings, since their earlier psychology-based procedure for measuring empathic accuracy was time-consuming. They shortened the experimental procedure while trying to keep it valid, and compared the shortened instrument with the original. Data from the shortened version showed excellent internal consistency and enough variation between people, and it produced results similar to the original longer measure.

857.title: The Impact of Gender on Individual Perceptions and Team Psychological Safety in Engineering Design Teams
857.summary: The authors explored how a team's gender mix affects psychological safety, the sense that it is safe to speak up. They followed 38 engineering design student teams, half all-male and half mixed, over an 8-week project, measuring psychological safety five times and collecting peer ratings at the end. Mixed and all-male teams did not differ overall, but women felt safer with female teammates than with male ones, and felt less safe with men than men felt with women.

858.title: The Influence of Team Goal Alignment and Awareness on Human-Centered Design Team Decision-Making Strategy
858.summary: The authors explored how well-aligned a design team's goals are and how that relates to the way the team makes decisions. They analysed the strategies behind 90 choices of design methods by six student teams during a human-centered design project, alongside measures of shared goals and awareness of teammates' personal goals. Teams with lower goal alignment appeared to rely more on decisions driven by individuals, and better-aligned teams more on process-driven decisions, though the results were not consistently significant.

860.title: Manufacturing Fixation in Design: Exploring the Effects of Manufacturing Assumptions on Design Ideas
860.summary: The authors introduced Manufacturing Fixation in Design, an unconscious tendency to stick to familiar manufacturing processes when generating ideas. After reviewing the fixation literature and ways it might be assessed, they ran an exploratory case study at a Design for Additive Manufacturing workshop for professional engineers at an aerospace company. The results were used to explore how this fixation shows up and how its impact might be measured, with next steps for validating it.

861.title: Can I Get a Word In? the Impact of Turn-Taking and Gender on Engineering Design Students’ Psychological Safety
861.summary: The authors studied how taking turns in conversation and gender relate to psychological safety in student design teams. They analysed video of members of fifteen engineering design student teams during concept generation, counting turns and self-turns and measuring perceived psychological safety. Taking more turns significantly raised an individual's sense of the team's psychological safety, though not at the team level, and gender did not affect turn-taking but did affect individuals' perceived safety.

862.title: Does It Matter Where Design Teams Come From in Design Studies?
862.summary: The authors asked whether work culture shapes how professional design teams behave, and whether teams from different companies can safely be pooled into one sample in design studies. They compared teams of three engineers from two large international companies, each designing a next-generation personal assistant and entertainment system, and analysed their interactions with statistical techniques. The two cohorts showed some different behaviors but also a common overall approach to team design thinking.

863.title: An Empirical Study of the Impact of Task Expectation Framing on Design Decision Delegation
863.summary: The authors examined how the way a design task is described to someone it is delegated to affects the result, a little-studied part of engineering systems design. A total of 472 engineering students played an engineering-themed computer game, randomly given instructions framed either as traditional design requirements or as maximizing a single value measure. Requirement-based framings led to better task performance than value-driven framings, suggesting theoretical arguments for value-driven design may overlook human behavior.

864.title: Influence of Different Representation of Requirements on Idea Generation: An Experimental Study
864.summary: The authors tested whether the way design requirements are presented changes the concept sketches engineers produce. In an experiment, 52 final-year mechanical engineering students tackled two design problems, each given with two of three formats: requirements embedded in a problem statement, a traditional requirements list, or contextualized scrum stories. Scrum stories significantly improved the novelty of ideas and how many requirements were addressed, without changing quantity, variety or sketch detail, and more sketches did not mean more requirements met.

865.title: Measuring Risk Attitudes for Strategic Decision-Making in a Collaborative Engineering Design Process
865.summary: The authors evaluated whether a standard lottery-style questionnaire can capture people's attitudes to risk well enough to predict their strategic choices in collaborative design. A total of 124 participants completed the questionnaire and 29 tasks in two-person design games, and the authors compared how well different risk assumptions predicted their decisions. A risk-neutral model predicted 62.2% of decisions, questionnaire-based risk attitudes only raised this to 63.3%, while attitudes inferred from behavior reached 77.5%, suggesting risk attitudes in engineering are context-dependent.

866.title: Predicting a Paradigm Shift: Exploring the Relationship Between Cognitive Style and the Paradigm-Relatedness of Design Solutions
866.summary: The authors examined whether a person's cognitive style predicts whether they produce ideas that stay within an existing paradigm or break from it. They studied 60 engineering student teams over 4- and 8-week design projects, using the KAI measure of cognitive style and testing crowdsourcing to rate the ideas. More innovative-leaning individuals were more likely to produce paradigm-breaking ideas, teams with more diverse styles produced more paradigm-challenging ideas, and crowdsourced ratings proved workable.

873.title: Towards Characterizing Cognitive Style Coping Behavior in Engineering Design
873.summary: The authors investigated what happens when the way a design problem is framed clashes with a designer's preferred problem-solving style, which Kirton's adaption-innovation theory says people manage through coping behavior. Using a mixed-methods analysis, they examined how cognitive style and problem framing affected solutions and which strategies and behaviors participants of different styles showed. The problem frame influenced the types of solutions designers developed and their cognitive experience, with some behaviors indicating coping.

874.title: Exploring the Effects of Individual Differences in Function Structure Modeling Behaviors
874.summary: The authors explored how differences between individual designers affect how they build function structure models and what the final models look like. Using surveys of systemizing tendency, goal orientation, risk propensity and thinking style, plus an earlier protocol study of modeling behavior, they ran regression analyses linking inputs, process and outputs. They identified several possible correlations and proposed three testable hypotheses and a follow-up experiment for future work.

876.title: Connecting Design Actions, Reasoning, and Outcomes in Concept-Selection
876.summary: The authors investigated why designers often select concepts that are not the best available, by linking their actions, reasoning and outcomes. Fifty-seven participants chose a robotic gripper design from a predefined design space on an interactive interface that logged their actions, followed by a survey on their reasoning. Strategies such as design manipulation and willingness to submit an alternative influenced outcomes, but the factors designers said they considered did not correlate with better results.

877.title: Evaluating the Potential for a Novel Irrigation System Controller to Be Adopted by Medium-Scale Contract Farmers in East Africa
877.summary: The authors assessed whether a new controller for solar-powered drip irrigation could be viable for farmers in East Africa, where high system costs limit adoption. The proposed controller plans irrigation schedules from local weather forecasts and farm details while optimizing the system's lifetime performance, and tells farmers how to operate low-cost manual valves; it was evaluated through storyboard-based interviews with farmers and market stakeholders. These lead users gave initial positive feedback, suggesting the controller could be a viable product.

879.title: Triggered: Using Human-AI Dialogue for Problem Understanding in Collaborative Design
879.summary: The authors explored whether AI-generated text can bring unfamiliar opinions and experiences into designers' conversations, so that problems are interpreted more inclusively. In an exploratory study, three pairs of designers tackled a complex socio-technical problem, two pairs interacting with an AI text generator and one pair working without it as a baseline. The AI prompted more nuanced interpretations of the problem and ideas, and designers assigned the AI different roles to suit their creative purposes.

880.title: Understanding Household Energy Challenges in Himalayan Communities Using Participatory Design Approaches
880.summary: The authors set out to understand why improved, cleaner cookstoves are slow to be adopted in rural Himalayan communities, where smoky biomass stoves harm health. They surveyed households in villages in Uttarakhand, India, about cooking and space-heating routines and attitudes. Households used both gas and biomass fuels, cooking and heating were linked and seasonal, traditional stoves had cultural significance and were built from local materials, supporting participatory design with local communities.

882.title: A Framework for Centralizing Ethics in the Design Engineering of Spatial Computing Artifacts
882.summary: The authors examined whether and how ethics are built into the process of creating spatial computing products such as virtual, augmented and mixed reality systems. They interviewed spatial computing practitioners and combined the findings with existing models from design and human-computer interaction research. Practitioners were aware these products are especially vulnerable to harm but lacked processes and tests to reduce it, so the authors proposed a three-phase framework for ethical spatial computing design.

884.title: Reflections on Designing in the Wild: How Theories of Design Information Manifest in Practice
884.summary: The authors explored how their earlier Information Archetypes Framework, which categorizes the kinds of information used in design, shows up in professional practice. They carried out an in-depth qualitative analysis of interviews with eight experienced practicing designers reflecting on their work. The designers deliberately adapted how they handled information to the needs of each situation, moving between competing information dimensions through trajectories and loops.

885.title: Universal Design Analysis for Improving the Usability of Fused Filament Fabrication 3D Printers
885.summary: The authors applied universal design principles to make desktop 3D printers easier to use for people of all ages and abilities, since current machines assume good hand strength, ability to stand and vision. They examined the physical challenges of interacting with desktop fused filament printers and surveyed 3D printer users about difficulties in operation and troubleshooting. Users found leveling the print bed the hardest task, so the authors began a redesign of bed leveling by developing design specifications.

887.title: Investigation of Mechanical Engineering Students’ Perceptions of Design Process Models
887.summary: The authors explored how engineering students view the design process models meant to guide how they design. In a preliminary study, they conducted semi-structured interviews with six upper-level mechanical engineering students about three design process models. Students judged the models' usefulness along eight dimensions, such as impacts considered, stakeholder interactions and solution novelty, and also by iteration and level of detail, suggesting students would benefit from multiple models, including ones that account for society and people.

888.title: Improving Customer Attribute Management Within the House of Quality by Integrating the Non-User
888.summary: The authors sought to make it easier to build and prioritize the list of customer attributes in the House of Quality, a complex product-planning tool. Using robot vacuums as a case, they interviewed users and non-users with a clear interview structure, examined types of and reasons for non-use, and translated the answers into attributes. Non-users' reasons for not using the product produced more attributes than users' complaints, and industry feedback suggested non-user attributes can stand in for user attributes.

893.title: The Cognitive Costs of Design Tasks: The Evolution of Cognitive Load in Design and Its Relationship With Design Outcomes
893.summary: The authors examined how mental workload changes over the design process and whether it is linked to the quality of design results. Twenty participants completed a design task while their cognitive load was recorded at each stage, and their ideas and prototypes were then evaluated. Cognitive load differed significantly between stages and was correlated with idea generation outcomes, but it did not appear to be tied to prototyping outcomes.

894.title: Understanding Professional Designers’ Knowledge Organization Behavior: A Case Study in Product Teardowns
894.summary: The authors studied how professional designers organize knowledge, with the aim of informing better data-driven design support tools. Twenty-three professional designers worked virtually with data from a teardown of a consumer product, grouping data, nesting subgroups and drawing links between items. Designers found grouping better for learning but linking more useful for sharing knowledge, used links far more than nests, and treated design features, housing, cost and manufacturing as separate central themes.

895.title: The Effects of Representation Modality on Subsystem Clustering
895.summary: The authors wanted to understand how the way a system is drawn affects how designers group its parts into subsystems. In a human-subjects experiment at two universities, participants saw a hair dryer, a food mixer or a toilet shown as a function structure, function graph or component graph, along with a troubleshooting scenario. The effect of representation was consistent across universities but varied between products, suggesting representation can shape systems thinking.

897.title: Design-Engineers’ Selection of Agency: Harm Mitigation in Ambient Intelligent Environments
897.summary: The authors examined how much independent agency designers give to ambient intelligence, the sensors and actuators that make buildings respond to people, and how that relates to unintended harm. They ran a case study of VyZee, a retailer converting its stores into smart stores, testing an Agency/Intelligence Axis from their earlier work. The company seemed unaware of the link between agency and harm but used varied agency levels, and the authors proposed a six-property model of ambient intelligent agents.

898.title: Co-Evolution of Communication and System Performance in Engineering Systems Design: A Stochastic Network-Behavior Dynamics Model
898.summary: The authors aimed to quantify how communication between engineering disciplines and system performance influence each other over time. They built a stochastic network-behavior dynamics model and fitted it with Bayesian inference to two datasets, one of students designing a car engine and one of NASA engineers designing a spacecraft. Design interdependence and social network effects strongly drove interactions in both groups, and more interactions slightly improved performance, though excessive interaction combined with inflexible exploration reduced it.

901.title: Design Embedding: Representation Learning of Design Thinking to Cluster Design Behaviors
901.summary: The authors sought a computational way to capture design thinking, which is hidden inside designers' heads, through the behaviors it produces. They defined five design behaviors from design theory, characterized each with techniques such as Markov chains, Doc2Vec and an LSTM autoencoder to create 'design embeddings', and clustered designers using data from a high school solar system design challenge. Designers fell into several distinct patterns for each behavior, supporting the use of design embeddings to group design behaviors.

903.title: The Effect of Dynamic Speed Information and Timing of Displaying EHMI on Automated Vehicle and Pedestrian Interactions
903.summary: The authors examined how a self-driving car's visible slowing down and the timing of an external display signaling that it will yield affect pedestrians' decisions to cross. They ran an online study of a two-way street with a marked but unsignalized crosswalk. Pedestrians crossed more often and felt more trust and safety when the display appeared earlier, while visible deceleration did not change crossing decisions but raised trust and perceived safety.

904.title: Human-Centric Design Requirements and Challenges for Enabling Human-AI Interaction in Engineering Design: An Interview Study
904.summary: The authors asked what the users of interactive AI tools in engineering design need, so that such tools can be designed around people. They interviewed engineering design faculty members about who would benefit from human-AI interaction and what the tools would require. The faculty mainly pointed to engineers, designers and students, and the requirements centered on understanding users' thinking and design contexts, suggesting AI agents need a 'theory of mind' to infer user preferences.

905.title: Addressing Challenges to Problem Complexity: Effectiveness of AI Assistance During the Design Process
905.summary: The authors investigated how AI assistance changes the way people design and how effective their designs are. Participants worked on a complex drone design task in the HyForm research platform with or without AI assistance, and their processes were analysed with Hidden Markov Models and network analysis. AI assistance helped most with moderately complex objectives and less with highly complex ones, and designers with AI searched more exploratively while those without spent more effort tuning parameters.

908.title: Supporting Designer Learning and Performance in Design Space Exploration: A Goal-Setting Approach
908.summary: The authors tested whether telling designers to focus on learning or on finding good designs changes what they get out of exploring a design space. In a between-subject experiment, 14 participants used a design exploration tool for mechanical metamaterials, rewarded either for correct answers on later learning tests or for the performance of their designs. Learning-focused participants scored better on the tests and design-focused participants produced better designs, suggesting a trade-off between the two goals.

910.title: A Network-Based Computational Model for Creative Knowledge Discovery Bridging Human-Computer Interaction and Data Mining
910.summary: The authors aimed to support creative knowledge discovery, finding valuable but unnoticed links between concepts, by combining data mining with human-computer interaction. They proposed a network-based model, built a web tool called B-Link, and evaluated it with longitudinal interviews and a questionnaire using a case study method called MILCs. Users found novel items and inspiration, and survey ratings were positive on all five creativity metrics.

911.title: A Proposed Quality Metric for Ideation Effectiveness
911.summary: Idea quality is hard to measure reliably and efficiently, so the authors set out to develop a quality metric for judging ideation that is meaningful, repeatable and efficient. Their metric is a weighted sum of quality dimensions from the literature, with weights tuned to each design problem through a quick experimental method. Inter-rater reliability showed repeatability, agreement with raters' intuitive judgments showed meaningfulness, and the rating process proved efficient, so the metric looked promising for further testing.

914.title: Divergent Thinking Ability + Interest = Creative Ideas: Exploring the Relationships Between Cognitive Creativity Assessments and Product Design Idea Generation
914.summary: The authors tested whether common creativity tests predict the creativity of real product design ideas. Participants took the Remote Associates Test, Alternative Uses Test and Torrance Test, and industry leaders rated their product ideas using the Consensual Assessment Technique, with product familiarity and interest tested as moderators. Only the Alternative Uses Test predicted rated creativity, and people less familiar with but more interested in a product translated their skills into creative ideas more readily.

915.title: Design Methods Used During Early Stages of Product Development: Three Company Cases
915.summary: Most design methods are developed and tested with student teams, so the authors examined which methods professionals actually use in the early stages of product development. They carried out case studies of design teams developing new physical products at three companies in consumer electronics, footwear and medical devices. All three teams relied heavily on internal and external benchmarking and reverse engineering to generate concepts, and all produced evolutionary rather than revolutionary products.

917.title: Teaching Students to Innovate: Evaluating Methods for Bioinspired Design and Their Impact on Design Self Efficacy
917.summary: The authors compared five methods for teaching bioinspired design, which draws on nature for engineering ideas. In an engineering elective course at Texas A&M University, students used the Directed, Case Study, AskNature.org, BioTRIZ and Functional Modeling methods, and the authors assessed the ideas produced, students' self-efficacy and student feedback. Each method produced many high-quality ideas, and the course improved students' design confidence, outcome expectancy and anxiety while maintaining their motivation.

919.title: Unpacking Subjective Creativity Ratings: Using Embeddings to Explain and Measure Idea Novelty
919.summary: Human judgments of idea novelty are subjective and hard to explain, so the authors developed a way to reveal how people judge similarity between ideas. They built two-dimensional idea maps from comparisons of the form 'Is idea A more similar to B or to C?', tested on sketches of coloured polygons and of milk frothers. The maps revealed the factors raters used to judge similarity, allowed novelty to be estimated from distances and were tested with sparse or noisy ratings.

921.title: The Way Makers Prototype: Principles of DIY Design

922.title: A Comparison of Variety Metrics in Engineering Design
922.summary: The authors compared ways of measuring the variety of a set of design ideas, since it was unclear whether the three existing metrics agree. They analysed 104 design ideas from 29 sophomore mechanical engineering students using the three existing metrics and a new one they developed, comparing them statistically and qualitatively. The four metrics showed varying levels of significant correlation, yet each offered a distinct view of variety suited to different situations.

923.title: Comparing the Effects of Design Interventions on the Quality of Design Concepts As a Reflection of Ideation Flexibility
923.summary: The authors compared three interventions meant to help students generate ideas: cognitive-style based teaming, problem framing and design heuristics. They analysed the quality of 966 design ideas from 152 engineering and industrial design undergraduates at two Midwestern universities, with and without each intervention. The teaming and problem framing interventions produced statistically significant differences in idea quality, with implications for how educators use such interventions.

924.title: To Classify or Combine: The Effects of Idea Generation Mechanisms on the Novelty and Quantity of Ideas
924.summary: The authors compared two ways of pausing during idea generation, classifying earlier ideas or combining them, to see which leads to more and more novel ideas. Sixty-one participants did an alternate uses test, applied one of the two techniques to their first-round ideas, then generated ideas again, and the ideas were scored for quantity and novelty. Both techniques raised novelty, but classifying produced significantly higher novelty scores and more unique ideas than combining.

925.title: My Idea Is Best! Ownership Bias and its Influence on Engineering Concept Selection
925.summary: The authors investigated whether engineering students favour their own ideas when choosing concepts, and how personality affects those choices. Thirty-seven engineering students generated and then selected design concepts within teams, and the authors analysed whose ideas were chosen alongside personality measures. Personality affected the proportion of ideas selected, and male students chose more of their own ideas, showing ownership bias, while female students more often picked teammates' concepts.

926.title: Object Reorientation and Creative Performance
926.summary: The authors investigated whether people who mentally reorient objects are more creative, as a way of understanding functional fixedness. Participants completed an Alternative Uses Test with reorientation cues, the Wallach-Kogan pattern meanings test and a Need for Closure scale. Reorientation was strongly and significantly correlated with several creativity measures and with the predictability part of the Need for Closure scale, and qualitative analysis suggested further possible creativity metrics.

927.title: Visual Similarity to Aid Alternative-Use Concept Generation for Retired Wind-Turbine Blades
927.summary: Retired wind-turbine blades have few disposal options and should not be reused in their original function, so the authors explored using visual similarity to find new uses. They developed a method that finds images visually similar to blade photos and derives reuse ideas from objects in those images, and compared it with two concept-generation sessions at German universities. The visual-similarity method produced fewer concepts that ignored the blades' large scale, offering a new way to find uses for large objects.

928.title: The Sketch Quality Bias: Evaluating Descriptions of Product Ideas With and Without Visuals
928.summary: The authors examined how much the quality of a product sketch sways people's judgement of the idea behind it. A total of 400 participants evaluated a set of product ideas presented either with or without a sketch. When sketches were shown, ratings of an idea's value were heavily influenced by sketch quality, and ratings differed somewhat without sketches, suggesting that how an idea is drawn shapes how worthwhile it seems.

929.title: Patterns of Creative Design: Predicting Ideation From Problem Formulation
929.summary: The authors examined how the way designers frame a problem relates to the creativity of the ideas they later produce. Twenty-five graduate students recorded their problem formulations for two design problems in the web-based Problem Map tool and sketched concepts, and regression models built on the first problem predicted ideation scores for the second. Models for variety and quality gave more accurate predictions, while some novelty and quality models were statistically more reliable.

930.title: Comparing Facets of Divergent Thinking in Engineering Freshmen and Upperclassmen
930.summary: The authors examined whether engineering education changes students' divergent thinking, expecting people to think more divergently on unfamiliar tasks. Forty upperclassmen and 40 freshmen completed an online survey with two ideation tasks, and their ideas were sorted into categories and scored for fluency, flexibility and originality. Contrary to the hypothesis, originality did not differ significantly between groups, and both produced their most original ideas on the generally familiar task.

931.title: Rate of Variety and its Relation to Creativity Factors
931.summary: The authors studied designers' ideation styles by looking at outcomes rather than think-aloud protocols, measuring how quickly each person explores the solution space, which they called rate of variety. In a quantitative study of problem solving, they related this exploration rate to the novelty and quality of ideas. Broad searching correlated significantly with novelty and detailed searching with quality, consistent with earlier protocol studies, while the number of ideas was a possible confounding factor.

932.title: Evaluating Crowdsourced Design Concepts With Machine Learning
932.summary: The authors developed a machine learning method to filter, categorise and rate the large sets of design concepts that crowdsourcing can produce. The method uses unsupervised learning trained on open-source databases to tag keywords and topics in plain-language concept descriptions, and it was tested on four ideation cases with over 4,000 concepts. In head-to-head comparisons, concepts picked by the machine learning metrics beat those selected by a time-limited human.

933.title: The Effects of Elaboration in Creativity Tests as it Pertains to Overall Scores and How it Might Prevent a Person From Thinking of Creative Ideas During the Early Stages of Brainstorming and Idea Generation
933.summary: The authors studied whether elaborating on early ideas holds people back from reaching original ones in creativity tests. Some 460 participants listed alternative uses for a paperclip, and 89 of them also took the Abbreviated Torrance Test for Adults. Later ideas were more original than early ones, and people who wrote longer, more elaborate responses had lower originality scores, suggesting that dwelling on first ideas during time-limited brainstorming can hinder creativity.

934.title: Understanding Effects of Analogical Distance on Performance of Ideation: Key Observations and Findings
934.summary: The authors investigated how the distance between a source of inspiration and a design problem affects the novelty and quality of the resulting concepts. They analysed 138 concepts for spherical rolling robots generated with patents as stimuli by 105 students in 21 teams, measuring distance between patent technology classes and the problem domain. Closer technologies were used more often, more distant stimuli led to more novel concepts, and closer stimuli led to higher quality.

935.title: Inspired Internal Search: Using Neuroimaging to Understand Design Ideation and Concept Generation With Inspirational Stimuli
935.summary: Inspirational stimuli such as analogies help designers, but little is known about the thinking processes behind them, so the authors looked inside the brain during ideation. In a functional MRI experiment, 21 participants generated design concepts with and without inspirational words given at different distances from the problem. Any stimulus, near or far, increased the number of ideas, and successful use of stimuli produced a distinct pattern of brain activation the authors called 'inspired internal search'.

936.title: Measuring and Optimizing Design Variety Using Herfindahl Index
936.summary: The authors proposed a new way to measure the variety of a set of designs, based on the Herfindahl index used in economics, along with a procedure for testing variety metrics against expert judgements. Using two new datasets built from experts' pairwise comparisons, they compared the new metric with commonly used tree-based ones. The new metric matched human ratings better, can be optimised efficiently, can be tuned to new domains, and distinguishes random design sets more sensitively.

939.title: Exploring the Use of a Full Factorial Design of Experiment to Study Design Briefs for Creative Ideation
939.summary: The authors examined how four kinds of information in a design brief, (quantitative requirements, a video example, a physical example and contextual information) affect the creativity of design outcomes. They used a full factorial experiment to capture main and interaction effects, rating ideas on novelty, appropriateness and usability. Briefs with no extra information gave novel but less appropriate and usable ideas, video examples did the reverse, and physical-contextual briefs scored reasonably well on novelty and usability.

940.title: Interpreting Measures of Rarity and Novelty: Investigating Correlations Between Relative Infrequency and Perceived Ratings
940.summary: The authors examined whether two common ways of measuring the novelty of design ideas, how rare an idea is within a set and how novel judges rate it, actually agree. They applied three previously published methods to the same ideas and compared the results. They found moderate agreement between a rarity measure and the ratings, enough to make recommendations for future research, but enough disagreement that the two kinds of measure should be named and analysed separately.

941.title: Discovery of Mental Metadata Used for Analogy Formation in Function-Based Design
941.summary: The authors set out to learn what kinds of similarity designers use when drawing analogies, to guide the design of databases that help designers find analogies. Ten mechanical engineering graduate students completed a design task followed by an interview, and the information they drew on was coded and linked to whether each concept used single, compound or no analogy. Function, flow and form information were all used, with little difference between compound and single analogies.

942.title: Design Whodunit: The Relationship Between Individual Characteristics and Interaction Behaviors in Design Concept Generation
942.summary: The authors studied how individuals' cognitive styles relate to the way they interact in design teams generating concepts. They measured team members' preferences with the Kirton Adaption-Innovation inventory and coded team interactions with the Interaction Dynamics Notation. Individual characteristics were significantly correlated with specific interaction behaviours and idea statements, and certain interaction sequences were associated with a higher chance of new ideas emerging.

943.title: Fixated on Fixation? An Exploration of the Benefits and Deficits of Design “Fixation” in Engineering Design
943.summary: Design fixation is usually seen as harmful, but the authors asked whether reusing parts of example products can actually help creativity. Designers took part in a product dissection activity with different types of products before generating ideas, and eye tracking was used to check whether their reuse of parts was unconscious. Reusing parts was positively related to individual creativity, and eye fixations were unrelated to design fixation, suggesting the reuse may be deliberate.

944.title: Computationally Derived Adaptive Inspirational Stimuli for Real-Time Design Support During Concept Generation
944.summary: The authors explored giving designers inspirational examples chosen by computer in real time, based on what they were currently designing. Midway through ideation, participants received a semantically near example, a semantically far example, or none, selected from a database using Latent Semantic Analysis. Near and far stimuli could be reliably distinguished, near stimuli made designs more feasible, and the overall innovativeness of the stimulus had a strong effect on final design outcomes.

945.title: Reducing Sketch Inhibition During Concept Generation: Psychophysiological Evidence of the Effect of Interventions
945.summary: The authors tested whether warm-up activities can ease students' reluctance to sketch during concept generation. Participants did no warm-up, simple warm-ups or art-based activities designed to reduce sketch inhibition before a short design task, while brain activity, skin response and self-reported workload were measured. Warm-ups reduced stress and art-based activities improved engagement for younger participants, but none changed the number of ideas or other performance measures.

946.title: Mining for Creativity: Determining the Creativity of Ideas Through Data Mining Techniques
946.summary: The authors aimed to find an efficient and reliable way to rate the creativity of large numbers of early design ideas, since human ratings are slow and inconsistent. They developed and tested a machine learning approach that predicts the creativity of ideas from their written descriptions. Machine learning predicted creativity with relatively high accuracy and sensitivity, showing potential for rating ideas in design research.

947.title: The Ends or the Means? Understanding How Students Use Causal and Effectual Information During Design Activities
947.summary: As part of building a framework of the kinds of information designers use, the authors studied effectual information, which sets goals from available resources, versus causal information, which pursues a fixed goal by any means. In a controlled pilot study, students addressed a design problem through a web interface while their use of design information was observed. The authors analysed these interactions and the creativity of the outcomes, giving early insight into the role of effectual information in design reasoning.

948.title: Dimensions of Product Similarity in Design by Analogy: An Exploratory Study
948.summary: The authors explored which kinds of similarity designers look for when choosing reference products for design by analogy. Fifty mechanical engineering students were given products to design, picked other products they would find useful references, and said along which dimensions (function, form, energy flow, material flow, motion) they were similar. Participants chose references based on several dimensions at once, with function the most dominant, followed by energy, motion, material and form.

949.title: In Search of Effective Design Problems for Design Research
949.summary: The authors explored how the choice of design problem in design research experiments may influence the results. They proposed a small set of problem characteristics that might affect outcomes and ran two experiments, one comparing evaluation metrics across two design problems and a follow-up relating the characteristics to differences in results. Participants' familiarity with and knowledge of a problem influenced the metrics, and the design method and problem could interact.

950.title: Demographic Factors and Their Influence on Designer Creativity and Empathy Evoked Through User Extreme Conditions
950.summary: The authors asked whether a designer's background changes how well simulated extreme user scenarios evoke empathy and creativity, to help designers choose suitable ideation tools. They studied 81 participants (49 female, 32 male) across three workshops, each simulating a different extraordinary user scenario. Having a personal connection to the simulated population significantly affected how much creativity and empathy the scenario evoked, while gender showed no significant effect.

952.title: An Extreme User Approach to Identify Latent Needs: Adaptation and Application in Medical Device Design
952.summary: The authors adapted a step-by-step approach for choosing simulated "extreme user" perspectives, such as physical or cognitive impairments, to help designers uncover hidden needs that ordinary users do not voice. Six teams with 25 participants from a healthcare product design course applied the approach, based on user activity diagrams, to six medical devices, and a new latency metric was evaluated. The approach captured latent needs for all six devices, and the authors discussed future uses of the metric.

953.title: Investigating Spontaneous Flexibility in Concept Generation
953.summary: The authors investigated how spontaneous flexibility, the tendency to produce many varied responses, relates to engineering concept generation. Fifty-two participants generated ideas for three items on a spontaneous flexibility test and three problems on an engineering ideation test, and their responses were scored for fluency and flexibility. Both fluency and flexibility were strongly correlated between the two tests, suggesting the engineering test complements the standard measure.

954.title: Investigating Problem Similarity Through Study of Between-Subject and Within-Subject Experiments
954.summary: The authors wanted to know whether different design problems are equivalent enough to be swapped in repeated-measures studies of students' design ability, since the same problem cannot be given twice. They ran idea generation sessions with between-subject and within-subject designs on four problems: peanut shelling, corn husking, coconut harvesting and a personal alarm clock. Solutions were scored on quantity, quality, novelty, variety and completeness, and the peanut and corn problems, and the alarm and coconut problems, proved similar.

955.title: Function Ordering Within Morphological Charts: An Experimental Study
955.summary: Morphological charts list options for each function of a product, and the authors tested whether the order of functions in the chart affects how designers explore it. Sixty-seven junior mechanical engineering students combined options from prepopulated charts for two problems, with functions arranged in five orders, including by importance, input to output and random. Students focused on the first columns regardless of order, and ordering functions from most to least important led to broader, more even exploration.

956.title: Does Visual Fixation Affect Idea Fixation?

957.title: Creativity Predictors: Findings From Design-by-Analogy Ideation Methods’ Learning and Performance
957.summary: The authors explored how psychological and situational factors relate to creative performance when using design-by-analogy ideation methods. Sixty-nine participants from 52 companies in Mexico and Singapore held two ideation sessions on a service design problem, being trained in WordTree, SCAMPER or no method in between, and rated 11 factors such as motivation and concentration. The authors analysed how learning the methods changed these self-ratings and how the factors related to fluency, novelty and fixation.

959.title: Systematic Framework to Apply Extraordinary User Perspective to Capture Latent Needs Among Ordinary Users

963.title: Design Heuristics: Analysis and Synthesis From Jet Propulsion Laboratory’s Architecture Team
963.summary: The authors studied the rules of thumb that expert designers at NASA's Jet Propulsion Laboratory use in early space mission design, and presented a method for extracting, classifying and characterising them. They interviewed ten experts, collecting 101 heuristics, and used follow-up surveys in which participants rated each heuristic's origin, applicability, frequency of use, reliability and tendency to evolve. Statistical analysis showed correlations between how often a heuristic was used, how reliable it seemed and how much it evolved.

964.title: Should it Stay or Should it Go?: A Case Study of Concept Screening in Engineering Design Industry
964.summary: The authors studied how professionals actually decide which design ideas to keep during concept screening, since most earlier research used students or hypothetical tasks. They shadowed a research and development team at a small electromechanical company from early concepts to a final executive pitch, and conducted surveys and interviews. Both idea generators and executives advanced ideas with high market potential and avoided risk, but only executives favoured highly feasible ideas, while idea generators showed no preference on originality or feasibility.

967.title: Human Validation of Computer vs Human Generated Design Sketches
967.summary: The authors explored how people perceive design sketches produced by a deep learning model compared with those drawn by humans, and whether people are biased against computer-generated ideas. A total of 619 participants rated the visual and functional characteristics of 50 human-made and 50 computer-generated 2D sketches. Participants judged the computer-generated sketches as more functional, labels did not change this, and they could not tell the two kinds apart better than chance.

970.title: Design Heuristics: A Conceptual Framework and Preliminary Method for Extraction
970.summary: Because fully rational decisions are computationally hard, designers fall back on rules of thumb, so the authors proposed a conceptual framework for these heuristics. In a preliminary study, participants with at least two years of robot design experience spent 45 minutes on a robotics design problem, and the authors developed a method to extract the heuristics they used. Trends in the extracted heuristics led to an initial taxonomy classified by design phase, field of study and action intent.

971.title: Uncovering Ownership Bias: The Influence of Idea Goodness and Creativity on Design Professionals’ Concept Selection Practices
971.summary: The authors investigated whether design professionals favour their own ideas when choosing concepts in a team setting, and what drives this. In two workshops with 45 professionals from two engineering companies, participants generated and selected ideas during a two-hour team design challenge, with ideas rated by teams for future value and by experts for creativity. Ownership bias appeared only for ideas of little value, and professionals generally preferred useful but less unique ideas, suggesting a bias against creative concepts.

972.title: Investigating Information: A Qualitative Analysis of Expert Designers’ Information Representation and Structuring Behaviors
972.summary: The authors looked closely at how experienced designers organise and use information when generating ideas. Four software design professionals each took part in a three-hour session, generating ideas to reduce distraction-related pedestrian accidents using specially prepared information sheets. The designers sorted information in individual ways but all judged it by whether it informed constraints, resources or user requirements, and their experience and design tools helped them turn information into insights.

975.title: Divergence in Problems Rather Than Solutions: Design Processes of Microfluidic Engineers in Academia
975.summary: Design process models stress exploring many alternative solutions early on, and the authors investigated how engineers actually explore alternatives in a specific setting. They interviewed 10 academic engineers working in microfluidics about their front-end design processes. Rather than starting from a problem, these engineers began with an existing solution and searched for problems to fit it, diverging widely on problems but hardly on solutions, which traditional design process models fail to capture.

977.title: Empirical Studies of Functional Decomposition in Early Design
977.summary: The authors studied how functional decomposition, breaking a product down into its functions, is used in early design. They compared three decomposition methods across 25 novice design teams and examined 78 design reports from industry engineers in a distance learning course. Top-down and energy-flow methods performed similarly and better than enumeration, and decomposition aided team communication, but its use showed no correlation with final design quality in the industry reports.

979.title: An Empirical Study of a Decision-Making Process Supported by Simulation in the Automotive Industry
979.summary: Modelling and simulation consume large resources in product development, so the authors set out to understand how design decisions supported by simulation are actually made. They conducted an empirical study at a car manufacturer, mapping the decision-making process in the development phase and analysing decision makers' difficulties and needs qualitatively. Decisions were often postponed and escalated as complexity and uncertainty grew, and limited knowledge of simulation limits, design ambiguity and uncertainty led to iterations and delays.

984.title: Designing Self-Organizing Systems With Deep Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning
984.summary: The authors proposed using deep multi-agent reinforcement learning so that robots in self-organizing systems can learn their own task knowledge and social rules, rather than having them predefined, for complex tasks. They trained agents in simulations of a box-pushing problem and tested how well the learning scaled with different team sizes and environmental noise. Systems trained with many agents generalised to other settings, but networks trained with small teams did not scale up, so training should use larger teams.

986.title: Validating a Tool for Predicting Problem-Specific Optimized Team Characteristics
986.summary: The authors tested whether the best way for a team to work can be predicted from the properties of the design problem, challenging the common assumption that interacting teams always do better. They defined a new problem of designing a system of internet-connected products to control home temperature, and used computationally derived response surfaces to predict ideal team characteristics. The tool predicted that members should work independently and pick the best individual solution, and a cognitive study confirmed this prediction.

990.title: Exploration of Entrepreneurial Student Teams Performance and Student Team Members’ Personality via the Big Five Test
990.summary: The authors investigated which personality traits make an interdisciplinary entrepreneurial student design team successful. Forty students in seven teams developed a technology-based product, each member took the Big Five personality test, and teams were analysed by average personality and by personality spread, then ranked on interviews, idea generation, prototyping and final presentation. The best teams had high variability in neuroticism and extraversion and average levels of extraversion and agreeableness.

992.title: Assessing the Impact of Cognitive Assistants on Mental Workload in Simple Tasks
992.summary: The authors investigated how working with a voice-based cognitive assistant, similar to Siri or Alexa, affects people's mental workload. Participants performed the Wisconsin Card Sorting Task with or without a simulated assistant called Mary while also completing a secondary speed and accuracy test. Performance was higher with the assistant, mental workload did not differ significantly, and participants working with the assistant were less frustrated.

994.title: Creativity of Concept Ideation Methods As Affected by Team Personality
994.summary: Building on work showing that individual personality type affects ideation results, the authors ran a pilot study on whether a team's average Myers-Briggs (MBTI) personality affects how creative its ideas are. They compared ideation outcomes using three creativity metrics: quantity, quality and variety. Teams near the extremes of the thinking-feeling spectrum produced more creative results, and teams with neutral or highly varied personalities could choose ideation methods to favour particular metrics.

995.title: Design Sprint for Complex System Architecture Analysis
995.summary: Complex system design usually relies on a single in-depth analysis by domain experts, and the authors tested whether a quick hackathon-style sprint by non-experts could also yield useful insights. Seven teams spent a few hours analysing an industry case about risks from a system's long lifecycle and delivery time, using design structure matrices of the product architecture and several analysis tools. Each team produced unique recommendations, and the sprint was judged a useful complement to traditional analysis.

999.title: Modeling Trust in Self-Organizing Systems With Heterogeneity
999.summary: Self-organizing systems such as robot swarms can malfunction when individual agents perform poorly or differ in capability, so the authors proposed a trust-based model for designing them. In simulations of agents cooperatively pushing a box, each agent's trust in others was measured with a beta probability distribution based on positive and negative interactions. Compared with systems without trust, the model encouraged favourable interactions, increased system effectiveness and in some conditions improved efficiency.

1002.title: Can Wearable Sensors Be Used to Capture Engineering Design Team Interactions?: An Investigation Into the Reliability of Sociometric Badges
1002.summary: Studying design team interactions usually means coding hours of video, so the authors tested whether wearable sociometric badges could capture team conversations reliably instead. They examined the badges' accuracy, precision and ability to detect who dominated speech in engineering design teams. The badges captured total speaking time accurately but were affected by environmental conditions and often overestimated when someone was speaking, making them suitable for high-level measures such as participation.

1003.title: Design Processes of Design Automation Practitioners
1003.summary: As computers play a bigger role in design, the authors examined how expert architects and engineers plan to use computation when tackling a design problem. They studied how practitioners planned a solution to a sample design problem using computers and computation. Their process could be modelled in four phases, discovery, evaluation, extrapolation and interpolation, with evaluation usually coming before extrapolation, and the authors also identified common computational strategies and challenges.

1004.title: Graduate Students’ Mental Models: An Investigation Into the Role of Function in Systems Understanding
1004.summary: The authors examined whether teaching functional modelling improves how well graduate students understand and explain engineering systems. They measured students' mental models of a hair dryer, a clothes dryer and a vacuum cleaner before and after instruction on functional modelling and decomposition, using scoring rubrics. Average scores improved significantly for all three products, suggesting that such teaching strengthens students' understanding of systems and their ability to communicate it.

1008.title: The Prototyping Behaviors of Startups: Exploring the Relationship Between Prototyping Behavior and the Financial Success of Startups
1008.summary: The authors investigated how prototyping practices relate to the success of tech start-ups, many of which fail before reaching market. They surveyed 34 start-up representatives and used cluster analysis to group the companies. Three groups emerged, differing in funding, use of prototyping best practices and difficulty with start-up tasks; high-performing start-ups had the most funding, found tasks less difficult and used prototyping best practices more often.

1010.title: Eye Gaze Experiment Into the Recognition of Intended Affordances
1010.summary: The authors tested the common design claim that people know how to use an object by visually perceiving its intended affordances. Sixty-one participants viewed images of artifacts for ten seconds while their gaze was tracked, then said how they would interact with each one. No eye-tracking measure reliably predicted recognising the intended use, but recognition was strongly linked to mentioning the artifact's function or category, suggesting analogical priming may explain usage better than affordances.

1011.title: Should Teams Collaborate During Conceptual Engineering Design? An Experimental Study
1011.summary: Individuals working alone have been shown to beat teams in brainstorming and configuration design, and the authors tested whether this also holds for open-ended conceptual engineering design. In a behavioural study, first-year engineering students solved a conceptual design problem either in teams or individually, and some individuals were asked to think aloud to test whether verbalising hurts performance. Individuals produced higher-quality solutions than teams, and verbalising did not affect individual performance.

1012.title: The Trajectory of Psychological Safety in Engineering Teams: A Longitudinal Exploration in Engineering Design Education
1012.summary: The authors set out to measure psychological safety, how comfortable team members feel sharing their views, in engineering student teams and to track how it changes over a project. They followed 12 engineering design teams for four weeks, collecting data at six time points. The study provided some of the first evidence that psychological safety can be measured reliably in engineering student teams and began to identify what builds or erodes it.

1014.title: A User Study on Exploring the Sequencing of Unit Cell Design Guidelines
1014.summary: The authors examined whether the order in which designers apply four guidelines for redesigning unit cells, the repeating structures in cellular materials, affects the results, since the guidelines are somewhat subjective. In a user study, designers applied the guidelines to increase shear flexure in twelve different sequences. Certain sequences produced more novel ideas than others that used less subjective guidelines.

1015.title: Toward a Model-Based Experimental Approach to Assessing Collective Systems Design
1015.summary: The authors aimed to understand the trade-offs and risks faced by independent but interacting design actors in decentralised engineering systems. They built a conceptual model combining value-driven design, game theory and simulation, in which actors first explore coupled design spaces and then choose a strategy in a classic strategy game. A preliminary multi-agent simulation assessed whether the proposed design spaces were valid and generated hypotheses for later studies with human participants.

1018.title: Risky Business: The Driving Factors of Creative Risk Taking Attitudes in Engineering Design Industry
1018.summary: The authors explored what drives engineering professionals' willingness to take risks on creative ideas early in design, since little research had looked beyond students. They surveyed 46 design professionals at a global manufacturing company about education, job type and years of experience. Education level and experience were related to willingness to take creative risks, and people in R&D and management were more financially risk averse than those in traditional engineering roles.

1019.title: Extending Lead User Theory to Participatory Co-Design: A Case Study in a Base of the Pyramid Context
1019.summary: Choosing the right users to co-design with is critical for products aimed at the world's poorest consumers, and the authors examined whether lead user theory could guide that choice. Using a case study of an improved cook stove design in Gujarat, India, they compared themes from stakeholder interviews with Von Hippel's lead user theory. Being 'ahead of trend' was not critical, and an extended model including expected benefit, design communication skills and social network access to user preferences was proposed.

1020.title: Manufacturing Vulnerability: How Resource Scarcity Hinders Team Coordination During Manufacturing in Nigerian Factories
1020.summary: The authors set out to learn how less-skilled and highly-skilled workers coordinate in Nigerian factories, where the education gap between them can be large. Using ethnographic methods, the study was carried out in two factories and two universities across four Nigerian states in summer 2018. Resource scarcity hindered coordination through unclear roles and processes, poor attitudes to work, under- and overuse of employees, and worker demoralisation.

1021.title: Measuring the Evoked Hardness of Design Problems Using Transient Microstates
1021.summary: The authors explored whether brain signals can reveal how hard a design problem feels to the person solving it. They applied microstate analysis to EEG recordings of subjects performing creative tasks of varying difficulty and defined a measure of transient microstates based on the complexity of the segmentation. Problems and subtasks of different perceived difficulty showed different levels of transient microstates, and the brain appeared to use 1 to 20% of its transient microstate capacity.

1022.title: Integrating Design and Optimization Tools: A Designer Centered Study
1022.summary: Designing additively manufactured parts usually means switching between separate software for design, analysis and optimization, so the authors tested whether combining them in one tool helps designers. In a controlled human subjects study, they built three tools with different levels of integration and gave them to designers working on two structural truss problems. Greater integration improved design quality, speed and efficiency, and the best designers with the fully integrated tool explored designs that users of other tools never reached.

1023.title: Inclusive Toy Design From a Lead User With Extraordinary Needs
1023.summary: The authors explored whether designing toys for one child with extraordinary needs could produce toys that engage other children too. Undergraduate engineering students designed and prototyped three toys for a four-year-old with hemiplegic cerebral palsy, and the toys were tested with him and with daycare children aged 16 to 33 months. The lead user completed 6 of the 9 designed functions, including 4 that fewer than half the daycare children completed, and the toys engaged all children in two-handed play.

1024.title: Collaborating With Style: Using an Agent-Based Model to Simulate Cognitive Style Diversity in Problem Solving Teams
1024.summary: The authors built KABOOM, a computer model that simulates how differences in team members' problem-solving styles affect collaborative problem solving. The model simulated teams of agents with varied cognitive styles working on two design problems. Some cognitive styles were more effective than others depending on the problem, and deliberately matching agents' styles to their roles improved team performance.

1025.title: Studying Human Design Teams via Computational Teams of Simulated Annealing Agents
1025.summary: The authors set out to simulate human design teams computationally, to reduce the cost of studies with human participants. They introduced CISAT, an agent-based framework built on simulated annealing that models several known cognitive behaviours of designers, and used it to simulate a previous cognitive study of teams. Simulated results were compared directly with human team results, and the model was used to identify which team characteristics helped or hindered performance most.

1026.title: Understanding Designers Behavior in Parameter Design Activities
1026.summary: The authors studied how engineers behave when adjusting design parameters, aiming to inform better tools and strategies for complex, constrained design problems such as aerospace and automotive systems. Thirty participants solved parameter design problems with both coupled and uncoupled variables while their actions were recorded. Designers' actions were related to gender, recorded errors, problem complexity and performance.

1028.title: Requirements Culture: A Case Study on Product Development and Requirement Perspectives
1028.summary: The authors examined whether a large power tool company had a shared culture around engineering requirements and how views on requirements differed across departments. Five interview teams conducted ten semi-structured interviews over two months with engineers, designers, project managers and vice presidents, and analysed the transcripts and documents. The company did have a clear requirements culture, consistent handover of requirements between departments was essential, and people involved early in development engaged more with requirements.

1031.title: Establishing a Protocol to Observe Leadership Behaviors Within Engineering Design Teams
1031.summary: The authors set out to create a protocol for identifying leadership behaviours in engineering design teams, drawing on leadership theory and research on collaborative design. Three raters applied the protocol to a video of a graduate student team building a function structure model. The protocol showed high agreement within raters and acceptable reliability between raters, and the pilot suggested refinements to clarify leader and follower behaviours and link them to design activities.

1033.title: Considering Different Motivations in Design for Consumer-Behavior Change
1033.summary: The authors aimed to design products that encourage sustainable behaviour by appealing to different personal motives. They proposed a model of egoistic, sociocultural and altruistic motives, checked it against reader comments about an international environmental agreement, and had online respondents evaluate concepts targeting each motive in two rounds. Results partly deviated from expectations because concepts were perceived unexpectedly, and the authors proposed a design tool combining motive types with levels of persuasion.

1034.title: Function Modeling: Comparison of Chaining Methods Using Protocol Study and Designer Study
1034.summary: The authors set out to learn whether the way a function structure model is built up, known as the chaining method, changes the resulting model, and whether designers prefer one method. In a designer study and a protocol study, participants completed function models from seed models built by forward chaining, backward chaining or nucleation, at 10%, 40% or 80% completion. The resulting models were to be compared by counting functions and flows and with a previously developed scoring method.

1035.title: How Engineering Design Students’ Creative Preferences and Cognitive Styles Impact Their Concept Generation and Screening
1035.summary: The authors explored how individual traits affect how students generate and screen creative ideas in engineering design. In an exploratory study, 19 undergraduate engineering students completed the Preferences for Creativity Scale and Kirton's Adaption-Innovation inventory, and their ideas for a design task were rated for creativity, quality and originality. Creative preferences predicted students' tendency to select creative concepts, explaining 74% of the variation, but not idea generation, while cognitive style predicted creative and original idea generation with small effects.

1036.title: Motivations for Users Participating in Co-Innovation Communities: A Case Study of Local Motors
1036.summary: The authors set out to identify why users take part in online co-innovation communities, where customers help firms develop products. Drawing on expectancy theory, they used netnography, collecting data on users' actual participation in the Local Motors community through web mining and defining four behaviour properties. They identified six motivations: most users took part out of interest and curiosity, social relations also mattered, monetary rewards drove contributions to complex technical work, and a few sought status or individuality.

1037.title: Parameter Design Strategies: A Comparison Between Human Designers and the Simulated Annealing Algorithm
1037.summary: The authors compared how human designers and a computer optimisation algorithm search for good design parameters. After interviews showed that veteran desalination designers relied on trial and error, mostly student subjects completed a series of simulated design tasks for seawater reverse osmosis plants. The top performers behaved like a well-tuned simulated annealing algorithm, while the worst performers searched almost randomly, pointing to ways of combining human and computer strengths in design tools.

1038.title: What is a Prototype?: Emergent Roles of Prototypes From Empirical Work in Three Diverse Companies
1038.summary: Prototyping is central to product development but little studied in companies, so the authors examined how prototypes are used in practice as part of building a prototyping framework. They carried out a qualitative study in three companies making consumer electronics, footwear and medical devices, and described their research design, data collection, analysis and validity checks. From the findings they proposed a modified definition of a prototype and identified three roles that prototypes play.

1039.title: Implicit and Explicit Trust Behavior: Does Stereotype Congruence Affect User Trust in a Home Automation Device?
1039.summary: Expanding on a pilot study, the authors examined whether matching or violating gender stereotypes in a home automation device affects how much users trust it. Participants interacted with a smart lock simulation whose agent either confirmed or violated social expectations, and both explicit trust behaviours and implicit measures such as reaction time were recorded. Users showed more trusting behaviour toward stereotype-congruent systems, and explicit and implicit trust measures differed.

1040.title: Antecedents and Outcomes of Designer Empathy: A Retrospective Interview Study
1040.summary: The authors explored what triggers empathy in designers during projects and what it leads to, distinguishing understanding users' views (cognitive empathy) from emotional reactions (affective empathy). They thematically analysed ten semi-structured interviews with product and service designers. Designers described many triggers, from recalling similar experiences to seeing users struggle; cognitive empathy was seen to drive design changes, while affective empathy raised recognition of user problems and motivation to help.

1042.title: Evaluating the Discriminatory Value and Reliability of Ideation Metrics for Their Application to Concept Development and Prototyping
1042.summary: Prototyping is a costly and poorly understood stage of product development, and there are no rigorous metrics for judging how ideas change after concept selection. The authors tested whether metrics originally developed to rate ideas during concept generation, such as originality, novelty and quality, can reliably distinguish functional prototypes and the concepts developed during prototyping. They concluded that new metrics are needed to track how product characteristics carry through from first concept to finished product.

1043.title: Function Modeling: An Analysis of Pause Patterns in Modeling Activities
1043.summary: The authors studied when and how long designers pause while building function structure models, to understand their thinking. In a protocol study, mechanical engineering students built a function model for a novel design problem on video, and their pauses and subsequent actions were coded. Participants spent an average of 38% of their time pausing, deleted elements more often after long pauses and edited after short ones, and paused more before adding flows and labelling functions.

1044.title: Application of a Protocol to Observe Leadership Behaviors in Engineering Design Teams
1044.summary: The authors studied how informal leadership emerges and is shared in student engineering design teams. They applied a previously presented protocol to video recordings of novice teams building a function model, coding leadership behaviours and tracking them over each session. Most leadership behaviours concerned planning and action rather than relationships, people who led early often stayed dominant, yet leadership functions were still shared across team members.

1045.title: Which One Should I Pick? Concept Selection in Engineering Design Industry
1045.summary: The authors explored how professional designers view creativity and which tools they use when selecting design concepts, since most research has focused on students. They conducted an online survey of 27 professional designers. The responses were used to identify the factors that affect concept selection in industry and to increase understanding of the creative process in professional engineering design.

1046.title: Measuring Information Content of Freehand Sketches Using a Cognitive Chunk Visualization Protocol
1046.summary: The authors aimed to measure how much information a freehand design sketch contains, based on the mental 'chunks' designers form as they draw. They automated an earlier manual protocol for detecting chunks in real time into a software program and validated it in a new protocol study with new participants. The study replicated earlier evidence of chunking, and the authors showed how to represent sketches as entity-relation models and compute their information content with four metrics.

1047.title: Patterns of Cortical Activation When Using Concept Generation Techniques of Brainstorming, Morphological Analysis, and TRIZ
1047.summary: The authors compared brain activity when engineers generate ideas using three techniques: brainstorming, morphological analysis and TRIZ.
