Twelve engineering students completed three design tasks, one per technique, while functional near-infrared spectroscopy measured blood oxygenation across the prefrontal cortex. Brainstorming produced an early but short-lived high response in a region linked to working memory and flexible thinking, while morphological analysis and TRIZ produced sustained responses and denser coordination across brain regions, suggesting greater cognitive effort.

1048.title: It Rings a Bell! Memory’s Impact on Information Utilization by Novice Designers in the Early Design Process
1048.summary: The authors investigated how memory shapes the way novice designers use information when generating ideas. Undergraduate students received a design problem and information pieces based on an Information Archetypes Framework, generated ideas, and then recalled the information, and their text was analysed with the LIWC language tool. The study showed that memory use during conceptual design has both semantic and linguistic components.

1050.title: Prototyping Methods for a Small-to-Medium Manufacturing Enterprise in a Resource-Constrained Setting: A Case Study
1050.summary: The authors examined how small and medium manufacturers in resource-constrained settings prototype their manufacturing systems, and what limits them. Through a site visit and interviews with engineers at a renewable fuel manufacturer in Rwanda, they studied prototyping methods, constraints and effects on design outcomes. The main aim was to reach high-fidelity, functional physical prototypes through simple prototyping and iteration, constrained by variable inputs, limited manufacturing capabilities and the limits of modelling predictions.

1051.title: “A Makerspace Is More Than Just a Room Full of Tools”: What Learning Looks Like for Female Students in Makerspaces
1051.summary: Universities have invested heavily in makerspaces on the assumption that making stimulates learning, and the authors asked how female students actually experience learning in an academic makerspace. They interviewed five female students in depth, selected through maximum variation and snowball sampling, and developed a preliminary coding scheme from part of the data. The students were learning by doing and solving design problems, and were also overcoming fears, developing patience and learning to communicate ideas.

1052.title: Effect of Team Size on Problem-Solving and Solution Quality: An Empirical Study
1052.summary: The authors examined how team size affects the way designers tackle a problem and the quality of their solutions. In a protocol study of teams of one, three and five people, they coded problem-solving strategies and scored final designs on constraints, manufacturability, feasibility and cost. Larger teams analysed more and proposed less, five-person teams revisited earlier ideas more often, and three-person teams, balancing proposing and analysing, produced the best designs.

1053.title: Discovery and Evaluation of Design Methods in Practice: An Empirical Study
1053.summary: The authors studied how practising engineers and designers discover, choose and judge design methods, since existing resources mostly offer search by method name or stage. They interviewed practitioners across a range of disciplines about searching for, selecting, assessing and sharing experiences of methods. Practitioners found, selected and assessed new methods in similar ways, but differed in how they exchanged experiences with peers.

1055.title: Understanding the Design Neurocognition of Mechanical Engineers When Designing and Problem-Solving
1055.summary: The authors set out to find out whether mechanical engineers' brains work differently when designing than when solving well-defined problems. They adapted tasks from an earlier brain-imaging study of design and recorded participants' brain activity with EEG, focusing on how responses changed over time. Brain activation was higher during designing than during problem-solving, and the time-related patterns linked to specific brain areas helped clarify engineers' thinking in open design tasks.

1056.title: A Pilot Study of Customer Requirement Derivation Methods Among Engineering Students
1056.summary: The authors set out to evaluate methods for turning customer need statements into formal design requirements, as no systematic way to judge their quality existed. They developed a framework of eight metrics from the literature and used it in a pilot study with sophomore engineering students to compare a traditional textbook method with methods based on affordance modelling. No method was best overall, but the methods differed on most metrics.

1057.title: Origins of Design Principles: The Case of Nuclear Reactor Design Projects
1057.summary: The author explored where design principles come from and how they shape design decisions, taking nuclear reactor design as the case. She analysed in-depth, open-ended interviews with designers across 26 reactor design projects in different organisations. Designers used both principles they were aware of and implicit ones recurring across projects, and their ability to generate principles grew with the number of prior designs in their field; criteria for developing design principles are proposed.

1059.title: Proposing a Design for Tangibility Framework: A Digital Payments Case Study
1059.summary: The authors proposed a framework for making abstract interactions, such as managing money, more tangible, and tested it on cashless payments, which tend to increase spending. Drawing on psychological mechanisms behind spending, they designed, built and tested a prototype that adds a physical interaction to digital transactions. The interaction increased people's sense of ownership over digital money, but its effect on spending behaviour was inconclusive.

1063.title: Collaborative Mind-Mapping: A Study of Patterns, Strategies, and Evolution of Maps Created by Peer-Pairs
1063.summary: The authors studied how pairs of people work together to build mind-maps, a common brainstorming tool whose collaborative side is little understood. They observed peer-pairs creating several mind-maps, rated the maps for creativity, and analysed exploration patterns, emerging strategies, inhibition and how maps evolved over time. The authors reported these patterns and strategies and discussed what they mean for designing computer support for mind-mapping.

1067.title: Prediction of Design Team Performance on a Conceptual Design Task Using an Automatable, Topic-Independent Analysis of Language Use
1067.summary: The authors tested whether analysing how team members match each other's language style can predict how well a design team performs. Building on the Language Style Matching measure, they developed new measures and applied them to 30-minute conceptual design meetings involving brainstorming. They identified two conversational patterns, "dwelling" and "forward-moving", and found the forward-moving pattern was associated with better-rated results, using an automatable method that does not depend on the topic.

1071.title: Risk Perception and Product Safety in User-Centered Design
1071.summary: The authors examined how customers' perceptions of risk should feed into product design itself, since earlier work focused mainly on warning labels. They studied how consumers perceive product risk and how this relates to design, using automobile safety as the main example. Perceived safety could differ from objective risk measures, was shaped by personal experience, regulations and standards, and individual traits, and was affected by design features relating to comfort, aesthetics and performance.

1072.title: An Investigation of Design Requirement Volatility, Risk and Priority in Early Stage Design Projects
1072.summary: The authors examined how changes in design requirements, their risk and their priority relate to project success in early-stage design. They studied requirements in projects within a graduate product development course for mid-career professionals. A pattern of decreasing requirement risk, especially for high-priority requirements, was a key predictor of success, suggesting that tracking requirement risk and priority could help monitor project health.

1073.title: Scenario-Based Conjoint Analysis: Measuring Preferences for User Experiences in Early Stage Design
1073.summary: Conjoint analysis usually measures how much consumers value individual product features late in development, and the authors wanted to extend it to user experiences in early concept design. They proposed scenario-based conjoint analysis, which asks people to evaluate experience scenarios rather than features, to complement qualitative design research. They demonstrated it on a case study of a flexible wearable for parent-child communication and tracking, and discussed its results and limitations.

1075.title: Manipulating Trust of Autonomous Products With Affective Priming
1075.summary: The authors tested whether putting people in a positive, neutral or negative mood beforehand changes how much they trust an autonomous product. Participants viewed emotion-evoking images, then interacted with a mock-up of the Amazon Echo through ten question-and-answer sets, rating its competence and their trust. Overall, the mood primes had no significant effect, but for participants whose expectations were met, both the primes and perceived competence affected trust, showing that meeting user expectations is key.

1076.title: Informing Early Design via Crowd-Based Co-Creation
1076.summary: The authors proposed using customers as a source of initial design concepts through online co-creation, rather than only asking for preferences on designers' ideas. They built a web interface for creating virtual prototypes of a computer mouse, a bicycle seat, a pen holder and a cola bottle, and ran a crowdsourcing study with 253 users. The approach captured varied form and function requirements, identified innovative concepts and revealed how perceptions related to product form.

1077.title: The Creation of an Ontology to Examine Customer Needs
1077.summary: Design texts offer no agreed way to categorise customer needs, so designers struggle to tell how much of the need space they have explored. The authors built an ontology for classifying customer needs, refining it over 11 iterations with repeated inter-rater reliability tests. They discussed how the ontology can be used early in design to check that collected needs cover all categories and to compare need-gathering techniques.

1078.title: The Influence of Physical Examples on Originality and Fixation in Engineering Design
1078.summary: The authors examined whether giving engineering students a physical example product affects how original their ideas are and how fixated they become on it. Freshman and senior mechanical engineering students designed garbage collection systems with or without an example product, and the concepts were scored with established metrics. Seniors were more original than freshmen in both conditions, students who saw the example were more fixated, and among them higher fixation went with lower originality, especially for seniors.

1079.title: Analysis of Designer Emotions in Collaborative and Traditional Computer-Aided Design
1079.summary: The authors developed a way to map designers' emotions to what they are doing in collaborative CAD software, where several people edit the same model at once. Using automated facial emotion detection and cursor tracking, they studied nine participants working either alone or in pairs in the same CAD environment. Paired designers showed more emotion, and specific activities predicted emotions to some degree, with chatting linked to joy for pairs and graphics-area work the most common trigger for solo users.

1081.title: Designing for Trust: Understanding the Role of Agent Gender and Location on User Perceptions of Trust in Home Automation
1081.summary: Lack of trust holds back smart home devices, so the authors explored whether a device's location and the gender of its voice affect how trustworthy it seems. In an exploratory pilot study, participants used a simulated smart lock system in a laboratory, with the agent set in an office or a home and speaking with a female or male voice. Users trusted stereotype-congruent agents, a male voice in the office and a female voice at home, more than incongruent ones.

1082.title: Effects of Immersion on Virtual Reality Prototype Design Reviews of Mechanical Assemblies
1082.summary: The authors investigated whether making virtual prototypes more realistic to view and handle helps people spot errors during design reviews of mechanical assemblies. They ran two experiments in which participants reviewed assembly models for errors: the first varied how the display behaved, through moving the viewpoint or rotating the model, and the second varied the controller setup used for input. The authors expected that more realistic rendering and controller input would lead to more accurate design reviews.

1083.title: ARCHIE: An Automated Data Collection Method for Physical Prototyping Efforts in Authentic Design Situations
1083.summary: The authors set out to make it easier to collect research data on physical prototyping in real design projects, which can run for months and are disrupted by researchers. They built ARCHIE, a device that photographs designers' prototypes, links the photos to designers' descriptions and keeps a record of how the design evolves. They described its rationale, method and implementation and tested it on student design projects, suggesting it could support machine learning analysis of prototypes.

1086.title: The Economies and Dimensionality of Prototyping: Value, Time, Cost and Fidelity
1086.summary: The authors set out to understand the trade-off between the design information gained from early prototypes and the time and money spent building them. They conducted an inductive study of industry projects across several disciplines, collecting and analysing data on their physical prototyping. They proposed ways to quantify prototyping value, supported an asymptotic relationship between value and fidelity, and identified practical rules of thumb for getting high value from both low- and high-fidelity prototypes.

1087.title: Similarity in Engineering Design: A Knowledge-Based Approach
1087.summary: The authors developed a way to measure how similar engineering design problems are that reflects findings from cognitive science and the role of scientific knowledge. The approach models knowledge with probabilistic graphical models and measures dissimilarity in terms of performance, illustrated with a shaft design for fatigue and tested in an experiment with 167 students. The approach captured known features of similarity judgements, such as dependence on direction, context and the individual, and their change over time.

1088.title: A Validation Study of Disability Simulation Suit Usage as a Proxy for Customer Need Statements From Persons With Disabilities
1088.summary: The authors tested whether a disability simulation suit lets people without disabilities experience products like people with disabilities, so designers can gather customer needs more safely and easily. They designed a suit and ran validation trials comparing the physical and perceptual behaviour of suit wearers with that of people with disabilities. Initial results showed the suit gave a valid empathic experience, producing similar customer needs and similarly reduced dexterity.

1091.title: Balancing Design Freedom and Brand Recognition in the Evolution of Automotive Brand Styling
1091.summary: The authors examined how car designers can balance making a new model look fresh against keeping it recognisable as part of its brand. In an experiment, customers responded to vehicle designs created interactively, and changes in ten styling attributes linked to design freedom and brand recognition were measured. Brand recognition depended strongly on the manufacturer, but tradeoffs between design freedom and brand recognition could be measured with predictive models to inform design decisions.

1092.title: “Thus, I Had to Go With What I Had”: A Multiple Methods Exploration of Novice Designers’ Articulation of Prototyping Decisions
1092.summary: The authors wanted to understand how novice designers use prototypes to communicate, and how they argue for the design decisions behind them. They ran a controlled prototyping study with 46 undergraduate engineering students and analysed both quantitative and qualitative data on their choices and explanations. The results showed close links between how students made decisions about materials and how they justified those decisions.

1094.title: Products’ Shared Visual Features Do Not Cancel in Consumer Decisions

1097.title: When Are Designers Willing to Take Risks? How Concept Creativity and Prototype Fidelity Influence Perceived Risk
1097.summary: The authors studied how a prototype's level of finish, the creativity of the concept and a person's attitude to risk affect how risky a concept seems and whether it gets chosen. They ran a between-subjects study with 72 engineering students. Students showed a "goldilocks" effect, picking concepts with just the right amount of novelty when quality was adequate, and unique concepts seemed less risky when shown as higher-fidelity prototypes.

1098.title: Promoting Energy-Efficient Driving Using Associative Graphical Displays: Can a Cup of Coffee Encourage You to Drive More Smoothly?
1098.summary: The authors explored whether a simple dashboard display could nudge drivers towards smoother, more energy-efficient driving, since training and information campaigns have had little effect. They designed a display showing an animated coffee cup that reacts to harsh acceleration and braking, and surveyed 92 participants online through Amazon Mechanical Turk. Participants significantly preferred the coffee cup over two other displays, after accounting for demographics, offering early evidence that such behavioural nudges could promote eco-driving.

1099.title: Prototyping for Desirability by Design of Experiments: A Case Study of a Hardware Startup
1099.summary: The authors explored whether prototyping combined with statistical design-of-experiments principles can guide early product development at a small start-up. They built a range of physical prototypes of an alarm device varying four design parameters, ran 44 user tests, and fitted a response surface model of perceived desirability. The model identified the main drivers of desirability, and a follow-up experiment confirmed it could predict how desirable specific prototypes would be.

1100.title: Exploring Situational Factors and Attitudes Affecting Sustainable Electric Kettle Usage
1100.summary: The authors explored what situations and attitudes lead people to heat more water than they need in electric kettles. Five residents in Denmark logged their kettle use, its purpose and context for two weeks, followed by interviews. Excess water varied with purpose and time pressure, the minimum fill marker had no visible effect, sustainability did not shape purchase or use, and four factors drove waste, including uncertain future need and worries about limescale.

1101.title: Back to Basics: Sketching, Not CAD, Is the Key to Improving Essential Engineering Design Skills
1101.summary: The authors tested whether teaching freehand sketching with an industrial design approach in a freshman CAD course would come at the expense of students' spatial visualization skills. They measured spatial visualization at three points during the course and compared this approach with a more traditional engineering approach. The industrial design sketching approach improved spatial visualization as much as the traditional one, and it was the sketching portion, not the CAD, that drove the gains.

1102.title: Exploring the Effectiveness of Providing Structured DfE Design Strategies During Conceptual Design
1102.summary: The authors tested whether giving designers specific environmental design strategies during concept generation helps them create more sustainable products. They added targeted strategies to the GREEn Quiz, a web-based Design for the Environment tool, and ran two experiments with expert and novice designers. Respondents using the strategy-based quiz produced concepts with more sustainable design decisions and higher solution quality than earlier respondents and control groups.

1104.title: A Wizard-of-Oz Experiment to Demonstrate Water Reduction and User Training With an “Autonomous” Faucet
1104.summary: The authors tested whether an apparently smart faucet could both reduce water use and train people to keep using less water afterwards. They built a custom faucet secretly operated by a researcher to seem autonomous, and had participants wash several sets of dishes with it and then with a normal faucet. Participants used 26.5% less water with the smart faucet and still 10.9% less afterwards with a normal faucet.

1106.title: Predicting Multi-Disciplinary Design Performance Utilizing Automated Topic Discovery
1106.summary: The authors explored how to predict a multidisciplinary design project's performance from the competencies of the people on it. Using students' capstone design projects, they automatically extracted topics from text describing competencies and projects, and compared three topic models with five regression-based prediction models. Representing both inputs and outputs as distributions of topics and using support vector regression gave the most accurate mapping between ability and performance.

1107.title: Students’ Exploration Strategies in a Sustainability-Focused Structural Optimization Task

1109.title: Investigating User Emotional Responses to Eco-Feedback Designs
1109.summary: The authors explored the emotions people feel when using eco-feedback products, which show resource use, and how those emotions relate to conservation behaviour. In lab experiments, 30 participants viewed sketches of four eco-feedback concepts and reported how they would feel and act in different scenarios. Immediate actions such as turning off lights were linked to negative emotions like guilt, while ratings of aesthetics and quality went with positive emotions, and figurative designs stirred stronger emotions in younger participants.

1110.title: Towards an Information Archetypes Framework: Exploring the Types of Information Used in Open Source Design Engagements
1110.summary: The authors set out to understand what types of information designers draw on when making decisions, as part of building an Information Archetypes Framework. They analysed interviews in detail with designers who do open source work as part of their jobs. The findings gave empirical evidence of the information types used in design, supported existing archetypes, and revealed new ones arising from combinations of information dimensions.

1111.title: Effects of Collage Priming on Sustainable Design Idea Creation and Assessment
1111.summary: The authors tested whether a collage-making priming exercise could help designers produce ideas covering all three pillars of sustainability and judge other people's ideas more fairly. Graduate design and engineering students did collage priming, a reading exercise, or no activity before designing and rating ideas. Collage priming produced ideas users saw as more environmentally friendly, though not more socially or economically sustainable, and it reduced designers' bias towards their own ideas, which reading did not.

1112.title: Successes and Challenges in Implementing Lean Product Development
1112.summary: The authors set out to understand why few companies have adopted lean product development, despite lean thinking's success in production. An industry-academia research roundtable identified successful practices and the challenges industry faces in implementing it. Challenges included nomenclature, visual management and metrics, knowledge repositories, and lean education and training, and the authors proposed a research roadmap to support adoption.

1119.title: Effects of Abstraction on Selecting Relevant Biological Phenomena for Biomimetic Design
1119.summary: The authors tested whether describing biological phenomena in more abstract terms helps designers pick useful analogies for biology-inspired design without being swayed by familiar words, organisms or preconceived solutions. In two experiments, novice designers chose between or rated biological phenomena whose descriptions had biological nouns replaced with more general terms. Neither experiment showed the expected benefits; instead, the abstraction led designers to latch onto the remaining specific words and made the descriptions harder to understand.

1120.title: The Four-Box Method of Problem Specification and Analogy Evaluation in Biologically Inspired Design
1120.summary: The authors addressed a problem they saw in a biologically inspired design course: interdisciplinary student teams struggled to judge which biological analogue best fits a design problem. They developed a Four-Box method that matches biological analogues to the problem on four dimensions, function, operating environment, constraints and performance criteria, and tried it out in the classroom. Initial results suggested that student designers found the method both useful and easy to use.

1122.title: The Impact of Sustainability on Consumer Preference Judgments of Product Attributes
1122.summary: The authors investigated how knowing a product's environmental impact changes what consumers value in its form, function and price. Using conjoint analysis on single-use spoons, reusable water bottles and washing machines, participants first rated form designs and then made two rounds of form-function-price choices, the second showing life cycle-based environmental impact values for each option. With impact information, functional attributes became more important, form became less important and price slightly less important.

1123.title: Identifying and Categorizing Opportunities for Design for Sustainable User Behavior
1123.summary: The authors developed a way to find where design could steer households toward using less energy, treating any use above the minimum needed for a task as a failure. In a living-laboratory study, participants cooked a simple dish first as usual and then while trying to save energy, with energy use recorded and interviews afterwards. All participants cut their energy use significantly when asked, but did not do so routinely, pointing to opportunities for better awareness and for redesign.

1128.title: Leveraging Mechanical 3D CAD Systems Through Improved Model Quality Based on Best Practices and Rubrics
1128.summary: The authors examined how teaching novice product designers best practices could improve the quality of their 3D CAD models, since current practice does little to enforce quality. They reviewed the dimensions of CAD model quality and ran pilot studies that conveyed best practices through rubrics during CAD training. Rubrics need to be adapted to the concept practised at each stage of training, and the lessons learned are framed as hypotheses for future, statistically powered experiments.

1129.title: Explicit Communication of Geometric Design Intent in CAD: Evaluating Annotated Models in the Context of Reusability
1129.summary: The authors tested whether adding 3D annotations to CAD models, to make the designer's intent explicit, helps others modify and reuse those models. They measured user performance on model alteration tasks in two scenarios: where designers might make wrong modelling assumptions, and where they had to pick the best of several possible solutions. In both scenarios annotated models gave statistically significant benefits, supporting annotation as a way to communicate design intent.

1130.title: Using Human Computation to Assist Biologically Inspired Design: Evaluating a Game-With-a-Purpose
1130.summary: The authors sought a way to collect machine-readable descriptions of biological strategies that is broader than expert-built databases but still accurate, to help designers find biological inspiration. They built the Biology Phenomenon Categorizer, a cooperative online game, and deployed it in a small engineering graduate class where students formed statements about the biological process of cell division. The statements were rated for factual correctness, which revealed measurable indicators of true statements, and areas for improving the game were identified.

1131.title: Crowd-Sourcing the Evaluation of Creativity in Conceptual Design: A Pilot Study

1132.title: A Dual-Process Analysis of Design Idea Generation
1132.summary: The authors applied dual-process theory from psychology, which separates fast intuitive thinking from slow analytical thinking, to understand how each affects the novelty of design ideas. They ran an exploratory pilot design experiment and used retrospective protocol analysis to link ideas to the type of thinking that produced them. Intuitive thinking was associated with higher average novelty up to a point, and an equal balance of intuitive and analytical thinking gave the greatest potential for novelty.

1133.title: Preliminary Sketching and Prototyping: Comparisons in Exploratory Design-and-Build Activities
1133.summary: The authors examined what role sketching plays when designers build quick, preliminary prototypes during hands-on design-and-build activities. They compared three groups, one free to sketch throughout, one allowed to sketch only at the start and one not allowed to sketch, in two rounds using an Erector set and foam core, evaluating prototype performance and sketch quality. Fast, preliminary prototypes proved as useful as sketching for exploring designs of simple mechanisms, though this may differ for complex tasks.

1134.title: Ideation Methods: A First Study on Measured Outcomes With Personality Type
1134.summary: The authors investigated whether a designer's personality type relates to how well they perform with different idea generation methods, with a view to tailoring methods to individuals. They observed designers developing a real product using several ideation methods and correlated the quality, quantity and variety of their ideas with their Myers-Briggs personality types. Personality type and ideation outcomes were significantly correlated, consistent with theory from psychology and business management.

1135.title: Analyzing Requirement Type Influence on Concept Quality and Quantity During Ideation: An Experimental Study
1135.summary: The authors tested whether the type of requirements given to designers affects how many concepts they generate and how good those concepts are. Student groups sketched solutions for a burrito-folding device with either no requirements, functional requirements, non-functional requirements, prioritised mixed requirements or randomly mixed requirements. Groups given non-functional requirements produced more and better-quality concepts than those given functional requirements, and the no-requirements group out-produced the functional-requirements group.

1138.title: Biased Information Passing Between Subsystems Over Time in Complex System Design
1138.summary: The authors studied how subsystem teams in large engineering projects share design information and how biased sharing affects system-level results. They interviewed twelve practitioners at a large aerospace organisation, then modelled the practice of adding conservative "margins" in optimisation simulations with no bias, constant bias and decreasing bias. Biased information passing increased the number of iterations needed and reduced the Pareto optimality of system-level solutions.

1139.title: Cognitive-Based Search Strategies for Complex Bio-Nanotechnology Design Derived Through Symbiotic Human and Agent-Based Approaches
1139.summary: The authors sought to improve how people search for good designs in complex systems, using synthetic muscle-like myosin systems as a test case. They tracked users solving design tasks of three difficulties, turned the behaviours of the best and worst users into strategies tested by computer agents, then gave the best strategies back to new users. Users following the agent-tested strategy, combining one-variable-at-a-time learning with greedy local search, performed significantly better than earlier users.

1141.title: Impact of Requirements Elicitation Activity on Idea Generation: A Designer Study
1141.summary: The authors asked whether having students work out design requirements themselves before generating ideas helps them address those requirements. Senior design students were split into three groups: one given only the problem statement, one given five requirements and one given ten requirements, with the first two asked to elicit requirements first. The group given all ten requirements and no elicitation task addressed requirements best, suggesting elicitation offered little benefit at the concept stage.

1142.title: The Role of Individual Risk Attitudes on the Selection of Creative Concepts in Engineering Design
1142.summary: The authors investigated why designers often reject creative concepts, focusing on personal attitudes towards risk and ambiguity. Nineteen first-year engineering students generated ideas and selected concepts, and their risk aversion and ambiguity aversion were measured. Risk attitudes were related both to creative ability and to the selection of creative concepts, but a student's ability to generate creative ideas was unrelated to their preference for creative ideas during selection.

1143.title: Serious Gaming for Design and Systems Engineering Research
1143.summary: The authors examined whether serious games are a reliable research tool for studying decision-making in design and systems engineering. They built a game around a crewed Mars mission to study the sunk cost effect and compared players' choices with responses to a survey describing the same scenario. Game players fell for the sunk cost effect regardless of treatment while survey respondents in the control did not, suggesting games can induce unrepresentative behaviour.

1146.title: Protocol Analysis: Studying Physical Manipulatives During Conceptual Design
1146.summary: The authors set out to document how individual designers interact with physical objects while generating mechanical concepts. They developed a protocol for recording people's interactions with artifacts and used it to observe three participants individually solving a design problem in a controlled setting. The most common behaviour patterns showed participants learning from or being inspired by handling the physical objects, and the authors also identified ways to improve the protocol and experimental methods.

1147.title: Safety and Usability Design Method Based on Gaps Between Designer and User
1147.summary: The authors aimed to help designers find safety and usability problems that arise when users operate a product differently from what designers expect. They proposed a model of gaps between designers and users and a program, GAP, that simulates operations as state transitions and detects gaps using time intervals. Applied to tractor operations by eight members of the public and four employees of a tractor maker, the method correctly detected potential safety and effectiveness gaps.

1148.title: Quantitative Comparison of High- and Low-Performing Teams in a Design Task Subject to Drastic Changes
1148.summary: The authors studied how engineering teams cope when a design problem changes drastically and unexpectedly partway through. Teams worked on a design task that underwent two large changes in problem formulation, while their design activity was recorded continuously. High-performing teams kept designs simple and explored small regions of the design space thoroughly, whereas low-performing teams produced complex designs with little focused exploration, differences the authors interpret through cognitive load and goal theory.

1149.title: Validity and Predictive Ability of Wilde’s Cognitive Teamology Model to Design Team Outcomes
1149.summary: The author tested whether Wilde's Teamology model, which forms teams based on personality-derived cognitive styles, actually predicts design team results. Myers-Briggs data were collected over five years from more than 661 capstone design students in 120 teams and converted into Teamology cognitive scores. The model explained about 10% of the variation in team outcomes, with the Imagination, Community and Evaluation factors statistically associated with outcomes.

1150.title: Searching for Inspiration: An In-Depth Look at Designers Example Finding Practices
1150.summary: The authors wanted to understand how professional designers search for and collect examples for inspiration, since poorly chosen examples can cause design fixation. They observed 18 professional designers during a 90-minute design task and supplemented this with surveys and interviews. The authors related designers' example-finding behaviour to research on design fixation and drew implications for building better tools to help designers find examples.

1151.title: Using Shape Grammars to Identify Salient Features in Support of Product Family Design
1151.summary: The authors explored whether shape grammars can identify which visual features make products in a family look alike. Survey respondents rated the style similarity of design variants against a baseline, and candidate shape parameters were screened for aesthetic importance with a fractional factorial experiment. Demonstrated on a family of medical ultrasound transducers, the screening was confirmed by a full factorial experiment with practising transducer designers and engineers.

1152.title: The Fuzzy Front End: Concept Development in the Automotive Industry
1152.summary: The authors examined the early, uncertain "fuzzy front end" of product development in the car industry and how it compares with academic definitions. They conducted semi-structured interviews with eleven employees at seven automotive manufacturers. A major challenge was developing concepts that would win internal support, partly because costs and customer benefits were hard to estimate, and the common academic view of the front end missed early work on transformational innovations.

1154.title: Effects of Over-the-Counter Medication Product Family Packaging Design on Knowledge Acquisition and Consumer Preferences
1154.summary: The authors studied how packaging design within over-the-counter medicine product families affects whether consumers choose the right medication. Sixty-four participants took a health literacy test, selected medications to match given symptoms, and rated package labels across two brands and five package designs. Differences in labelling and family packaging design significantly affected how accurately and quickly people chose medications, suggesting packaging could help reduce medication errors.

1156.title: Collaborative Sketching With skWiki: A Case Study
1156.summary: The authors developed skWiki, a web-based tool for collaborative sketching on tablets, and evaluated it both as an ideation aid and as a research tool. They followed an undergraduate design team that used skWiki throughout the concept generation and development phase of a course project. The team's sketches showed ideas being built on both sideways and in depth across members, and skWiki proved effective for studying such collaborative design processes.

1157.title: Analogy Seeded Mind-Maps: Testing of a New Design-by-Analogy Tool
1157.summary: The authors introduced Analogy Seeded Mind-Maps, a method to help designers find solutions by analogy across different domains. Starting from a key function such as "eject part", related words at varying distances from the seed word were placed in a mind-map, and senior engineering students in two studies used them individually and in teams. The method proved useful for generating analogous solutions, with quantity and uniqueness of solutions also examined against word distance.

1159.title: A Novel Method for Providing Global Assessments of Design Concepts Using Single-Word Adjectives and Semantic Similarity
1159.summary: The authors aimed to create a quick way to rate the creativity and feasibility of large numbers of design concepts during concept selection. Their SCAT method has evaluators pick single-word adjectives and uses semantic similarity to score concepts, and it was tested with 10 engineering designers on three design tasks against established rating methods. SCAT ratings could serve as a proxy for assessing design concepts, though modifications could improve its usefulness.

1160.title: Relationship Between Product Aesthetic Subject Preference and Quantified Gestalt Principles
1160.summary: The authors tested whether Gestalt principles, which describe how people visually group shapes, can serve as a measure of a product's aesthetic appeal. In a survey, participants rated their preference for 2-D drawings of car wheel rims designed in pairs with lower and higher Gestalt scores, holding complexity constant within each style. Higher Gestalt increased preference, and designs with different geometry but equal Gestalt were not rated significantly differently.

1161.title: Customer Needs Extraction Using Disability Simulation for Purposes of Inclusive Design
1161.summary: The authors explored whether people without disabilities, wearing a disability simulation suit, can stand in for people with disabilities when gathering customer needs for inclusive products. They collected customer needs on pairs of products that perform the same function, one designed inclusively and one not, and extended earlier work linking need statements to product modules. Only preliminary data were presented, intended to support future inclusive design guidelines.

1162.title: An Investigation on the Inconsistency of Consumer Preferences for Product Appearance: A Case Study of Residential Solar Panels
1162.summary: The authors examined how consistent consumer preferences for product appearance are, using residential solar panels as a case study. About 200 survey respondents rated solar panel designs using visual conjoint analysis, first seeing standalone panels and then panels installed on a roof. Preferences shifted significantly once panels were shown in context, which the authors suggest has implications for how designers uncover user needs.

1163.title: Creation of Empathic Lead Users From Non-Users via Simulated Lead User Experiences
1163.summary: The authors tested whether designers who are not users can be turned into "empathic lead users" through simulated experiences, using lower-limb prosthetics for amputees in developing countries as the case. Participants attended a training session on amputees' needs, especially in Bolivia, then wore a mock prosthetic, and were interviewed before, between and after. These participants identified 95% of the needs of Bolivian lead users and of US users, and doubled the number of latent needs identified.

1167.title: An Unsupervised Deep Learning Model to Discover Visual Similarity Between Sketches for Visual Analogy Support
1167.year_note: Crossref gives 2021; the corpus filename gives 2020
1167.summary: The authors developed a computational method to find sketches with similar shapes to a designer's rough sketch, to inspire visual analogies. They proposed a deep clustering model that learns underlying shape features across many sketch categories and groups sketches at the same time, and evaluated its clustering in different configurations. The method found similar-looking sketches, helped explain visual links between categories, and showed potential for generating visual stimuli for designers.

1169.title: Influence of Conceptual Sketches on Variety, Typology, and Novelty of Elicited Requirements
1169.year_note: Crossref gives 2021; the corpus filename gives 2020
1169.summary: The authors tested whether sketching an early concept before writing design requirements improves those requirements, since students often have solutions in mind before defining the problem. Third- and fourth-year mechanical engineering students generated requirements with or without a preliminary sketch, and the requirements were analysed for variety, type and novelty. Sketching first significantly improved the type and novelty of requirements but not their variety, and identifying key features in the sketch had further influence.

1171.title: How Should We Measure Creativity in Design Studies? A Comparison of Social Science and Engineering Approaches
1171.year_note: Crossref gives 2021; the corpus filename gives 2020
1171.summary: The authors compared the social science and engineering approaches to measuring creativity in design studies, because researchers lack agreement on how to rate the creativity of ideas. They rated nearly 1,000 engineering design ideas with both methods and studied expert raters thinking aloud. The two methods gave similar ratings of idea quality but significantly opposite ratings of novelty, and quasi-experts and experts agreed on novelty but not on quality.
1171.doi_note: papers.json gives 10.1115/1.0001911v (the conference presentation); this is the proceedings paper's DOI, title confirmed by Crossref

1172.title: Mirroring Neurostimulation Outcomes Through Behavioral Interventions to Improve Creative Performance
1172.year_note: Crossref gives 2021; the corpus filename gives 2020
1172.summary: The authors asked whether simple behavioural tasks that engage the same brain regions targeted by neurostimulation could boost creativity, since electrical stimulation raises safety and ethical concerns. Thirty undergraduates did a Stroop task and a finger-tapping task at easy and hard levels, then completed the Alternative Uses Test. Harder tasks led to more ideas and more categories of ideas, with the Stroop task showing the most promise as a creativity intervention.
1172.doi_note: papers.json gives 10.1115/1.0001963v (the conference presentation); this is the proceedings paper's DOI, title confirmed by Crossref

1173.title: Dimensions of Similarity Used to Identify Products As Sources of Analogy
1173.year_note: Crossref gives 2021; the corpus filename gives 2020
1173.summary: The authors explored which kinds of similarity lead designers to pick an existing product as a source of analogy when designing something new. Fifty participants chose useful source products for a target design from five candidates and explained their choices in writing, yielding 2,440 coded instances. At least six dimensions mattered, and working principle, structure and human interaction were more influential than function, previously thought to be the main driver.
1173.doi_note: papers.json gives 10.1115/1.0002188v (the conference presentation); this is the proceedings paper's DOI, title confirmed by Crossref

1174.title: Memory and Idea Generation Applied to Product Repurposing
1174.year_note: Crossref gives 2021; the corpus filename gives 2020
1174.summary: The authors tested whether recalling specific personal memories helps engineers generate ideas, using the problem of repurposing retired wind-turbine blades. Thirty-eight fourth-year engineering students generated ideas for common objects and for wind-turbine blades after either a memory induction or a control induction. After the memory induction, ideas for common objects were more flexible and elaborate, and blade repurposing ideas were more appropriate and feasible.
1174.doi_note: papers.json gives 10.1115/1.0001955v (the conference presentation); this is the proceedings paper's DOI, title confirmed by Crossref

1175.title: The Stakeholder Agreement Metric (SAM): Quantifying Preference Agreement Between Product Stakeholders
1175.year_note: Crossref gives 2021; the corpus filename gives 2020
1175.summary: The authors proposed the Stakeholder Agreement Metric to help design teams make go/no-go decisions when a product must satisfy several stakeholders besides the end user. The metric uses the distance between the best designs implied by each group's preferences, and was compared with the analytical hierarchy process in a case study of a hand tool for informal electronic waste workers in Thailand. The metric's estimate matched later stakeholder satisfaction, while the hierarchy process proved harder to use in practice.

1176.title: The Presence of Culture in Student Designer Perceptions When Making Design Requirements: A Pilot Study
1176.summary: The authors investigated what aspects of target users' culture student designers consider when writing design requirements, since overlooked cultural factors often derail humanitarian engineering projects. In a pilot quasi-experimental study, they compared a control group with a group using a formal method that prompts designers to assess requirements against user culture. The method increased attention to user culture, but the intervention alone did not clearly change the requirements produced.

1178.title: Novice Designers' Approaches to Justifying User Requirements and Engineering Specifications
1178.year_note: Crossref gives 2021; the corpus filename gives 2020
1178.summary: The authors studied how novice designers justify the user requirements and engineering specifications they write for their projects. They analysed the design reports of capstone design teams and coded the justifications given. Teams leaned on sponsor interactions and their own perceptions of user needs rather than data from users, and several specifications had no clear justification, suggesting novices need support tools for this step.
1178.doi_note: papers.json gives 10.1115/1.0001756v (the conference presentation); this is the proceedings paper's DOI, title confirmed by Crossref

1179.title: Sequential Design Decision Making Under the Influence of Competition: A Protocol Analysis
1179.year_note: Crossref gives 2021; the corpus filename gives 2020
1179.summary: The authors investigated how knowing an opponent's past performance affects when contestants in engineering design contests stop searching for better designs. Participants competed against opponents with strong or weak records in a behavioural experiment and were then interviewed about their decisions. People stopped searching on reaching thresholds such as a target quality, a resource budget or a desired improvement, and these thresholds shifted with how competitive they perceived their opponent to be.
1179.doi_note: papers.json gives 10.1115/1.0002010v (the conference presentation); this is the proceedings paper's DOI, title confirmed by Crossref

1180.title: Early-Stage Uncertainty: Effects of Robust Convex Optimization on Design Exploration
1180.year_note: Crossref gives 2021; the corpus filename gives 2020
1180.summary: The authors examined how robust optimization, which builds uncertainty directly into design models, affects how engineers explore designs early on compared with safety factors or Monte Carlo simulation. They reviewed how aerospace models currently handle uncertainty and ran a human-subjects experiment comparing ways of representing it. Robust optimization led to much more efficient exploration, with a typical participant's trade-off curve outperforming the best curves produced using industry-standard methods.
1180.doi_note: papers.json gives 10.1115/1.0001904v (the conference presentation); this is the proceedings paper's DOI, title confirmed by Crossref

1181.title: Measuring Human Learning in Design Space Exploration to Assess Effectiveness of Knowledge Discovery Tools
1181.summary: The authors set out to define and measure what designers learn while exploring a design space, so that knowledge discovery tools can be assessed and compared. Drawing on learning goals from education research, they developed seven measures targeting different kinds of learning and tested them in a human-subject experiment. They examined how consistent and correlated the measures were and discussed implications and issues for using them in future studies.

1182.title: Method Selection in Human-Centered Design Teams: An Examination of Decision-Making Strategies
1182.year_note: Crossref gives 2021; the corpus filename gives 2020
1182.summary: The authors explored why novice design teams choose particular human-centered design methods and what shapes those choices. They built a framework classifying strategies as agent-, outcome- or process-driven and used it to code 297 method selections from three semester-long engineering design courses. Outcome-based strategies were least common, teams shifted from user-focused to product-focused outcomes over time, and strategy explained more variation in method choice than project type.

1183.title: Motivating Sustainable Behavior Using Cognitive Interventions in Product Design
1183.year_note: Crossref gives 2021; the corpus filename gives 2020
1183.summary: The authors tested whether cognitive interventions in product design, such as messages and feedback, can encourage people to use fewer napkins in cafés. They compared positively and negatively framed information and consumption feedback by tracking napkins per transaction, then surveyed 295 people about their reactions. Positive messages produced a short-term reduction and negative messages a longer-term one, feedback had no effect, and each message evoked distinct emotions.

1186.title: Only As Strong As the Strongest Link: The Impact of Individual Team Member Proficiency in Configuration Design
1186.summary: The authors asked whether the most or the least proficient member of a configuration design team has the bigger effect on team performance, since past research focused on team averages. They ran a behavioural study of design teams and used hidden Markov modelling to compare the strategies of members with different proficiency. Teams depended most on their strongest member, who helped them reach performance targets faster and produced simpler designs that teammates then adopted.

1187.title: A Topic Modeling Approach to Study the Impact of Manager Interventions on Design Team Cognition
1187.year_note: Crossref gives 2021; the corpus filename gives 2020
1187.summary: The authors used topic modelling to study how a human process manager's interventions affect what design teams talk and think about while solving a problem. They trained a topic model on the conversations of managed and unmanaged teams from an earlier experiment and compared discussion before and after each intervention. The two kinds of team differed on several topics, and interventions immediately shifted the team's discussion toward the topic of the intervention.

1188.title: Can Design Teams Be Empathically Creative? A Simulation-Based Investigation on the Role of Team Empathy on Concept Generation and Selection
1188.year_note: Crossref gives 2021; the corpus filename gives 2020
1188.summary: The authors investigated how a team's overall level and spread of empathy affect concept generation and selection, since empathy research had focused on individuals. They simulated 13,482 teams of non-interacting brainstormers by statistically resampling a repository of 806 ideas from first-year engineering students. Higher average team empathy improved the generation and selection of unique ideas, while more varied empathy within a team improved the generation of useful ideas.

1189.title: Back and Forth: Using Conversation Analysis to Explore Dialogues of Sharedness of Mental Models
1189.year_note: Crossref gives 2021; the corpus filename gives 2020
1189.summary: The authors examined the different ways design team members come to share mental models, which are known to improve team performance. Using conversation analysis, they studied two teams in a lab as they agreed on a ranked list of design principles and then generated solutions from it. They identified conversational features designers used to build shared understanding and showed how team mental models emerged from patterns in open-ended discussion.
1189.doi_note: papers.json gives 10.1115/1.0002179v (the conference presentation); this is the proceedings paper's DOI, title confirmed by Crossref

1190.title: How Engineering Design Students’ Psychological Safety Impacts Team Concept Generation and Screening Practices
1190.summary: The authors explored how psychological safety, the sense that a team is safe for taking interpersonal risks, affects idea generation and screening in engineering design teams. They studied 53 student teams over 4- and 8-week design projects, measuring the number and quality of ideas and how teams screened concepts. Psychological safety was unrelated to the number of ideas but linked to higher-quality ideas, and safer teams selected a larger share of their teammates' ideas.

1191.title: Paired Computer-Aided Design: The Effect of Collaboration Mode on Differences in Model Quality
1191.year_note: Crossref gives 2021; the corpus filename gives 2020
1191.summary: The authors compared two ways for pairs to collaborate in a fully synchronous computer-aided design (CAD) tool, inspired by research on pair programming. In an experiment, pairs completed CAD tasks either working in parallel or sharing a single control. Shared control produced significantly better, more complete and more consistent models, while parallel work showed a weak trade-off between speed and quality, suggesting the benefits depend on how designers collaborate.

1193.title: Reading the User's Mind: Designers Show High Accuracy in Inferring Design-Related Thoughts and Feelings
1193.year_note: Crossref gives 2021; the corpus filename gives 2020
1193.summary: The authors examined how accurately designers can infer what users think and feel, linking human-centered design to the psychology of understanding others' minds. Twenty-four designers watched recorded needfinding interviews with six users and inferred their thoughts and feelings, which were scored for empathic accuracy. Feelings were inferred somewhat more accurately than thoughts, and designers were consistently more accurate on design-related thoughts and feelings than on unrelated ones.

1194.title: Human Inductive Biases in Design Decision Making
1194.year_note: Crossref gives 2021; the corpus filename gives 2020
1194.summary: The authors set out to identify the built-in assumptions, or inductive biases, that people bring to sequential design search before they have any information. They reanalysed data from several earlier behavioural experiments on how participants search a design space and decide when to stop. Participants' very first choices were not spread evenly across the design space, suggesting that models of designer behaviour should use informed rather than neutral starting assumptions.

1196.title: Development of Spatial Abilities in Engineering Education: An Empirical Study of the Influence of Visualisation Media
1196.summary: The authors tested whether the visualisation media used for sketching and technical drawing tasks affect how much engineering students' spatial abilities improve. Seventy students in a fundamental design engineering class took the Mental Rotation Test before and after the semester, completing individual tasks with media offering different degrees of interaction. All students improved substantially in mental rotation, but the size of the improvement varied considerably with the visualisation media used.

1197.title: From Information to Ideas: How Designers Structure Information to Support Idea Generation
1197.year_note: Crossref gives 2021; the corpus filename gives 2020
1197.summary: The authors investigated how designers organise large amounts of information and how that organisation relates to the ideas they produce. Eight professionals, four software designers and four graphic designers, each spent three hours generating ideas to reduce pedestrian accidents in Nebraska using provided information. Designers structured information in three ways, called clusters, relations and nests, and both their background and their organising strategy shaped the features of their ideas.

1198.title: Evolution of Brain Network Connectivity in the Prefrontal Cortex During Concept Generation Using Brainstorming for a Design Task
1198.year_note: Crossref gives 2021; the corpus filename gives 2020
1198.summary: The authors explored how activity in the brain's prefrontal cortex changes over time while engineers brainstorm design concepts. Ten graduate engineering students brainstormed for a design task while their brain activation was measured, and graph theory was used to map changing network connectivity. Network centrality shifted between the right, middle and left prefrontal cortex, consistent with designers alternating between divergent and convergent thinking.

1200.title: Effects of Locus of Control Personality Trait on Team Performance in Cooperative Engineering Design Tasks
1200.year_note: Crossref gives 2021; the corpus filename gives 2020
1200.summary: The authors examined how the locus of control personality trait, whether people feel they control outcomes themselves, affects designer behaviour and team performance. Twelve pairs grouped by matching or mixed locus of control each completed six simplified cooperative parameter design tasks, yielding 72 data points. Pairs with mixed traits worked less efficiently, while pairs with similar traits performed better, echoing findings from outside engineering design.

1201.title: Advisory and Adaptive Communication Improves Trust in Autonomous Vehicle and Pedestrian Interaction
1201.year_note: Crossref gives 2021; the corpus filename gives 2020
1201.summary: The author investigated whether the way autonomous vehicles communicate with pedestrians can build appropriate trust, which is needed for the technology to be adopted and used safely. A preliminary online study tested informative, advisory and commanding message styles, delivered once or adaptively, during pedestrian crossing decisions. Advisory messages raised trust when the vehicle expected the pedestrian to cross, advisory and commanding messages both helped when it did not, and adaptive communication improved trust significantly when crossing was expected.

1202.title: Analysis of Virtual Communication Within Engineering Design Teams and its Impact on Team Effectiveness
1202.year_note: Crossref gives 2021; the corpus filename gives 2020
1202.summary: The authors studied how engineering design teams use the messaging platform Slack, to understand team communication and coordination. They analysed more than 400,000 messages from 32 teams of 17 to 20 students over four years of a three-month senior product design course, looking at social networks, emoji use and topics. Leaders held more central network positions, stronger teams had lower average centrality and used emojis more often, and emojis came mostly from leaders and well-connected members.

1203.title: Investigating the Challenges of Crowdsourcing for Engineering Design: An Interview Study With Organizations of Different Sizes
1203.year_note: Crossref gives 2021; the corpus filename gives 2020
1203.summary: The authors set out to identify the challenges of using crowdsourcing for engineering design and whether they differ with the size of the organization, since small and medium enterprises have lagged in adopting it. They interviewed industry professionals from five organizations of varying sizes. The interviews revealed key challenges in applying crowdsourcing, and the authors suggested support mechanisms for smaller firms and directions for further research.

1204.title: Creating a Design for Inspectability Framework: Investigating DfAM Heuristics for Inspection Technologies
1204.year_note: Crossref gives 2021; the corpus filename gives 2020
1204.summary: The authors developed a Design for Inspectability worksheet to help designers consider early on whether additively manufactured parts can be inspected for quality, since complex printed geometries are hard and costly to check. The worksheet lets designers assess whether a part can be inspected after production and guides later design iterations. A controlled laboratory study suggested that using the worksheet affected design outcomes.

1205.title: The Value of Prototyping: An Investigation of the Relationship Between the Costs of Prototyping, Perceived Value, and Design Outcome
1205.summary: The authors explored how the time and money invested in prototypes relate to designers' perceptions of their value and to final design outcomes. They studied 32 teams of mechanical engineering students over a 16-week design project. Effective early prototyping uncovered knowledge and reduced uncertainty, leaving more time for testing later, but the cost of a prototype was not significantly related to either its perceived value or the final design outcome.

1206.title: Defining Function: How Student Definitions Compare to Literature to Function Model Generation
1206.year_note: Crossref gives 2021; the corpus filename gives 2020
1206.summary: The authors examined how mechanical engineering students define the concept of function and how their definitions relate to the function models they build. As part of a larger protocol study, they compared student definitions with those in the literature using topical analysis and with the size and completeness of students' models. Student definitions tended to focus on a single topic, certain terms were linked to larger or better-rated models, and building a model influenced how students defined function.

1207.title: “You Cannot Test It Before It Is Verified. When It Is Verified You Cannot Change It”: Prototyping Challenges in Industry
1207.summary: The authors investigated what challenges industry practitioners face when prototyping, what opportunities they see, and what trends are shaping prototyping. They gathered data from eight practitioners in Danish industry through a small survey and focus group discussions, then analysed the content qualitatively. They identified 23 challenges, 15 opportunities and 5 trends, including making decisions from few, limited prototypes, gaps between virtual and physical prototypes, and medical regulations.

1210.title: Analyzing the Characteristics of Cognitive-Assistant-Facilitated Ideation Groups
1210.year_note: Crossref gives 2021; the corpus filename gives 2020
1210.summary: The authors compared brainstorming groups led by human facilitators with groups led by a cognitive assistant, an AI tool using natural-language processing that could stand in when no trained facilitator is available. They coded co-located sessions with Interaction Dynamics Notation and used hidden Markov models to identify group states. Human facilitation was associated with interruptions and responses to them and a more equal share of speaking time, while the cognitive assistant was associated with deviations and silence.
