1211.title: Brand Affiliation Through Curved and Angular Surfaces Using the Example of the Vehicle Front
1211.year_note: Crossref gives 2021; the corpus filename gives 2020
1211.summary: The authors investigated whether curved versus angular surfaces, not just contours, can signal which brand a product belongs to, using car fronts as the example. They designed vehicle fronts varying face-like headlight and air-intake contours and surface types, then surveyed 150 people online about their impressions and brand affiliation. Both contours and surfaces could convey brand affiliation, and two user groups emerged that judged brand affiliation differently.
1211.doi_note: papers.json gives 10.1115/1.0005308v (the conference presentation); this is the proceedings paper's DOI, title confirmed by Crossref

1334.title: Back to the Drawing Board?: Computer-Mediated Communication Tools for Engineers
1334.year_note: Crossref gives 1990; the corpus filename gives 1991
1334.summary: The authors explored what information engineers involved in product design and manufacture would exchange through computer-mediated communication tools such as electronic mail and computer conferencing. In an exploratory study, they examined the nature and timing of the information exchanged by participants in an engineering design and manufacturing process. Tools supporting asynchronous, written exchanges appeared likely to be of little use to these engineers, and would need substantial augmentation before being widely adopted.

1337.title: The Use of Function and Form When Reading Mechanical Engineering Drawings by Experts and Non-Experts
1337.summary: The authors investigated how design experience shapes the function and form information people use when reasoning about mechanical engineering drawings, to inform intelligent CAD systems. They recorded what expert mechanical designers, graduate students and novices said while reading 13 line drawings, and analysed the descriptions for links between function and form. A discriminant analysis showed both similarities and differences in the design features each group relied on when reasoning about the drawings.

1340.title: Models of Visual Thinking by Novice Designers
1340.year_note: Crossref gives 1990; the corpus filename gives 1994
1340.summary: The authors examined visual thinking, in which spatial, numerical and descriptive information are combined to realise a design idea, with a focus on freehand sketching. In a series of experiments, they studied how novice engineering designers and industrial designers used sketches in their design work. They identified functional, geometric and pictorial sketches tied to stages of concept development, and proposed a model in which sketching is an interface, and potential barrier, between thinking and the physical world.

1342.title: A Cognitive Approach to the Analysis of Design Processes
1342.summary: The authors aimed to give design theory a scientific basis by proposing "design experiments", in which designers' sessions are recorded and analysed. They ran two kinds of experiment, one using conventional protocol analysis and one using a new CAD-like system that precisely records drawing, and analysed the data by extracting the knowledge used and by turning protocols into a semantic network. The network approach let them track what designers paid attention to and how that focus shifted during design.

1344.title: Recognizing Novel Uses for Familiar Plans
1344.summary: The author set out to model a common pattern in analogical design, where a designer gets stuck, puts the problem aside and later realises that a familiar plan can solve it in a new way. A computer system was described that uses a causal case memory to check the side effects and preconditions of incoming events against goals that were previously blocked. The system provides a mechanism by which design systems can recognise situations that help achieve earlier unmet goals.

1346.title: The Information Requests of Mechanical Design Engineers
1346.summary: The authors examined what information mechanical design engineers look for that standard design documentation fails to provide. They studied practising engineers making modifications to existing designs, paying close attention to the questions they asked and the conjectures they formed and tried to confirm or refute. They produced a taxonomy of these questions and conjectures, and proposed an intelligent CAD system that would capture, structure and replay this design information.

1348.title: Design History Knowledge Representation and its Basic Computer Implementation
1348.summary: The authors set out to record the reasoning behind a product's design, because final drawings and notes often cannot answer later questions from manufacturing staff or redesign teams. They described a Mechanical Design History that records the constraints developed and decisions made from initial specification to detailed design, along with its basic computer implementation. The history lets design, management and manufacturing staff query not only the final drawings but the rationale behind each object in a design.

1360.title: Identifying the Fundamental Geometric Attributes of Design: An Application of Distinctive Feature Theory
1360.summary: The authors looked for a basic set of geometric attributes that designers use to describe mechanical designs, by analogy with the distinctive features of spoken language. Five mechanical designers read and analysed thirteen engineering drawings of varying complexity, and the geometric attributes in their verbal descriptions were grouped by cluster analysis. Fifteen attributes were enough to cluster the 61 design features in the drawings, offering insights for designing human-machine interfaces for CAD.

1367.title: Evaluation of Group Design in Engineering
1367.summary: The author built a computer-based group design system (GDS) to study engineering design done in groups, which is hard to observe because of simultaneous input, communication and management. Three groups of engineering designers used the system, and observations covered management style, communication, the sequence of steps leading to a conceptual design decision, and member involvement. Systematic procedures appeared to encourage more equal participation, decisions less driven by individual choice, and a flatter authority hierarchy.

1370.title: Cumulative Results of Concept Generation by Individuals in a Mechanical Design Class
1370.summary: The authors studied how well individual students in a senior mechanical engineering design class generated concepts, to provide measures for comparing concept generation methods. Sixty-five students took two tests, with concepts defined using a categorisation scheme from Pahl and Beitz and scores standardised by the concepts the whole sample identified. Between sixty and seventy percent of concepts were found by fewer than ten percent of students, suggesting groups could generate more concepts by accepting members' uncommon ideas.

1372.title: Accelerating the Iterative Process in Design: An Experimental Evaluation of a Computer Based Expert Advisor
1372.summary: The authors tested whether a computer-based Expert Advisor System actually helps a knowledgeable designer reach results faster in a complex, trial-and-error design search. The task was adjusting the parameters of a discrete event simulation of a manufacturing system until it met given design specifications, a process widely seen as lengthy and tedious. They used designed experiments in which human subjects performed such tasks with and without the Expert Advisor.

1391.title: Quantification of Operator Perceived Vibrations for a Consumer Product Design
1391.summary: The authors needed a quantitative measure of how operators feel vibration while designing a new line of rear-engine riding lawn mowers. They devised a Goodness of Vibration factor, based on frequency weighting at the steering wheel, footrests and seat, and used it alongside spectrum analysis, modal analysis and finite element analysis. The approach produced a comfort-optimised mower and was presented as a generic process that could guide the design of other consumer power equipment.

1393.title: The Comparison of the Reliability of Three Psychometric Scales for Measuring Design Quality
1393.summary: The authors developed three subjective scales for judging the quality of design solutions, each using a different strategy to help the evaluator, because criteria such as aesthetics cannot be measured objectively. They ran an experiment comparing how reliable judgements made with each scale were over time, with a view to evaluating design tools and formalising concept evaluation. One of the scales proved unreliable, while the other two were reliable.

1394.title: Subjective Design Evaluation With Multiple Attributes
1394.year_note: Crossref gives 1990; the corpus filename gives 1991
1394.summary: The author presented a formal method for evaluating design alternatives during iterative design and redesign that reflects the decision maker's subjective preferences. Deterministic multiattribute utility analysis compared the overall value of alternative designs across several performance characteristics, and sensitivity analysis showed how a design should be modified to increase its value. The method was applied with 6 automotive companies in the United States and Europe in a case study of materials selection and design.

1414.title: Analogical Saturation and Affordance in Ideation
1414.summary: The authors tested whether showing designers more inspirational images, and giving them more boxes to sketch ideas in, would change how many ideas they produced and how detailed they were. In a controlled study, 318 design students brainstormed for 15 minutes on 8-cell or 20-cell sheets, with no images, six fixed images, or six new images every minute. More cells led to more ideas, and a continuous stream of new images produced both more ideas and more detailed ones.

1415.title: Understanding Design Fixation in Generative Artificial Intelligence
1415.summary: The authors examined why generative AI tends to produce similar, less novel design ideas, viewing the problem through the lens of design fixation. In an experimental study with ten designers, they looked at how fixation shows up in the design features produced by text- and image-generating models, and how designers noticed and responded to it. They recommend adopting this AI design fixation perspective in creativity research and when refining AI-based creativity support tools.

1417.title: The Development and Analysis of Knowledge Networks Within Engineering Design Experts
1417.summary: The authors set out to map the mental knowledge structures that experienced engineering designers draw on when exploring a design problem. They captured each practitioner's knowledge network through semi-structured interviews and a mind-mapping exercise, then used network analysis to examine the graphs, their properties and growth, and the effect of years of experience. The results shed light on how practitioners approach problems and how gathering information and reflecting on their mind maps change their mental models.

1418.title: An Explainable Artificial Intelligence Framework for Leveraging Large Language Models in Early-Stage Product Design
1418.summary: The authors evaluated how well large language models support early-stage design and proposed a way to make their suggestions easier to understand and trust. They compared AI and human solutions using psychology-based creativity tests, then built a framework combining interactive clustering, semantic distance maps and feature attribution, and ran a preliminary comparison against a standard AI workflow. AI produced more but less original ideas, and the explainable approach appeared to help designers filter and refine AI concepts.

1419.title: Musical Playlists to Improve the Ideation Environment: An Exploratory Study
1419.summary: The authors explored whether background music affects idea generation, since the ideation environment has received little research attention. Participants generated ideas while listening to classical, pop or video game playlists or no music, and their ideas were evaluated for quantity, diversity and creativity. Participants produced the most ideas with, and preferred, the pop playlist, while the video game playlist led to ideas they rated as most creative and diverse.

1423.title: Influence of AI Use on Creativity in a Speculative Design Process
1423.summary: The authors investigated how using AI affects the creativity of ideas in speculative design, where engineering and creative-writing studies disagree on whether AI raises or lowers novelty. Experts rated 120 ideas from a professional Futures Wheel activity that were made by humans, by humans using AI as a tool, or by AI alone. AI-involved ideas were rated better crafted, novelty did not differ, and AI-only ideas covered a narrower design space.

1424.title: A Real-Time Automatic Interaction Dynamics Notation Communication Analysis System
1424.summary: The authors set out to automate Interaction Dynamics Notation, a framework for analysing how design team members interact that normally requires slow manual coding. They built a system that combines automatic speech recognition with a large language model to assign notation symbols in real time, and tested it during a NASA design sprint. It agreed with human coders 80.3% of the time, similar to agreement between humans, though it struggled with context-dependent moments such as humour and idea blocking.

1428.title: AI Judges in Design: Statistical Perspectives on Achieving Human Expert Equivalence With Vision-Language Models
1428.summary: The authors developed a statistical framework to test whether AI vision-language models can rate early design sketches as well as human experts, whose ratings are slow, costly and sometimes inconsistent. They applied it to four AI judges using different prompting techniques, rating uniqueness, creativity, usefulness and drawing quality, and to three trained novices. The best AI judge, which used text and image examples with reasoning, reached expert-level agreement on uniqueness and drawing quality and matched or beat the novices.

1429.title: Towards a Theory Driven Foundational Model for Design: Rethinking Requirement Elicitation for Special Needs
1429.summary: The authors examined how designers gather requirements for assistive devices for children with special needs, who often cannot express their needs. They tested an existing support tool, the Master List of Requirements, through a validation study with design and clinical experts. Experts disagreed on how sound the listed requirements were and how to prioritise them, noting that requirements are context-specific, so the authors proposed a foundational model built on an extended knowledge ontology to capture implicit needs.

1430.title: Leveraging the Wizard of Oz Method for Stimulating Design: Benefits and Challenges From an Application Case Study
1430.summary: The authors assessed the Wizard of Oz method, in which hidden people secretly simulate a technology that does not yet exist, as a way to study emerging design tools. In a case study, wizards simulated an AI design assistant that responded to designers' sketches across 17 sessions of an hour and a half each. The simulation worked well, with good timing and content and positive designer reactions, though wizard workload and ethics posed challenges, and the authors offer recommendations.

1431.title: Cognitive Demands and Individual Differences in Product Similarity Judgements: A Context-Dependent Model
1431.summary: The authors tested the common research assumption that judging how similar two products are is quick and intuitive for people. They ran a repeated-measures experiment in which participants rated pairs of products that were similar in appearance, in function, or neither, collecting more than 7,000 ratings. Judging appearance similarity took less mental effort, but judgements of functional similarity were more accurate, which the authors attribute to a mental schema they call the functionality context schema.

1432.title: A Multi-Player Educational Game for Teaching Solver-Aware Systems Architecting (SASA) Heuristics
1432.summary: The authors built a multiplayer web game to teach rules of thumb for solver-aware systems architecting, which means splitting a complex system design problem and deciding whether experts, crowds or specialists should solve each part. They piloted the game with 30 participants, who learned the basic concepts and then tackled increasingly difficult architecting problems. By the end, all participants showed acceptable command of the heuristics for system-level trade-offs, suggesting the game supports higher-order learning.

1434.title: Speaking of Users: Assessing the Frequency, Consistency, and Depth of User-Related Internal Communication of Strong and Weak Novice Engineering Design Teams
1434.summary: The authors explored whether student design teams' internal chat could show instructors how well teams engage with potential users. They analysed 251,744 Slack messages from 16 strong and 16 weak teams in a senior product design course, tracking mentions of users and applying topic modelling. Strong teams discussed users more consistently over the semester, all teams talked about users most during convergent phases, and strong teams linked users to process topics while weak teams linked them to tasks.

1435.title: Decoding Conflict: Linguistic Markers of Disagreement in Hackathon Design Teams
1435.summary: The authors studied how the language design teams use changes during conflict, focusing on fast-paced hackathons where disagreement is common. They coded conflict episodes in transcripts from two hackathon teams, one of strangers and one of existing teammates, and compared conflict and non-conflict talk using the LIWC text analysis tool. Conflict talk showed less negative emotion and less prosocial language, and sentence complexity and cohesion differed depending on whether teammates already knew each other.

1436.title: The Impact of Design Representation on Equal Contribution In Engineering Design Teams
1436.summary: The authors asked whether the type of design representation a team works with affects how equally its members contribute. Teams worked with CAD models, written descriptions or hand sketches, and the researchers measured each member's speaking time, word count and turns taken. Contrary to expectations, there were no statistically significant differences between conditions, suggesting the choice of representation does not change how evenly team members participate.

1437.title: Impact of Team Size on Requirements Variety
1437.summary: The authors investigated how team size affects the range of design requirements that engineering students come up with. In an experiment, 1,208 first-year students were organised into 378 teams of one, three or six members, wrote requirements for a design problem, and had their requirements sorted into seventeen categories such as geometry, safety and cost. Larger teams spread their requirements across more categories and covered the most common categories more fully.

1438.title: How Personal Sense of Power Influences Concept Selection of AI-Generated Designs
1438.summary: The authors examined whether a person's sense of power affects how they evaluate and choose among AI-generated designs. In two experiments with bike helmet concepts, 23 participants rated designs labelled as human- or AI-generated, and 66 participants rated AI concepts after being put in a high, neutral or low sense of power. Labelling designs as AI-generated had no effect and power had mixed effects, suggesting the link between power and concept selection depends on context.

1439.title: Impact of Team Size on Requirements Completeness
1439.summary: The authors investigated whether team size affects how complete the design requirements written by engineering students are. In an experiment, 1,208 first-year students were grouped into 378 teams of one, three or six members, documented requirements for a design problem, and had their requirements analysed by parts of speech. Individuals leaned on objects and modifiers, while teams of three and six used more modal terms and target values, suggesting collaboration turns vague wording into measurable requirements.

1440.title: Shaping Dynamic Design Capabilities (DDC) in the Public Sector: Insights From Innovation Practices
1440.summary: The authors examined how public-sector organisations build dynamic design capabilities, the ability to use design to sense and act on change, which has mostly been studied in private companies. They interviewed 15 professionals in innovation and development departments of municipalities, governing bodies and ministries in the Netherlands and Sweden. These capabilities were still underdeveloped but emerging, and the authors identified six, including building a design culture, cross-department collaboration and strategic stakeholder engagement.

1441.title: Designing Complex Socio-Technical Systems for Participation: Community Engagement in Utility-Scale Solar
1441.summary: The authors investigated how developers of large grid-connected solar projects make decisions and engage with local communities, treating these projects as complex socio-technical systems. They conducted semi-structured interviews with five solar developers to identify key decision points, interaction patterns and barriers to including community views. Landowners and local officials dominated decisions while neighbours and the wider public had limited roles, and developers kept engagement cautious to manage risk, leaving room for participatory design approaches.

1444.title: Redesigning Engineering Design Tools to Center Social Impact
1444.summary: The authors tested whether redesigning a common engineering design tool, the Pugh Design Specifications, could get students to think more about the social and ethical effects of their designs. Forty-two students were randomly split between the original tool and a version emphasising social and ethical aspects, and tackled a design challenge set in a local context. Students using the redesigned tool engaged more deeply with the problem and said it helped them consider social and ethical issues.

1445.title: Bringing Justice to Design: How Researchers and Practitioners View and Incorporate Justice Into Design
1445.summary: The authors set out to learn how researchers and practitioners in the design theory and methodology community think about and include social justice in their work. They ran a special session on design justice at the 2024 International Design Engineering Technical Conferences and qualitatively analysed participants' responses. Participants discussed handling power dynamics, creating teaching materials and centring community experience, and both groups wanted stronger links between research and practice.

1446.title: From Dismissal to Adoption: Examining and Visualizing Stakeholder Perspective-Taking in Design
1446.summary: The authors studied how designers take community stakeholders' viewpoints into account when making design decisions. Seven participants in three teams were given six stakeholders' perspectives and had 30 minutes to propose a solution, and the recorded sessions were analysed. The researchers found 89 instances of perspective-taking, ranked on six levels from dismissal to full adoption, and introduced graphical 'signatures' that showed clear differences between teams and individuals.

1449.title: Human-Machine Collaboration for Coordinating Design Customization and Production Systems
1449.summary: The authors aimed to speed up machine setup for customised products, which relies on operators' trial and error and can take up to 30% of production time. They developed a method that captures operators' implicit know-how using SHAP explanation values and uses it to guide Bayesian optimisation, and tested it on roll-forming of customised HVAC parts. The method needed 14.6% fewer trials than human experts and 76.7% fewer than standard Bayesian optimisation, with much more consistent results.

1451.title: Investigating How Engineers Use Computer-Aided Design Versus Pen-and-Paper for Conceptual Design – A Methodology Review and Mixed-Method Pilot Study
1451.summary: The authors set out to design a sound way to compare how CAD and pen-and-paper affect creativity in conceptual design, a question that remains unresolved. They reviewed the main methodological challenges and built an experiment combining creativity tests such as the Torrance Tests with EEG brain recordings and eye-tracking, using an IKEA Hacking Task adapted for both tools. The resulting methodology offers a blueprint for future studies of how engineers interact with design tools.

1452.title: Human-Gen AI Co-Design: Exploring Factors Impacting Trust Calibration
1452.summary: The authors explored what makes designers' trust in a generative AI system rise or fall while they generate ideas with it, since well-calibrated trust is key to using such tools effectively. They analysed 12 hours of think-aloud co-design sessions with a custom image-generating AI that took text and sketch prompts, coding every trust-related moment. They identified 23 factors forming a complex network that affects trust, offering guidance for designing AI systems that build trust faster.

1453.title: Opportunities and Challenges in Using Large Language Models As Interviewees for User Needs Elicitation in Design Research
1453.summary: The authors examined whether large language models can stand in for real people in user interviews, a slow but vital design step. They compared real interviews with simulated ones from language models, with and without demographic details, extracted themes with three AI tools, and had human reviewers cluster them into user needs. The AI interviewees relied heavily on the questions asked and could not flag irrelevant topics, but they surfaced some areas worth checking with real users.

1454.title: Designing Trust: How System-Level Design Attributes Shape AI-Assisted Design Ideation
1454.summary: The authors investigated how the design of an AI chatbot affects users' trust when it helps them generate design ideas. They built the AI Design Assistant (AIDA) and ran a controlled experiment varying its appearance, performance and empathetic behaviour, supplemented by conjoint analysis of user preferences. Performance and empathy both increased trust, empathy improved users' views of the system even when performance was low, and users' initial trust and age also shaped how trust developed.

1456.title: Facilitating Identification of Ergonomic User Needs Through AI-Assisted Observation
1456.summary: The authors developed an AI tool to make observing users faster and less biased when identifying ergonomic needs early in design. The tool uses computer vision, including pose estimation and object segmentation, to analyse videos of people's posture and object use for signs of physical discomfort, and was evaluated in a human-subject experiment. It did not change the number or types of needs found, but it made the process more detailed and efficient and increased participants' confidence.

1460.title: An Empirical Study Measuring the Effects of Generative AI on Early-Stage Engineering Design and Neurocognition
1460.summary: The authors investigated how using generative AI early in a design task affects later design work and the brain effort involved. Sixty engineering undergraduates identified constraints for redeveloping a campus site, either alone or with generative AI, and then all developed concepts without AI while their brain activity was measured. The AI-assisted group found more constraints and later produced more sustainability-related concepts, and showed lower mental effort in a brain region linked to abstract thinking.

1461.title: Simulating Design Theory Using LLM Agents: A Case Study of C-K Theory
1461.summary: The authors explored whether computer simulation, usually used for analysis, could help develop design theory itself. Using C-K design theory as a case study, they built a simulation of agents powered by large language models that followed the theory's wording and framework, and evaluated the results qualitatively and quantitatively. Concept-to-concept transitions dominated and idea diversity declined across conditions, pointing to gaps in C-K theory and showing that design theories can be simulated.

1478.title: Understanding Complex Sketch Recognition Strategies for Intelligent Sketch-Based Design Tools

1497.title: A Designer’s Spreadsheet
1497.summary: The authors observed that many designers use spreadsheets for preliminary parametric design calculations because they are flexible and easy to use, even though commercial spreadsheets were built for finance and accounting. They proposed a fundamentally different kind of spreadsheet for preliminary parametric design, describing its features and the theoretical basis for implementing it. They also reported the results of preliminary tests with users.

1505.title: Testing of a Relative Comparison Method for Evaluating Design Concept Alternatives
1505.summary: The authors compared two methods in a software tool for assessing design concept alternatives early in design, one using relative comparisons and one using absolute ratings. They evaluated both methods for reliability, sensitivity and validity, building on earlier work showing that the relative comparison method was easier to use. The relative comparison method did not perform as well as the absolute rating method on reliability and validity.

1506.title: A Study of the Information Handling Behavior of Designers During Conceptual Design
1506.summary: The authors examined design from an information perspective, aiming to understand how designers generate, access and analyse information so that new tools can fit their technical and social work. They ran an experimental study of conceptual design using the verbal protocol method. They explored a measure of the amount of information designers handle and presented a framework for analysing designers' information handling behaviour.

1509.title: Testing Design Methodology Through Task Performance
1509.summary: The authors tested design methodology in practice, since industry often dismisses it as too abstract despite its acceptance at universities. At the Technical University of Berlin, 13 mechanical engineers performed the same design task in a laboratory, seven with conventional tools and six with the KALEIT design system, while being videotaped and assessed for stress and strain. The results helped answer criticism of methodology and yielded specifications for improving design methods.

1511.title: Integrating the Results of a Laboratory Study Into the Development of a System for the Support of Simultaneous Engineering
1511.summary: The authors described a system being developed at the Technical University of Berlin to support simultaneous engineering, including distributed work and computer-based communication. They drew on a laboratory study of stress and strain during CAD design work, in which engineers' heart rates were recorded and they reviewed videotapes of their most strained moments. Building in the requirements found in that study was intended to make the software more useful in practice and better meet users' expectations.

1516.title: An Exploration of Engineering Learning
1516.summary: The authors explored how students learn engineering, especially how they develop engineering intuition, noting that curricula teach design and analysis in separate classes. They developed "synalysis exercises" that combine problem formulation, analysis and synthesis, and used video analysis to see how students applied formal knowledge, how they learned and the social context of learning. Combining dissimilar activities prompted students to ask questions and supplied resources for answering them, and the exercises showed promise for assessment.

1522.title: Non-Intrusive Protocol Study of Design Idea Generation
1522.summary: The authors studied how designers generate ideas, pairing two designers so that their natural conversation replaced the more intrusive method of one person thinking aloud. They developed a framework for analysing the mental processes of idea generation, including identifying activity objects, building state diagrams and statistically analysing interaction densities. The role of experience and analogies in idea generation was identified, and although the data were limited, the approach could be used in future experiments.

1527.title: Analyzing Inter and Intra Group Information Exchanges in Conceptual Collaborative Design
1527.summary: The authors developed a technique to study information exchanges within and between groups during the conceptual stage of collaborative design, which no existing technique tracked. Adapting sense-making theory to engineering design, they transcribed, labelled and interpreted session records to map information seeking, help received and decisions over time. In the first session, most needs arose in establishing the knowledge base and identifying the design process, with a strong need for exchanges within and between groups.

1535.title: Critical Thinking: Evolution of a Freshman Graphics Course
1535.summary: The authors reworked the freshman engineering graphics course at Santa Clara University to use graphic communication as a way into the design process, aiming to build students' critical thinking. Drawing on theories of students' intellectual development, they added a small design project to the course and refined their teaching over three years. Integrating critical thinking turned the course into their own iterative design process for developing a more effective teaching method.

1550.title: Mathematical Resolution of MBTI Creativity Data Into Personality Type Components
1550.summary: The author proposed a way to make Myers-Briggs Type Indicator (MBTI) scores easier for engineers to interpret, as part of understanding people in design teams. Each set of four MBTI scores was treated as a vector and resolved along new axes pointing toward personality types such as "Strategist", supported by simple word labels. The method was used to analyse results from two ASEE faculty workshops on creativity in design education, which showed a statistically significant improvement in a creativity measure.

1563.title: Manufacturability: Metrics and Perceptions
1563.summary: The authors benchmarked how Sun Microsystems applied design for manufacture and assembly (DFMA) on two of its computer workstations. They applied standard DFMA metrics and indirect process metrics, and interviewed development team members about how manufacturable they thought each product was. The two products were similar, but perceptions did not always match the analysis, and perceptions strongly influenced design decisions when DFMA metrics were not readily available.

1569.title: Elementary Education and Engineering Design: Concrete Experiences in Mathematics and Science
1569.summary: The authors presented DTEACh, a program started in 1992 that uses hands-on engineering design lessons to teach integrated mathematics and science in elementary schools. They focused on its two-part teacher preparation program, describing a new teaching model, the engineering and design fundamentals it covers, and an evaluation of the program. Teachers became more confident and better equipped to teach mathematics, science and engineering principles.

1570.title: Modeling the Information Access Methods of Engineering Designers
1570.summary: The authors sought to understand how engineering designers access the design information they need, given growing information overload. They developed Information Access Diagrams, based on observations of designers in practice and the IDEF1X modelling technique, and applied them in twenty case studies. The diagrams showed the routes designers took to information across different kinds of design work, such as original, adaptive and variant design, and led to recommendations for future research.

1571.title: Understanding Design Information Handling Behavior Using Time and Information Measure
1571.summary: The authors set out to characterise how designers handle information during conceptual design, so that tools could cut the time designers spend dealing with it. They ran six verbal protocol experiments and sorted information handling by activity, descriptor, subject class, level of detail and level of abstraction, measuring each with a design information measure. The insights gained were intended to guide the development of computational tools that improve the conceptual design process.

1584.title: Understanding Emotion in Sound
1584.summary: The authors aimed to understand the emotional messages in a speaker's voice, which listeners can grasp regardless of language and which matter for collaboration. They distinguished truly emotional expressions from those meant to convey feelings to others, and analysed speech sounds using the cepstrum method. Preliminary work showed that anger could be extracted from sound and characterised by its pitch frequency and amplitude variation.

1588.title: ELK: A Method for Eliciting Knowledge From Customers
1588.summary: The authors developed ELK, a method for eliciting customers' requirements on the issues a design team faces, because teams need clearer insight into customer expectations when defining a product. The method combined a taxonomy of design issues organised around customer needs with a knowledge elicitation technique used in building expert systems. An experimental study compared ELK with a traditional qualitative marketing research strategy.

1589.title: Set-Based Concurrent Engineering and Toyota
1589.summary: The authors presented a paradigm for concurrent engineering, which they call set-based design, that explains apparent paradoxes in Toyota's product development strategy. They drew on interviews at U.S. and Japanese automakers and suppliers, including two in-depth case studies. Toyota made little use of commonly cited elements such as co-located, dedicated teams, yet its seemingly inefficient process made sense under set-based design, and the authors discussed the paradigm's potential benefits.

1593.title: Transforming Design Practice in a Small Manufacturing Enterprise
1593.summary: The authors described the in-house design style of a small, innovative Australian company making award-winning hydraulic cylinders, since small firms are largely ignored in design research. With help from the University of Queensland, the company adopted more formal design methods, including quality function deployment, during a three-year product development project. The change did not follow a linear model of technology transfer but a cycle of shared learning and mutual discovery across practice, research and teaching.

1596.title: A Method for the Study of Information Use Profiles for Design Engineers
1596.summary: The authors studied how designers at two aerospace companies organise and use technical information, because computer-based design information systems need to rest on that understanding. They proposed Design Information Profiles and gathered them through structured interviews and workplace observation of ten engineers at different design stages and in different styles of workgroup, plus an audit of their personal and group information stores. Designers in different contexts differed markedly in how much personal, local group and company-wide information they used.

1597.title: The Relationships Between Data, Information and Knowledge Based on a Preliminary Study of Engineering Designers

1623.title: Facilitating Tacit Knowledge Capture and Reuse in Conceptual Design Activities
1623.summary: The authors wanted to understand where design knowledge is created during conceptual design, because the reasoning behind many early decisions is never recorded. They carried out an empirical study of design activity to test whether concept generation happens mostly in informal media such as brainstorming sessions and conversations. The study supported this, showing that ideas emerge where capture tools are weakest, and the authors described Recall, a computer system for capturing and indexing informal media so it can be reused.

1626.title: Educational Interactive Multimedia Software: Can it Effectively Teach Engineering Concepts?
1626.summary: The authors asked whether interactive multimedia software can effectively teach engineering concepts, using a course module on DC motors and motorized systems. The module combined the software with lectures and a design project, and pre- and post-tests plus preference questionnaires measured what students learned and from which resources. The module succeeded and the software contributed to that success; it was especially effective for female students, and four student preference groups responded differently to the teaching techniques.

1629.title: Clarifying the Fuzzy Front End of New Product Development: Teaching Engineering and Industrial Design Students Ethnographic Methods to Foster Interdisciplinary Inquiry Into Consumer Needs
1629.summary: The authors described a way of teaching new product development that brings engineering and industrial design students together and uses ethnographic methods to tie the poorly understood early stage to real users. The approach drew on five years of teaching an Integrated Product Development course, including observation of 25 design teams across 350 project meetings and 100 presentations, plus interviews with industry teams. Qualitative methods helped students navigate the fuzzy front end, with lessons that may carry over to industry.

1634.title: The Role of Shape in Communicating Designers’ Aesthetic Intents
1634.summary: The authors aimed to describe how product designers convey intended aesthetic impressions through a product's shape, as groundwork for a computer tool that supports conceptual design. They developed a theory that maps shape characteristics to aesthetic characteristics and used it to run experiments on how respondents perceived and appreciated product shapes. Analysing the results, they concluded that a first version of the mapping between shape and aesthetic qualities could be established.

1636.title: Artefacting in a Cross-Discipline Design Team
1636.summary: The authors looked at how physical objects, gestures and actions combine with talk in design conversations, which earlier studies had largely treated separately. They analysed in fine detail the everyday work of a cross-discipline rehabilitation engineering team of therapists, engineers and prosthetics specialists. They described this combination of purposeful physical interaction and accompanying talk as "artefacting", a way team members communicate complex messages with design implications.

1638.title: Experimental Investigation of Progressive Idea Generation Techniques in Engineering Design
1638.summary: The author studied three team-based idea generation methods in which ideas develop in stages: Method 6-3-5, Collaborative Sketching (C-Sketch) and the Gallery Method. Experiments over nearly 3 years, totalling over 200 hours of data from roughly 44 subjects, examined how the recording medium and communication between team members affect idea generation. Work in progress addressed design fixation, written versus sketched ideas, misinterpretation as a creative stimulus, and exploratory processes during sessions.

1648.title: Augmenting a Design Capture and Reuse System Based on Direct Observations of Usage
1648.summary: The authors studied how student teams in Stanford's 30-week ME210 design course used a large archive of captured design information from earlier years. Design notes, drawings, reports, emails and other material from 1994 to 1996 were made available on a web server, and access to them was logged. Past work was heavily under-used, with only 8% of access going to earlier years and 15% to project-specific information, which led the authors to add ways to contextualise and reward reuse.

1656.title: Developing ‘Text Learning Capture’ to Examine How Students Learn From Texts and How Texts Learn From Students
1656.summary: The authors wanted to give the author of a freshman engineering textbook in development direct feedback on how students learn from it. They developed the Text Learning Capture Method, drawing on usability testing, and analysed the protocols it captured as students worked through the text. The feedback revealed issues of readability, comprehensibility and usability, and generated a list of questions about how students learn from engineering textbooks.

1657.title: An Experiment in Improving Student Estimation Skills
1657.summary: The authors tested whether upper-division mechanical engineering students could make sensible rough estimates, and whether practice could improve that skill. In the fall semesters of 1996 and 1997, seniors solved an in-class estimation problem about once a week, and their results on a final problem were compared with those of the whole junior class. Many students could not estimate within an order of magnitude or keep units consistent; practice helped slightly, and teams estimated much better than individuals.

1670.title: Creative Design Methodology and the SIT Method
1670.summary: The authors presented SIT (Structured Inventive Thinking), a method for supporting creative problem solving in engineering design. SIT has three steps: reformulating the problem, choosing a general search strategy and applying idea-provoking techniques, with reformulation based on a set of sufficient conditions for creative solutions. An empirical study using expert judges of creativity supported these conditions, and the method was illustrated with examples.

1685.title: Noun Phrases As Surrogates for Measuring Early Phases of the Mechanical Design Process
1685.summary: The authors explored whether project documentation could be used to evaluate the design process in a graduate design class with industry-sponsored projects. They analysed different representations of the project documents, including readability, word counts and the number of distinct noun phrases. Project grades were strongly associated with the number of distinct noun phrases (gamma above 0.7) but only weakly with the other measures, suggesting noun phrases could help measure design.

1694.title: Using Student Preferences to Guide Design Team Composition
1694.summary: The author described five years of experiments at Stanford that used students' questionnaire answers to guide how design teams were formed. The rules drew on a short questionnaire sampled from the Myers-Briggs Type Indicator, later adjusted using a survey of team satisfaction from another design course. Teams formed this way won more prizes in the national Lincoln Foundation Design Competition than in the previous thirteen years, including all but two of twelve prizes in 1995.

1695.title: The Role of Simulation Software in an Ideal Learning Environment
1695.summary: The authors examined how computer simulation software affects students' learning while solving an engineering design problem. Three pairs of male undergraduates were videotaped designing a four-bar toggle clamp, one pair with paper tools only, one also with Working Model simulation software and one also with a Lego set, and the sessions were analysed using two learning theories. The pairs' approaches differed markedly, and the analysis compared which setting best promoted learning about the mechanisms.

1703.title: The Influence of Information Characteristics on Preliminary Design Concepts
1703.summary: The author studied how the information used in conceptual design relates to the quality of the resulting concept, to help specify computer support for early design. A recently developed observation method was tested and refined over 10 design sessions, and each concept was scored with a quality rating system. The amount of information communicated correlated significantly and positively with the design's rating, and analysis activities involved more communication than synthesis and evaluation.

1705.title: The Validation of a Taxonomy for Manufacturability Design Requirements
1705.summary: The authors tested a taxonomy of manufacturing issues meant to serve as a checklist when design teams define product requirements. Subjects received one of three levels of the taxonomy at one of two design stages and performed design tasks, and their use of it and the requirements they produced were compared with analysis of variance. The taxonomy helped designers manage product requirements early in design, but worked best when used methodically.

1727.title: Validation Studies of an Information-Flow Model of Design

1729.title: Dependence of Early Engineering Concepts on Information Characteristics
1729.summary: The authors studied how the information used during conceptual design relates to the quality of the resulting concept, to help specify future computer support tools. They observed 10 design sessions using a newly developed observation method and rated each design concept with a quality rating system. The amount of information communicated correlated significantly and positively with design quality, and analysis activities involved more communication than synthesis and evaluation.

1730.title: Required and Requested Information During Conceptual Engineering Design As Found by Categorization of Empirical Data

1731.title: Experiencing Product Realisation on the World Wide Web
1731.summary: The author described a new way for mechanical engineering students to experience product realisation, which is hard to provide at university with physical products. Student teams designed, prototyped and delivered a simple homepage about concurrent engineering, using the World Wide Web as a rapid prototyping and production medium, guided by an experiential model of learning. Structured reflection on their own process allowed the students to demonstrate what they had learned.

1732.title: Process Metrics for Asynchronous Concurrent Engineering: Communication in an Internet Newsgroup
1732.summary: The author set out to characterise and measure computer-mediated communication in a collaborative design process. Using a very large Internet newsgroup captured during a sophomore design course at Cornell, the author developed a weighted communication matrix, an Affinity Matrix linking topics and a topic space defining topic robustness, and grouped activity by Myers-Briggs type. Students leaning toward analytical and invention modes used the newsgroup actively, while those leaning toward affiliation and implementation used it little.

1733.title: Student Responses to Impromptu Estimation Questions
1733.summary: The authors examined how well undergraduates make rough estimates, a skill engineering designers rely on, especially early in design. Students were asked impromptu questions about basic engineering quantities of common engineering artifacts, and their responses to two such questions were analysed. Students had great difficulty estimating and applying engineering fundamentals, even at senior level, so the authors proposed shifting teaching from detailed analysis toward estimation.

1743.title: Functional Evaluation Based on Function Content
1743.summary: The authors addressed how to evaluate the functions of a design, since designers' evaluations rest on subjective, ambiguous and unstated standards. Within their Functional Evolution Process model, in which a design evolves through function description, actualization and evaluation, they proposed "function content", a measure modelled on Shannon's information content. They showed an example of optimising a design's functions using this measure.

1745.title: The Differences in Reading Schematic Drawings of Mechanisms by Expert and Naive Mechanical Designers
1745.summary: The authors studied how expert and inexperienced mechanical designers read schematic drawings of mechanisms, to inform better computer aids for conceptual design. They recorded the knowledge and reasoning used by 15 designers of different levels of expertise as they interpreted 8 mechanical engineering drawings. Results partly supported the idea that experts recognise drawings through functions they have met before, and experts used inverse reasoning more often and more successfully than novices.

1746.title: The Nature of Constraints and Their Effect on Quality and Satisficing
1746.summary: The authors set out to clarify the nature of design constraints, as part of a method for evaluating design tools by how well the resulting designs satisfy constraints. Drawing on two sets of think-aloud protocols of mechanical designers, including a redesign of cattle water tanks, plus other researchers' work, they built a taxonomy of constraints by design consideration, source, context, strength and use. They also proposed how introduced constraints affect design quality and a sharper, experiment-based definition of satisficing.
